back.title: Verse
back.html:
A transformer block is a residual stream of width d_model with two sublayers, each wrapped as x = x + Sublayer(Norm(x)) (pre-LN, the modern default). The original paper used post-LN Norm(x + Sublayer(x)), which needs LR warmup to stay stable. Sublayer 1 = multi-head self-attention; sublayer 2 = position-wise FFN (two linear layers + nonlinearity, inner dim ≈ 4·d_model, GELU/SwiGLU). The residual stream is the "highway" every sublayer reads from and writes to; its width d_model is the model's information bandwidth.

# pre-LN block (schematic)
def block(x, attn, ffn, ln1, ln2):
    x = x + attn(ln1(x))     # sublayer 1: mixes tokens
    x = x + ffn(ln2(x))      # sublayer 2: per-token transform
    return x

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Everything hinges on what the attention sublayer computes — so what is inside it? (1.02)

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Attention mixes tokens by content similarity:

$$\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$

with Q=XW_Q, K=XW_K, V=XW_V. The 1/√d_k scale exists because for unit-variance q,k the dot product q·k has variance d_k; without scaling, logits grow with d_k, softmax saturates toward one-hot, and gradients through it vanish. Dividing by √d_k restores unit-variance logits.

import torch, math
def attention(Q, K, V, mask=None):           # Q,K,V: [B, h, T, d_k]
    scores = Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(Q.size(-1))
    if mask is not None:
        scores = scores.masked_fill(mask == 0, float("-inf"))
    return torch.softmax(scores, dim=-1) @ V

back.title: Chain →
back.html: One head attends in only one subspace — how do we attend in several at once? (1.03)

cards.cue: Everything hinges on what the attention sublayer computes — so what is inside it?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Split into h heads of width d_k = d_model/h, attend independently, concatenate, project with W_O:

$$\text{MHA}(X)=\text{Concat}(\text{head}_1,\dots,\text{head}_h)W_O,\quad \text{head}_i=\text{Attention}(XW_Q^i,XW_K^i,XW_V^i)$$

Total parameter/FLOP cost ≈ one full-width head, but heads specialize (syntax, coreference, positional patterns). GQA/MQA later share K,V across heads to shrink the KV cache (see 4.26).

def split_heads(x, h):        # [B, T, d_model] -> [B, h, T, d_k]
    B, T, d = x.shape
    return x.view(B, T, h, d // h).transpose(1, 2)
# merge is the inverse, then @ W_O

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Attention is permutation-invariant — reorder tokens, output set is unchanged. How does the model know order? (1.04)

cards.cue: One head attends in only one subspace — how do we attend in several at once?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Order is injected explicitly.

  • Sinusoidal (fixed, additive): PE(pos,2i)=sin(pos/10000^{2i/d}), PE(pos,2i+1)=cos(...). Extrapolates modestly.
  • Learned absolute: trainable position table; cannot extrapolate past trained length.
  • RoPE (rotary): rotates Q,K by a position-dependent angle so the dot product depends only on the relative offset; strong extrapolation; default in modern decoders (Llama, Qwen).
  • ALiBi: adds a linear distance penalty to attention logits; cheapest, strong extrapolation.
import torch
def sinusoidal(T, d):
    pos = torch.arange(T)[:, None]
    i   = torch.arange(0, d, 2)[None, :]
    ang = pos / (10000 ** (i / d))
    pe = torch.zeros(T, d); pe[:, 0::2] = ang.sin(); pe[:, 1::2] = ang.cos()
    return pe

back.title: Chain →
back.html: These blocks stack identically, but encoder and decoder differ in the attention mask. What is an encoder? (1.05)

cards.cue: Attention is permutation-invariant — reorder tokens, output set is unchanged. How does the model know order?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
An encoder applies unmasked self-attention: every position attends to all positions, left and right. Output is a contextual representation of the whole input — ideal for understanding tasks: classification, NER, retrieval embeddings (BERT, RoBERTa). It cannot generate autoregressively because it "sees the future." Trained with masked language modeling (see 4.28).

# no causal mask: full [T, T] attention allowed
attn_mask = None            # only padding mask applied, never a causal triangle

back.title: Chain →
back.html: So what do we use when we must generate text token by token? (1.06)

cards.cue: These blocks stack identically, but encoder and decoder differ in the attention mask. What is an encoder?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
A decoder applies a causal mask: position t attends only to ≤ t. Implemented by adding -∞ to the upper triangle of QKᵀ/√d_k before softmax, forcing those weights to 0. This enforces autoregression p(x_t | x_{<t}), enabling generation (GPT family). At inference, past keys/values are cached (KV cache, see 4.26) so each new token costs O(seq) not O(seq²).

import torch
def causal_mask(T):
    return torch.tril(torch.ones(T, T)).bool()   # lower-triangular True = allowed

back.title: Chain →
back.html: What about tasks that must both fully understand an input and generate a different output? (1.07)

cards.cue: So what do we use when we must generate text token by token?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Seq2seq models (T5, BART, original Transformer) pair a bidirectional encoder with a causal decoder joined by cross-attention: the decoder supplies Q, the encoder's final states supply K,V. Decoding is thus conditioned on a fully-contextualized source — the natural fit for translation and summarization where source/target lengths and vocabularies differ. Cost: you pay for both stacks plus cross-attention.

# decoder layer has THREE attention calls:
h = h + self_attn(ln1(h), mask=causal)          # 1: causal self-attn
h = h + cross_attn(ln2(h), kv=encoder_states)   # 2: Q=decoder, K,V=encoder
h = h + ffn(ln3(h))                             # 3: FFN

back.title: Chain →
back.html: All three architectures emit hidden states we call embeddings — but what is an embedding, precisely? (1.08)

cards.cue: What about tasks that must both fully understand an input and generate a different output?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Objectives: 1.6, (1.8 support)

An embedding maps a discrete token id to a dense vector via lookup in the embedding matrix E ∈ ℝ^{V×d} (V = vocab size). Training arranges these vectors so geometric proximity ≈ semantic/functional similarity. Weight tying reuses E (transposed) as the output projection to logits, cutting parameters and coupling input/output representations. "Embedding" also names any later hidden state used as a sentence/document vector.

import torch.nn as nn
emb = nn.Embedding(V, d)          # lookup table E: [V, d]
lm_head = nn.Linear(d, V, bias=False)
lm_head.weight = emb.weight        # weight tying (input emb == output projection)

back.title: Chain →
back.html: How do we actually pull a usable sentence embedding out of an encoder? (1.09)

cards.cue: All three architectures emit hidden states we call embeddings — but what is an embedding, precisely?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Objectives: 1.3, 1.6

Two standard poolings over the encoder's last hidden state: the [CLS] token vector, or masked mean pooling over token vectors. Mean pooling usually wins unless the model was fine-tuned to make [CLS] a sentence representation (Sentence-Transformers exist precisely for this reason).

from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel
import torch
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")
enc = AutoModel.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased").eval().cuda()
b = tok(["a cat sat", "a dog ran"], padding=True, return_tensors="pt").to("cuda")
with torch.no_grad():
    h = enc(**b).last_hidden_state              # [B, T, d]
m = b.attention_mask.unsqueeze(-1)              # [B, T, 1]
mean_emb = (h * m).sum(1) / m.sum(1)            # masked mean pooling -> [B, d]

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Decoders have no [CLS] and attend only leftward — how do we get an embedding from one? (1.10)

cards.cue: How do we actually pull a usable sentence embedding out of an encoder?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Use the last non-pad token's final hidden state — under causal masking it is the only position that has attended to the entire sequence. This requires left padding so the true last token sits at index -1; right padding returns a pad vector and collapses your embeddings.

from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel
import torch
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2"); tok.padding_side = "left"
tok.pad_token = tok.eos_token
dec = AutoModel.from_pretrained("gpt2").eval().cuda()
b = tok(["a cat sat", "a dog ran too"], padding=True, return_tensors="pt").to("cuda")
with torch.no_grad():
    h = dec(**b).last_hidden_state              # [B, T, d]
last_emb = h[:, -1, :]                          # left-padded => real last token

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Now the decoder can produce hidden states and logits — how do we turn logits into the next token? (1.11)

cards.cue: Decoders have no [CLS] and attend only leftward — how do we get an embedding from one?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Objectives: 1.4, 1.5

From logits z, p = softmax(z). - Greedy = argmax; deterministic, myopic, repetitive. - Beam search keeps the b highest-probability sequences (summed, usually length-normalized log-probs); maximizes likelihood — good for constrained tasks (translation), bad for open-ended text (bland, degenerate loops). - Temperature rescales before softmax: p_i = softmax(z_i/T). T<1 sharpens (greedier), T>1 flattens (more random), T→0 ≡ greedy (implementations special-case it; literal z/0 is undefined).

import torch
def sample_temp(logits, T=0.7):
    p = torch.softmax(logits / max(T, 1e-6), dim=-1)
    return torch.multinomial(p, 1)

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Temperature reshapes the whole distribution — how do we instead cut off the unreliable tail? (1.12)

cards.cue: Now the decoder can produce hidden states and logits — how do we turn logits into the next token?

cards.front: Sampling II: top-k, top-p (nucleus), repetition penalty

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Objectives: 1.4, 1.5

  • Top-k: keep the k highest-prob tokens, renormalize, sample — fixed count regardless of confidence.
  • Top-p / nucleus: keep the smallest set whose cumulative probability ≥ p, then sample — an adaptive count that stays small when confident and widens when uncertain.
  • Repetition penalty: divide logits of already-generated tokens by r>1 to suppress loops.

Common recipe: temperature≈0.7, top_p≈0.9.

import torch
def top_p(logits, p=0.9):
    s, idx = torch.sort(logits, descending=True)
    cum = torch.softmax(s, -1).cumsum(-1)
    s[cum > p] = float("-inf")            # drop the tail beyond nucleus
    return idx[torch.multinomial(torch.softmax(s, -1), 1)]

back.title: Chain →
back.html: These are exactly the knobs a serving stack exposes — which sets up controlling model behavior from the prompt/decoding layer: Domain 2.

cards.cue: Temperature reshapes the whole distribution — how do we instead cut off the unreliable tail?

cards.front: Training a from-scratch transformer, attention weights collapse to one-hot and gradients vanish — recite the chain.

back.title: Recall
back.html: The block is a residual stream with attention + FFN sublayers (1.01). Inside attention we compute query-key dot products scaled by one-over-root-d-k (1.02); we scale because dot-product variance grows with d_k, and unscaled logits saturate the softmax and kill gradients — exactly the symptom. Fix: confirm the √d_k scaling is present.

cards.label: WR-1a · Walk & Recall
cards.front: Why more than one attention head?

back.title: Recall
back.html: One head sees one subspace; multi-head splits d_model into h heads of width d_model/h, each specializing, then concatenates and projects with W_O (1.03), at roughly the cost of one full head.

cards.label: WR-1a · Walk & Recall
cards.front: Model ignores word order — shuffling the input barely changes output. Recite.

back.title: Recall
back.html: Attention is permutation-invariant, so order must be injected: sinusoidal, learned-absolute, RoPE, or ALiBi (1.04). Missing positional encoding is the symptom.

cards.label: WR-1a · Walk & Recall
cards.front: Understanding task vs generation task — which stack?

back.title: Recall
back.html: Encoder = unmasked bidirectional, for understanding/embeddings (1.05); decoder = causal-masked, for autoregressive generation (1.06). The mask (upper triangle → −∞) is the only structural difference.

cards.label: WR-1b · Walk & Recall

back.title: Recall
back.html: Encoder-decoder: bidirectional encoder, causal decoder, joined by cross-attention where Q comes from the decoder and K,V from the encoder's final states (1.07). Then: all stacks emit embeddings — a token-id lookup in matrix E, optionally weight-tied to the output softmax (1.08).

cards.label: WR-1b · Walk & Recall
cards.front: My decoder sentence embeddings are garbage / identical across inputs — recite.

back.title: Recall
back.html: Decoders need the last non-pad token's hidden state, which requires left padding; with right padding you read a pad vector — the symptom (1.10). Encoders instead use CLS or masked mean pooling, mean usually better unless CLS was fine-tuned (1.09).

cards.label: WR-1b · Walk & Recall

back.title: Recall

Temperature rescales the whole distribution (T<1 sharpen, T>1 flatten, T→0 greedy); to cut the tail use top-k (fixed count) or top-p/nucleus (adaptive cumulative-p), plus repetition penalty to break loops (1.12).

cards.label: Q1 · Domain 1
cards.front: A team pretrains a transformer from scratch; attention distributions collapse to near one-hot early and loss plateaus. d_k=128. Most likely cause?

back.title: Why
back.html: Var(q·k) ≈ d_k; unscaled logits saturate softmax → vanishing gradients → early one-hot collapse. A: low LR slows learning, no saturation. C: fewer heads = less capacity, not saturation. D: vocab affects output layer, not attention.

cards.label: Q2 · Domain 1
cards.front: You must classify whole documents and power a semantic-search embedding index. Best architecture?

back.title: Why
back.html: Encoder-only gives bidirectional whole-input reps, ideal for classification and retrieval embeddings. A: decoders causal, weaker for pure understanding. C: overkill, adds a generation stack. D: not the LLM tool here.

cards.label: Q3 · Domain 1
cards.front: A translation product must condition generated target tokens on a fully bidirectional understanding of the source. Design + cross-component mechanism?

back.title: Why
back.html: Encoder-decoder + cross-attention (decoder Q, encoder K/V) conditions generation on a bidirectional source. A: decoder-only lacks a bidirectional source encoder. B: encoder can't generate. D: no bidirectional encoding or coupling.

options.html: Encoder-decoder with cross-attention (Q from decoder, K/V from encoder)

cards.label: Q4 · Domain 1
cards.front: GPT-style decoder embeddings are nearly identical across inputs. Code uses padding_side="right" + hidden_states[:, -1, :]. Best fix?

back.title: Why
back.html: Under causal masking only the last real token attended to the full sequence; right padding puts pads at index −1. Left padding fixes it. B/D: don't address the indexing bug. C: sampling knob, not embeddings.

cards.label: Q5 · Domain 1
cards.front: For a BERT model not fine-tuned for similarity, which sentence embedding is better and why?

back.title: Why
back.html: Without similarity fine-tuning, raw CLS is a poor sentence vector; masked mean pooling is empirically better. A: false for untuned models. C: decoder technique. D: no context.

options.html: Masked mean pooling, since raw CLS isn't tuned

cards.label: Q6 · Domain 1
cards.front: An open-ended chatbot using beam search (width 5) is bland and repetitive. Best single change?

back.title: Why
back.html: Nucleus + moderate temperature restores diversity and coherence. A: wider beams are more repetitive. C: greedy is least diverse. D: capacity isn't the issue.

cards.label: Q7 · Domain 1
cards.front: Which statement about temperature T in softmax(z/T) is correct?

back.title: Why
back.html: T→0 → greedy. A: T>1 flattens. C: T=0 is undefined (÷0), special-cased to greedy, not uniform. D: T<1 reduces diversity.

cards.label: Q8 · Domain 1
cards.front: Config sets top_k=50 and top_p=0.9. On a step where one token has p≈0.97, practical candidate-set difference?

back.title: Why
back.html: Top-k always allows up to 50; top-p adaptively shrinks to ~1 when one token has p≈0.97. A: ignores top-p adaptivity. C: reverses them. D: top-k wouldn't collapse to 1.

options.html: top-k keeps up to 50; top-p may keep ~1

cards.label: Q9 · Domain 1
cards.front: A model with a learned absolute positional table is fed sequences longer than any in training. Expected behavior?

back.title: Why
back.html: Learned absolute tables have no entry beyond trained max length → failure/undefined. A: describes RoPE/ALiBi. C: no auto switch. D: false.

back.title: Why
back.html: RoPE rotates Q/K so scores depend on relative position. A: ALiBi is a linear logit bias, not a table. C: sinusoidal extrapolates modestly, not "not at all." D: learned absolute is the worst extrapolator.

options.html: RoPE = rotates Q/K so scores depend on relative offset

cards.label: Q11 · Domain 1
cards.front: In the NVIDIA stack, which NeMo collection for an abstractive summarization seq2seq model?

back.title: Why
back.html: Summarization is seq2seq → T5 (encoder-decoder). A: GPT is decoder-only. B: BERT is encoder-only (no generation). D: not applicable.

cards.label: Q12 · Domain 1
cards.front: During autoregressive decoding, why does per-step cost stay ~O(seq) not O(seq²) after the first token?

back.title: Why
back.html: KV cache stores past keys/values so each new token attends over cached states → per-step work linear in sequence length. A: unrelated. C: parameter trick. D: training memory technique.

back.title: Watch out
back.html: Logit variance scales with d_k; unscaled → softmax saturation → vanishing gradients. Classic "why divide by root d_k" question (1.02).

back.title: Watch out

cards.label: Trap · Domain 1
cards.front: Assuming BERT [CLS] is a good sentence embedding out-of-the-box

back.title: Watch out
back.html: Without NSP/contrastive fine-tuning, raw CLS is weak; masked mean pooling usually beats it (1.09).

back.title: Watch out

back.title: Watch out

back.title: Verse
back.html:
A chat prompt is a structured sequence of roles — system (behavior/constraints), user (task), assistant (model turns) — rendered into the model's chat template (special tokens like <|system|>, [INST]). Delimiters (triple backticks, XML tags) separate instructions from data and reduce injection ambiguity. The system message is the highest-leverage, lowest-cost control surface before any fine-tuning.

messages = [
  {"role": "system", "content": "You are a terse SQL assistant. Output SQL only."},
  {"role": "user", "content": "users older than 30"},
]
prompt = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(messages, add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=False)

back.title: Chain →
back.html: With structure fixed, how does the model do a task it was given zero examples of? (2.02)

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Zero-shot = instruction only, no examples. Relies entirely on knowledge acquired in pretraining/instruction-tuning. Works when the task is common and unambiguous; fails when output format or a niche label set must be inferred. Cheapest prompt (fewest tokens), lowest steering.

Classify sentiment as positive/negative/neutral.
Text: "The battery drains too fast."
Sentiment:

back.title: Chain →
back.html: When zero-shot gets the format or label set wrong, what is the smallest fix? (2.03)

cards.cue: With structure fixed, how does the model do a task it was given zero examples of?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
One-shot = a single worked example before the query. The example fixes format and label vocabulary more reliably than instructions alone; it demonstrates rather than describes. Cheapest way to pin output shape when zero-shot drifts.

Text: "Loved it." -> Sentiment: positive
Text: "The battery drains too fast." -> Sentiment:

back.title: Chain →
back.html: One example fixes format; what if the task needs the model to generalize across several patterns? (2.04)

cards.cue: When zero-shot gets the format or label set wrong, what is the smallest fix?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Few-shot = k examples (typically 2–8). Accuracy rises with informative, diverse, class-balanced exemplars; degrades with redundant or skewed ones. Recency/order matters — models over-weight later examples. Retrieval-based selection (pick exemplars similar to the query) beats fixed sets on heterogeneous inputs. Bounded by context length and cost.

# 3-shot, class-balanced, then the query
pos -> "Loved it."
neg -> "Broke in a week."
neu -> "It's fine, nothing special."
query -> "The battery drains too fast."

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Examples fix pattern-matching; but how does adding examples actually change the model without touching its weights? (2.05)

cards.cue: One example fixes format; what if the task needs the model to generalize across several patterns?

back.title: Verse
back.html: In-context learning (ICL) = the model conditions on exemplars in the prompt and adapts its output distribution without any gradient step. Weights are frozen; "learning" is transient, living only in the forward pass's activations/KV cache. Implication: ICL cannot add durable knowledge or survive across sessions — that is what fine-tuning (Domain 5) is for. Distinguish sharply from prompt learning / P-tuning (2.12), which does train continuous prompt vectors.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: If plain examples aren't enough for multi-step reasoning, how do we make the model show its work? (2.06)

cards.cue: Examples fix pattern-matching; but how does adding examples actually change the model without touching its weights?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
CoT elicits intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer, improving multi-step arithmetic/logic/commonsense accuracy. It works because generation is autoregressive: written steps become context the model conditions on (externalized scratchpad). Trade-off: more tokens, higher latency/cost, and reasoning can be plausible-but-wrong.

Q: A shelf has 3 boxes of 12 and 2 boxes of 5. How many items?
A: Let's reason step by step. 3*12=36. 2*5=10. 36+10=46. Answer: 46.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: CoT needs a worked example — can we trigger reasoning with zero examples? (2.07)

cards.cue: If plain examples aren't enough for multi-step reasoning, how do we make the model show its work?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Append a trigger phrase — "Let's think step by step." — with no exemplars. Elicits reasoning cheaply on capable instruct models. Weaker/smaller models may need few-shot CoT (2.09). Often paired with a second "extraction" prompt that pulls the final answer out of the reasoning trace.

Q: If a train travels 60 km in 45 minutes, what is its speed in km/h?
A: Let's think step by step.

back.html: A single reasoning path can go wrong — how do we make reasoning robust? (2.08)

cards.cue: CoT needs a worked example — can we trigger reasoning with zero examples?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Sample multiple CoT traces (temperature > 0), then take a majority vote over final answers. Marginalizes over reasoning paths, correcting single-path errors; large accuracy gains on arithmetic/reasoning. Cost scales linearly with the number of samples — a compute-for-accuracy trade (a form of test-time scaling, 2.13).

answers = [extract(sample_cot(prompt, temperature=0.7)) for _ in range(8)]
final = max(set(answers), key=answers.count)   # majority vote

back.html: Voting fixes reasoning; but how do we give the model more examples of the reasoning itself? (2.09)

cards.cue: A single reasoning path can go wrong — how do we make reasoning robust?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Provide k exemplars that each include the reasoning trace, not just the answer. Teaches the model the style and granularity of reasoning for the domain. Best for smaller models or specialized formats where zero-shot CoT (2.07) underperforms. Exemplar quality dominates: one wrong trace can anchor the model to a bad pattern.

A: 17-5=12. 12+12=24. Answer: 24.

back.title: Verse
back.html:
ReAct interleaves Thought → Action → Observation loops: the model reasons, emits a tool call (search, calculator, retrieval), reads the result, and continues. Grounds reasoning in external state, reducing hallucination on knowledge tasks and enabling agents. Requires an orchestration loop that parses actions and feeds observations back.

Thought: I need the current population.
Action: search("population of Iceland 2024")
Observation: ~383,000
Thought: That answers it.

A template separates fixed instruction scaffolding from variable slots, making prompts versionable, testable, and injection-aware. Treat prompts as code: pin a version, diff changes, and A/B test (ties to Domain 9 versioning). Escape/validate user-filled slots to blunt prompt injection (2.25).

TEMPLATE = (

cards.front: Prompt learning: soft vs hard prompts

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Hard prompts are discrete natural-language tokens (everything above). Soft prompts are continuous, trainable embedding vectors prepended to the input; the model weights stay frozen while only these vectors are learned via backprop — parameter-efficient adaptation for small datasets/specialized domains. This is the bridge to P-tuning / prefix tuning in Domain 5 (5.15).

[p1][p2]...[pk]  <actual input tokens>
# p1..pk are learned float vectors, not tokens from the vocabulary

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Soft prompts help small data — but what if we just spend more inference compute to reason harder? (2.13)

cards.cue: Templates use discrete text — can we instead learn the prompt as vectors?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Test-time scaling trades inference compute for accuracy: longer reasoning traces, more self-consistency samples (2.08), or best-of-N with a verifier. Reasoning models expose a "thinking budget" (max reasoning tokens). Diminishing returns and latency/cost ceilings apply. NVIDIA framing: this is why serving must budget KV cache and tokens per request (ties to 8.02 prefill/decode, 9.03 metrics).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: More compute helps general tasks — but how do we adapt to a specialized domain purely through prompting? (2.14)

cards.cue: Soft prompts help small data — but what if we just spend more inference compute to reason harder?

back.title: Verse
back.html: For specialized domains or small datasets, adapt without fine-tuning: inject a domain glossary/style guide in the system prompt, use retrieved domain snippets (RAG, 2.23), and few-shot with in-domain exemplars. Decision boundary: prompt-only adaptation is free and instant but capped by context length and cannot add durable knowledge — cross over to PEFT/fine-tuning (Domain 5) when volume or consistency demands it.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Prompting adapts a pretrained decoder — but how is a decoder trained to predict text in the first place? (2.15)

cards.cue: More compute helps general tasks — but how do we adapt to a specialized domain purely through prompting?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Decoders are trained to predict the next token: minimize $\mathcal{L}=-\sum_t \log p(x_t \mid x_{<t})$ (cross-entropy over the vocabulary), with the causal mask (1.06) guaranteeing no future leakage. This single objective, at scale, yields the in-context abilities Domain 2 exploits. Contrast with MLM for encoders (4.28).

import torch.nn.functional as F
# logits: [B, T, V]; labels: [B, T] (input shifted left by 1)
loss = F.cross_entropy(logits[:, :-1].reshape(-1, V), labels[:, 1:].reshape(-1))

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Predicting x_t from x_{<t} during training — how do we feed the ground truth efficiently? (2.16)

cards.cue: Prompting adapts a pretrained decoder — but how is a decoder trained to predict text in the first place?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
During training the decoder is fed the ground-truth previous tokens (not its own predictions) — teacher forcing — so all positions train in parallel in one forward pass. Labels are the inputs shifted by one; loss is masked on padding and often on the prompt portion (train only on the completion). Exposure bias (train sees gold, inference sees own outputs) is the known downside.

labels = input_ids.clone()
labels[:, :prompt_len] = -100     # ignore prompt tokens in loss
labels[attention_mask == 0] = -100

back.html: With objective and labels defined, what does a minimal training loop look like? (2.17)

cards.front: Train a decoder with CLM (code sketch)

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Minimal HF loop: tokenize, let the model shift labels internally (pass labels=input_ids for pure LM), backprop cross-entropy. This is the substrate SFT (5.01) builds on.

from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
import torch
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2"); tok.pad_token = tok.eos_token
m = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("gpt2").cuda().train()
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(m.parameters(), lr=5e-5)
batch = tok(["hello world"], return_tensors="pt").to("cuda")
out = m(**batch, labels=batch.input_ids)     # HF shifts labels internally
out.loss.backward(); opt.step(); opt.zero_grad()
print(float(out.loss))

back.html: A trained decoder still emits free text — how do we force it into a strict output shape? (2.18)

cards.cue: With objective and labels defined, what does a minimal training loop look like?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Ask for machine-parseable output (JSON) and provide the schema in the prompt plus a one-shot example. Improves parse rates but does not guarantee validity — the model can still emit malformed JSON. Prompt-level structuring is necessary but not sufficient; pair with constrained decoding (2.19) for hard guarantees.

Return ONLY JSON matching:
{"intent": string, "entities": string[], "confidence": number}
Text: "book a flight to Tokyo next Friday"

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Prompting for JSON still allows invalid output — how do we make invalid tokens impossible? (2.19)

cards.cue: A trained decoder still emits free text — how do we force it into a strict output shape?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Constrained decoding restricts the sampling step to tokens allowed by a grammar (CFG/regex/JSON schema). At each step, tokens that would violate the grammar have their logits set to -∞ (masked), so invalid output is impossible by construction — a hard guarantee that prompting (2.18) cannot give. Cost: a grammar/state machine and per-step mask computation.

def masked_logits(logits, allowed_ids):
    mask = torch.full_like(logits, float("-inf"))
    mask[..., allowed_ids] = 0.0
    return logits + mask     # only grammar-allowed tokens survive softmax

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Even valid-shaped output can be wrong or unsafe — where does the validation live? (2.20)

cards.cue: Prompting for JSON still allows invalid output — how do we make invalid tokens impossible?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Wrap the model in a module that (1) builds the prompt from a template, (2) applies constrained decoding, (3) validates output against a schema/business rules, and (4) retries or repairs on failure. This is NVIDIA's "specialized LLM-wrapping module with built-in validation" — it turns a probabilistic generator into a dependable component and is where guardrails (Domain 10) attach.

def call(model, msg, schema, retries=2):
    for _ in range(retries + 1):
        out = model.generate(build_prompt(msg), grammar=schema)
        ok, parsed = validate(out, schema)
        if ok: return parsed
    raise ValueError("validation failed after retries")

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Validation catches format errors — but how do we stop the model asserting false facts? (2.21)

cards.cue: Even valid-shaped output can be wrong or unsafe — where does the validation live?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Reduce fabrication by grounding: supply authoritative context (retrieved documents, 2.23) and instruct the model to answer only from it and to say "I don't know" otherwise. Add citations so claims are checkable. Grounding attacks the root cause (missing knowledge in-context) better than post-hoc filtering. Deeper mitigation (fine-tuning, Guardrails) is in Domains 5 and 10.

Answer using ONLY the context. If the context is insufficient, say "I don't know."
Context: {retrieved_chunks}
Question: {q}

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Grounding constrains content — but who enforces the output policy at runtime? (2.22)

cards.cue: Validation catches format errors — but how do we stop the model asserting false facts?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Output control at runtime is owned by a guardrails layer: input rails (block malicious/off-topic prompts), output rails (block unsafe/PII/hallucinated content), and dialog rails (keep to allowed topics). NVIDIA's tool is NeMo Guardrails with the Colang policy language (full treatment in 10.09–10.10). Prompt engineering sets intent; guardrails enforce it independently of the model's cooperation.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Grounding needs relevant context — where does that context come from? (2.23)

cards.cue: Grounding constrains content — but who enforces the output policy at runtime?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Objectives: 2.1, 2.4

Retrieval-Augmented Generation = retriever + generator. An embedding model encodes the query; a vector store returns top-k relevant chunks; those chunks are injected into the prompt; the LLM generates grounded, citable answers. RAG adds fresh/proprietary knowledge without retraining and is NVIDIA's default enterprise pattern (NeMo Retriever + NIM). It is a prompt-context technique, which is why it lives in Domain 2, not a domain of its own.

[system] answer only from context
[context] <top-k retrieved chunks>
[user] <question>

back.title: Chain →
back.html: RAG hinges on retrieval quality — how are chunks embedded and searched? (2.24)

cards.cue: Grounding needs relevant context — where does that context come from?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Documents are split into chunks (size/overlap trade recall vs precision), embedded (1.09/1.10), and indexed for approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search by cosine/dot similarity. Query embedding → top-k chunks. Levers: chunk size, overlap, k, and re-ranking. Poor chunking (too large → diluted; too small → fragmented) is the top RAG failure mode. Evaluate with Ragas (6.08).

sims = query_emb @ chunk_embs.T          # [1, N]
topk = sims.topk(k).indices              # nearest chunks

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Injecting external text into prompts opens an attack surface — what is it? (2.25)

cards.cue: RAG hinges on retrieval quality — how are chunks embedded and searched?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Prompt injection: untrusted input (user text or retrieved content) carries instructions that override the system prompt ("ignore previous instructions…"). Indirect injection hides instructions in RAG-retrieved documents. Jailbreaks coax the model past its safety policy (role-play, obfuscation). Defenses: strong delimiters, treat retrieved text as data not instructions, output rails, and least- privilege tool access. Prompting alone is insufficient — enforce with guardrails (2.22, Domain 10).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Beyond safety, these same decoding knobs shape user experience — how? (2.26)

cards.cue: Injecting external text into prompts opens an attack surface — what is it?

back.title: Verse
back.html: The decoding params from 1.11–1.12 are product controls exposed per request in the serving stack (Dynamo-Triton / TensorRT-LLM): low temperature + low top_p for deterministic, factual, testable output (code, extraction); higher values for creative tasks. max_tokens bounds latency/cost; stop sequences and repetition_penalty prevent runaway/looping output. Consistency requirements (validation, evals) usually push production toward near-greedy settings.

back.title: Watch out
back.html: The blueprint has no RAG domain; RAG verses live in Prompt Engineering (context), Evaluation (Ragas), Deployment, and Safety.

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Cleaning removes noise that models otherwise memorize: exact/near-duplicate documents, inconsistent Unicode (NFC/NFKC normalization), stray whitespace/control chars, boiler- plate, and encoding errors (mojibake). Deduplication both improves generalization and prevents train/test leakage. NVIDIA accelerates this at scale with NeMo Curator (3.06) on GPU (RAPIDS).

import unicodedata, re
def clean(t):
    t = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", t)
    t = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", t).strip()
    return t

back.title: Chain →
back.html: After cleaning text, what about records with missing fields? (3.02)

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Options: drop rows/columns (safe when missingness is small and random), or impute (mean/median/mode for tabular features; forward/backward fill for sequences; model- based imputation). The mechanism matters: MCAR (missing completely at random) tolerates simple imputation; MNAR (missing not at random) biases the model if imputed naively. For text corpora, "missing" often means empty/short docs — filter by length.

import pandas as pd
df["age"] = df["age"].fillna(df["age"].median())   # robust to outliers vs mean
df = df[df["text"].str.len() >= 20]                 # drop degenerate short docs

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Once complete, are numeric features on comparable scales? (3.03)

cards.cue: After cleaning text, what about records with missing fields?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Standardize numeric features so no feature dominates by magnitude: standardization z=(x−μ)/σ (zero mean/unit variance) or min-max to [0,1]. Fit scalers on train only, then apply to val/test to avoid leakage. Mostly relevant to tabular/auxiliary features; token embeddings are learned, not scaled. LayerNorm/RMSNorm handle activation scaling inside the model (1.01).

from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
sc = StandardScaler().fit(X_train)     # fit on train ONLY
X_train, X_val = sc.transform(X_train), sc.transform(X_val)

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Balanced scales don't fix skewed labels — how do we detect imbalance? (3.04)

cards.cue: Once complete, are numeric features on comparable scales?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Skewed class frequencies make a model optimize the majority and ignore rare classes; accuracy becomes misleading (use per-class recall / macro-F1, see Domain 6). Mitigate with resampling (oversample minority / SMOTE, undersample majority), class- weighted loss, or focal loss. For instruction data, imbalance shows up as over-represented task types skewing behavior.

import numpy as np, torch
counts = np.bincount(labels)
weights = torch.tensor(counts.sum() / (len(counts) * counts), dtype=torch.float)
loss_fn = torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss(weight=weights.cuda())

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Beyond labels, what does the overall feature/token distribution look like? (3.05)

cards.cue: Balanced scales don't fix skewed labels — how do we detect imbalance?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Profile distributions before training: token-length histograms, vocabulary coverage, language/topic mix, outliers, and correlations. On large corpora this is IO/compute heavy — RAPIDS cuDF gives a pandas-like API on GPU for order-of-magnitude speedups (NVIDIA's recommended tool). Length distributions directly drive max_seq_len and padding/packing decisions (3.12).

import cudf                       # GPU DataFrame, pandas-like
df = cudf.read_parquet("corpus.parquet")
print(df["n_tokens"].describe())  # p50/p95/p99 to pick max_seq_len

back.html: Curating billions of docs by hand is impossible — what pipeline does NVIDIA provide? (3.06)

cards.cue: Beyond labels, what does the overall feature/token distribution look like?

back.title: Verse
back.html: NeMo Curator is NVIDIA's GPU-accelerated data-curation library for LLM pretraining/ fine-tuning corpora. Stages: download/extract → language ID → quality filtering → deduplication (exact + fuzzy) → PII/content filtering → decontamination against eval sets → format for training. Built on Dask + RAPIDS for multi-GPU/multi-node scale. It is the exam's expected answer for "how does NVIDIA curate pretraining data at scale."

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Within Curator, how is low-quality text separated from high-quality? (3.07)

cards.cue: Curating billions of docs by hand is impossible — what pipeline does NVIDIA provide?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Two layers: heuristic filters (document length, symbol-to-word ratio, mean word length, fraction of alphabetic chars, repeated-line/n-gram ratios, stop-word presence) cheaply drop junk; classifier-based filters (a small model scoring "high-quality like reference corpus") catch subtler low-quality text. NeMo Curator ships both. Over-filtering hurts diversity; tune thresholds against a validation sample.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Filtered text can still contain massive duplication — how is that removed at scale? (3.08)

cards.cue: Within Curator, how is low-quality text separated from high-quality?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Exact dedup: hash documents (e.g. document-level or via md5) and drop collisions — cheap, catches verbatim copies. Fuzzy dedup: MinHash + LSH estimates Jaccard similarity of shingle sets to catch near-duplicates (templated pages, reformatted copies) without O(n²) comparison. Dedup reduces memorization, improves generalization, and prevents eval-set contamination. NeMo Curator does both on GPU.

shingles -> MinHash signatures -> LSH bucketing -> compare within-bucket -> drop near-dups

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Deduped text may still contain sensitive data — how is that handled? (3.09)

cards.cue: Filtered text can still contain massive duplication — how is that removed at scale?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Detect and redact/replace personally identifiable information (names, emails, phone numbers, SSNs) via regex + NER models, and filter toxic/unsafe content. Reduces compliance risk and the chance the model regurgitates private data (ties to Safety, Domain 10). NeMo Curator provides PII modules. Redaction must precede training; you cannot un-train leaked PII.

import re
text = re.sub(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+", "<EMAIL>", text)
text = re.sub(r"\b\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}\b", "<SSN>", text)

back.html: Clean, deduped, redacted data still needs a shape to train on — what format? (3.10)

cards.cue: Deduped text may still contain sensitive data — how is that handled?

cards.front: Dataset formats: JSONL, prompt-completion, chat templates

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Standard training formats: JSONL (one example per line), prompt-completion pairs for SFT, and chat/messages arrays (role/content) rendered through the model's chat template (2.01) so training matches inference formatting. Mismatched templates between train and serve are a top silent bug. For preference data (DPO, 5.06): {prompt, chosen, rejected}.

{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "2+2?"},
              {"role": "assistant", "content": "4"}]}

back.title: Chain →
back.html: With a format chosen, how do we split data without cheating? (3.11)

cards.cue: Clean, deduped, redacted data still needs a shape to train on — what format?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Split into train/val/test. Prevent leakage: deduplicate across splits (3.08), split by group (user/document/time) when records are correlated, and decontaminate training data against benchmark/eval sets (a duplicate of a test item in train inflates scores). Fit all preprocessing (scalers, tokenizers, filters) on train only. Time- series/production data → temporal split, never random.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Splits defined — how do we feed terabytes efficiently to the GPUs? (3.12)

cards.cue: With a format chosen, how do we split data without cheating?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
For large corpora: pre-tokenize to binary shards (memory-mapped) so training reads without re-tokenizing or loading everything into RAM (NeMo/Megatron use .bin/.idx). Sequence packing concatenates short examples up to max_seq_len to eliminate padding waste — a major throughput win — with attention masking to prevent cross-example attention. Shard for parallel data loading across ranks (Domain 7).

docs -> tokenize -> pack to max_seq_len -> write .bin + .idx -> mmap at train time

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Both formatting and packing assume tokens exist — how are tokens produced? (3.13)

cards.cue: Splits defined — how do we feed terabytes efficiently to the GPUs?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Word-level tokenization explodes vocab and fails on OOV/rare words; character-level gives tiny vocab but very long sequences. Subword tokenization is the compromise: frequent words stay whole, rare words split into meaningful pieces, and any string is representable (no true OOV). This bounds vocab size while keeping sequences short — the basis of all modern LLM tokenizers.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: What is the dominant algorithm for building subword vocab from data? (3.14)

cards.cue: Both formatting and packing assume tokens exist — how are tokens produced?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
BPE starts from characters (or bytes, "byte-level BPE" — GPT-2/Llama) and greedily merges the most frequent adjacent pair repeatedly, recording an ordered merge list until the target vocab size is reached. Encoding re-applies merges in order. Byte-level BPE guarantees no OOV for any Unicode input. Used by GPT, RoBERTa, Llama.

init:  l o w </w>, l o w e r </w>, ...
merge most frequent pair (e.g. "l o" -> "lo"), repeat
final vocab = base chars + learned merges

back.title: Chain →
back.html: BPE merges by frequency — is there an alternative that merges by likelihood? (3.15)

cards.cue: What is the dominant algorithm for building subword vocab from data?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
WordPiece (BERT) also builds subwords but merges the pair that maximizes the likelihood of the training corpus under a unigram LM, not raw frequency: it picks the merge maximizing count(pair)/(count(a)·count(b)). Continuation pieces are marked with ## (e.g. play, ##ing). Encoding is greedy longest-match-first.

"playing" -> ["play", "##ing"]        # ## marks a non-initial subword

back.title: Chain →
back.html: With two algorithms in hand, how do we choose between them (and Unigram)? (3.16)

cards.cue: BPE merges by frequency — is there an alternative that merges by likelihood?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
• BPE: greedy frequency merges; ordered merge list; byte-level variant = no OOV. GPT/Llama/RoBERTa.
  • WordPiece: likelihood-maximizing merges; ## continuations; greedy longest-match. BERT.
  • Unigram LM: starts with a large vocab and prunes to maximize corpus likelihood; probabilistic segmentation. T5/ALBERT.
  • SentencePiece: a library/framework (not an algorithm) implementing BPE or Unigram directly on raw text (treats space as a symbol ▁), language-agnostic, no pre-tokenization needed.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Choosing an algorithm still leaves the vocab-size knob — how is a tokenizer trained and sized? (3.17)

cards.cue: With two algorithms in hand, how do we choose between them (and Unigram)?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Train on a representative sample; choose vocab size. Larger vocab → shorter sequences (fewer tokens/word, lower fertility), faster inference, but a bigger embedding + softmax matrix (more params/memory) and rarer tokens undertrained. Smaller vocab → longer sequences, more compute per document. Typical LLM vocabs: 32k–256k. Match the tokenizer to the target languages/domains (code, multilingual need larger vocab).

from tokenizers import ByteLevelBPETokenizer
tk = ByteLevelBPETokenizer()
tk.train(files=["corpus.txt"], vocab_size=32000, min_frequency=2)

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Beyond size, which tokens and edge cases decide real efficiency? (3.18)

cards.cue: Choosing an algorithm still leaves the vocab-size knob — how is a tokenizer trained and sized?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Special tokens: [CLS], [SEP], <pad>, <eos>, <bos>, chat-role markers — must be reserved in the vocab and never split. OOV: byte-level BPE has none; other schemes fall back to [UNK]. Fertility = average tokens per word; high fertility (e.g. on code or an unseen language) inflates sequence length, cost, and can exceed max_seq_len, silently truncating input. Measure fertility on your actual domain before committing (ties to 3.05, 8.02 cost).

back.html: Well-prepared, well-tokenized data is the input to optimization — Domain 4: Model Optimization.

back.title: Verse
back.html: Three orthogonal levers to shrink/accelerate a model: quantization (fewer bits per weight/activation), pruning/sparsity (remove weights/structure), distillation (train a smaller student from a larger teacher). They compose. Goals: cut memory footprint, raise throughput/lower latency, and fit hardware acceleration paths (Tensor Cores, sparse cores). NVIDIA's inference-optimization stack (TensorRT / TensorRT-LLM) consumes all three.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Start with quantization — what does it mathematically do to a value? (4.02)

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Quantization maps floats to low-bit integers via an affine transform:

$$q=\text{round}(x/s)+z,\qquad x\approx s\,(q-z)$$

  • scale s = (x_max − x_min) / (q_max − q_min) sets resolution.
  • zero-point z is the integer that maps to real 0.
  • Symmetric quantization forces z=0 (range [−a, a]); asymmetric/affine allows a nonzero z (range [x_min, x_max]), better for skewed activations (e.g. post-ReLU). Weights → usually symmetric; activations → often asymmetric.
def quantize(x, s, z, qmin=-128, qmax=127):
    return (x / s + z).round().clamp(qmin, qmax)

back.title: Chain →
back.html: One scale for a whole tensor is coarse — at what granularity should scales apply? (4.03)

cards.cue: Start with quantization — what does it mathematically do to a value?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Scale/zero-point can be shared at different granularities: - Per-tensor: one scale for the whole tensor — cheapest, least accurate. - Per-channel (per output channel of a weight matrix): a scale per row — standard for weights, much better accuracy at negligible cost. - Per-group / per-block (e.g. groups of 128 weights): finest, used by GPTQ/AWQ and low-bit (INT4) schemes to contain outliers.

Finer granularity → higher accuracy, slightly more metadata. Activations are usually per-tensor or per-token.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Granularity aside, do we quantize only weights or activations too? (4.04)

cards.cue: One scale for a whole tensor is coarse — at what granularity should scales apply?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Objectives: 4.1, 4.2

  • Weight-only (e.g. INT4/INT8 weights, FP16 activations): shrinks memory and is memory-bandwidth-bound decode's friend — the decode phase is dominated by weight loading, so smaller weights = faster. Compute still in FP16. GPTQ/AWQ are weight-only.
  • Weight + activation (e.g. W8A8 INT8, FP8): also quantizes activations so the GEMM runs in low precision on Tensor Cores, raising compute throughput — essential for compute-bound prefill/large batch. Harder: activations have outliers (→ SmoothQuant, 4.15).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Concretely, what does INT8 quantization look like end to end? (4.05)

cards.cue: Granularity aside, do we quantize only weights or activations too?

back.title: Verse
back.html: INT8 = 8-bit signed integers, range [−128, 127]. On NVIDIA Tensor Cores INT8 GEMM roughly doubles throughput vs FP16 and halves weight memory. Accuracy is preserved by per-channel weight scales + calibrated activation scales (4.10). INT8 is the A100 fallback for FP8 workflows: same "low-precision GEMM" concept, available on Ampere. Supported on A100 and H100.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: H100 adds an 8-bit floating format — how does FP8 differ from INT8? (4.06)

cards.cue: Concretely, what does INT8 quantization look like end to end?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
FP8 is 8-bit floating point with two formats: E4M3 (4 exponent, 3 mantissa — more precision, less range; used for weights/activations) and E5M2 (5 exponent, 2 mantissa — more range, less precision; used for gradients). Unlike INT8's uniform steps, FP8's floating format handles wide dynamic range better, so it needs less careful calibration. Hardware: Hopper (H100) and later via the Transformer Engine (7.13).

A100 fallback: use INT8 (4.05) or BF16 — same low-precision-GEMM concept without Hopper FP8 units.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: FP8/INT8 are 8-bit; how do the 16-bit float formats compare? (4.07)

cards.cue: H100 adds an 8-bit floating format — how does FP8 differ from INT8?

cards.front: FP16 vs BF16 vs TF32 numerics

back.title: Verse
back.html:
• FP16: 1-5-10 (sign-exp-mantissa). High precision, narrow range → overflow/ underflow; training needs loss scaling (7.10).
  • BF16: 1-8-7. Same exponent range as FP32 (no loss scaling needed), less mantissa precision. Preferred for LLM training stability. Ampere+.
  • TF32: 1-8-10 (19 bits used in Tensor Core matmul). A "free" FP32 speedup — FP32 storage, reduced-precision matmul. Default for torch matmul on Ampere+.

Rule of thumb: BF16 for training stability, FP16 where hardware/legacy demands, TF32 as a drop-in FP32 accelerator.

back.html: Below 8 bits lies FP4 — what should I know conceptually? (4.08)

cards.cue: FP8/INT8 are 8-bit; how do the 16-bit float formats compare?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
FP4 = 4-bit floating point; NVFP4 is NVIDIA's Blackwell-era format pairing FP4 values with fine-grained (micro-block) scaling factors to retain accuracy at extreme compression. Enables very high inference throughput and tiny memory footprints on Blackwell Tensor Cores (e.g. GB200), and FP4 training via the 2nd-gen Transformer Engine. Exam may reference it conceptually. If you have Blackwell (sm_100), it is a real, runnable path — see Lab 4's [GB200] NVFP4 branch; on A100/H100 fall back to INT8/FP8. Contrast: INT4 (uniform) vs NVFP4 (floating + micro-scaling).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Formats decided, how do we actually apply quantization after training? (4.09)

cards.cue: Below 8 bits lies FP4 — what should I know conceptually?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Post-Training Quantization: take a trained FP model, run a small calibration dataset (a few hundred representative samples) through it to record activation ranges, compute scales/zero-points, and convert. No retraining, fast, no labels. Accuracy usually holds for INT8/FP8; can degrade at INT4 or on sensitive layers. Calibration data must match the deployment distribution.

FP model -> forward calibration set -> collect activation histograms
         -> compute per-tensor/channel scales -> emit quantized model

back.title: Chain →
back.html: How exactly are activation ranges chosen from those histograms? (4.10)

cards.cue: Formats decided, how do we actually apply quantization after training?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Choosing the clip range from activation histograms: - Min-max: use observed min/max — simple but outlier-sensitive (one spike widens the range, wasting resolution). - Entropy / KL-divergence: pick the clip threshold that minimizes KL between FP and quantized distributions — TensorRT's default for INT8; robust to outliers. - Percentile: clip at e.g. 99.99th percentile — discards extreme tails.

TensorRT exposes these as calibrators (IInt8EntropyCalibrator2, etc.). Wrong choice → either clipped signal or wasted range → accuracy loss.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: PTQ can still lose accuracy — when must we instead train with quantization? (4.11)

cards.cue: How exactly are activation ranges chosen from those histograms?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Quantization-Aware Training inserts fake-quantize nodes (quantize→dequantize) into the forward pass so the model learns weights robust to quantization error. The non-differentiable rounding is bypassed in backprop by the Straight-Through Estimator (STE) — gradient passes through as identity. Requires training data, compute, and labels, but recovers accuracy that PTQ loses (especially at low bit-widths or sensitive models). Usually fine-tune from a trained checkpoint.

def fake_quant(x, s, z):
    q = (x / s + z).round().clamp(-128, 127)
    xq = (q - z) * s
    return x + (xq - x).detach()   # STE: forward=xq, backward=identity

back.html: With both PTQ and QAT available, which do I pick and when? (4.12)

cards.cue: PTQ can still lose accuracy — when must we instead train with quantization?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
PTQ QAT
Retraining none yes (fine-tune)
Data small calibration set, no labels labeled training data
Cost minutes hours–days
Accuracy good for INT8/FP8 best, recovers low-bit loss
Use when INT8/FP8, tight timeline INT4/aggressive, accuracy-critical, PTQ dropped too much

Rule: try PTQ first; escalate to QAT only if the measured accuracy drop is unacceptable. QAT is mandatory when target bit-width (e.g. INT4) or a sensitive model makes PTQ accuracy collapse.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: For LLM weights specifically, what PTQ algorithms beat naive min-max? (4.13)

cards.cue: With both PTQ and QAT available, which do I pick and when?

back.title: Verse
back.html: GPTQ is a one-shot, layer-wise weight-only PTQ method for LLMs. It quantizes weights column-by-column while using second-order (Hessian) information to update remaining weights and compensate for the error introduced — minimizing output error per layer. Enables accurate INT4/INT3 weight quantization with a small calibration set. Weight-only → accelerates memory-bound decode; compute stays FP16.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: GPTQ compensates weights; what if the activations are the problem? (4.14)

cards.cue: For LLM weights specifically, what PTQ algorithms beat naive min-max?

back.title: Verse
back.html: AWQ observes that a small fraction of weight channels are salient (aligned with large-magnitude activations) and dominate output error. It scales those salient channels before quantization (protecting them) rather than keeping them in high precision, achieving accurate INT4 weight-only quantization that generalizes across domains without heavy calibration. Popular for LLM deployment (supported in TensorRT-LLM).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: AWQ protects salient weights; the dual problem is activation outliers — what handles those? (4.15)

cards.cue: GPTQ compensates weights; what if the activations are the problem?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Activations in LLMs have large per-channel outliers that make W8A8 activation quantization hard. SmoothQuant migrates the difficulty from activations to weights by a per-channel smoothing factor: Y = (X · diag(s)^{-1}) · (diag(s) · W). Dividing activations by s and multiplying weights by s leaves the product unchanged but flattens activation outliers, enabling accurate INT8 weight+activation quantization (fast compute-bound GEMM). Complements weight-only GPTQ/AWQ.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Weights and activations aside, the KV cache is huge — can we quantize that too? (4.16)

cards.cue: AWQ protects salient weights; the dual problem is activation outliers — what handles those?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
At long context/large batch, the KV cache (4.26) dominates memory. Quantizing cached keys/values to INT8 (A100-OK) or FP8 ([H100-ONLY]) roughly halves KV memory, enabling longer context or higher concurrency, with small accuracy impact. Trade-off: extra quant/dequant per step and possible quality loss on very long context. TensorRT-LLM exposes INT8/FP8 KV-cache flags.

A100 fallback: INT8 KV cache demonstrates the same memory-halving concept without FP8 hardware.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Quantization shrinks values; the other memory lever is removing weights — what is pruning? (4.17)

cards.cue: Weights and activations aside, the KV cache is huge — can we quantize that too?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Unstructured pruning zeros individual weights by magnitude → high sparsity but irregular; needs specialized kernels to see speedup (dense hardware ignores the zeros). Structured pruning removes whole units (neurons, heads, channels, layers) → immediate dense speedup and smaller matrices, but coarser and usually needs fine-tuning to recover accuracy. Structured is deployment-friendly; unstructured maximizes theoretical sparsity.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: NVIDIA hardware accelerates a specific structured sparsity pattern — which one and what does it require? (4.18)

cards.cue: Quantization shrinks values; the other memory lever is removing weights — what is pruning?

back.title: Verse
back.html: NVIDIA Sparse Tensor Cores (Ampere A100 and later) accelerate 2:4 fine-grained structured sparsity: in every contiguous group of 4 weights, exactly 2 must be zero. This fixed pattern is what the hardware exploits for ~2× GEMM throughput — arbitrary/unstructured sparsity does not qualify. Workflow: train dense → prune to the 2:4 mask → fine-tune to recover accuracy → deploy (TensorRT). Only the 2:4 pattern gets the speedup.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: 2:4 sparsity pairs powerfully with low precision — how do they combine in TensorRT? (4.19)

cards.cue: NVIDIA hardware accelerates a specific structured sparsity pattern — which one and what does it require?

back.title: Verse
back.html: 2:4 structured sparsity and INT8 quantization stack: the Sparse Tensor Core runs an INT8 GEMM at ~2× the dense INT8 rate, compounding memory and throughput gains. NVIDIA's recommended workflow (per the "Sparsity in INT8" guidance): prune to 2:4, quantize (PTQ/QAT), fine-tune to recover, then build a TensorRT engine that enables both sparse and INT8 kernels. Verify the engine actually selected sparse+INT8 tactics (not a dense fallback).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Beyond quantization and pruning, how do we make an entirely smaller model? (4.20)

cards.cue: 2:4 sparsity pairs powerfully with low precision — how do they combine in TensorRT?

cards.front: Knowledge distillation: teacher, student, soft targets

back.title: Verse
back.html: Train a small student to mimic a large teacher. Beyond hard labels, the student learns from the teacher's soft targets (full probability distribution), which carry "dark knowledge" about class similarities. A temperature T softens the teacher's logits to expose that structure: p_i = softmax(z_i/T). Student learns far more per example than from one-hot labels alone.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: How is the distillation loss actually formed from those soft targets? (4.21)

cards.cue: Beyond quantization and pruning, how do we make an entirely smaller model?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
$$\mathcal{L}=\alpha\,T^2\,\text{KL}(p_T^{teacher}\;\|\;p_T^{student})+(1-\alpha)\,\text{CE}(y,\,p^{student})$$

  • KL term matches softened distributions (temperature T); the T² factor rescales gradient magnitude softened by T.
  • CE term keeps the student honest to ground-truth labels.
  • α balances the two.
import torch.nn.functional as F
def distill_loss(s_logits, t_logits, y, T=2.0, alpha=0.5):
    kl = F.kl_div(F.log_softmax(s_logits/T, -1), F.softmax(t_logits/T, -1),
                  reduction="batchmean") * (T*T)
    ce = F.cross_entropy(s_logits, y)
    return alpha*kl + (1-alpha)*ce

back.title: Chain →
back.html: What real model demonstrates this, and what variants exist? (4.22)

cards.cue: How is the distillation loss actually formed from those soft targets?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
DistilBERT: ~40% smaller, ~60% faster, retains ~97% of BERT's language understanding — distilled with a triple loss (MLM + distillation KL + cosine embedding alignment). Variant taxonomy: - Response-based: match output logits/soft targets (4.20). - Feature-based: match intermediate hidden states/attention maps. - Relation-based: match relationships between layers/samples.

Distillation composes with quantization and pruning for maximum compression.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Compression handled — how do we accelerate the model on the actual GPU runtime? (4.23)

cards.cue: What real model demonstrates this, and what variants exist?

back.title: Verse
back.html: TensorRT is NVIDIA's inference optimizer/runtime. It ingests a model (ONNX), then the builder applies layer/tensor fusion, kernel auto-tuning (picks fastest tactics for the target GPU), precision selection (FP16/INT8/FP8), and memory planning, producing a serialized engine optimized for that specific GPU. Precision flags (FP16, INT8 + calibrator, sparsity) gate which kernels are considered. Engines are hardware-specific — rebuild per GPU architecture.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: TensorRT is general; what specializes it for transformer LLMs? (4.24)

cards.cue: Compression handled — how do we accelerate the model on the actual GPU runtime?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
TensorRT-LLM is the LLM-specialized layer on TensorRT: optimized attention kernels, in-flight (continuous) batching (8.08), paged KV cache, tensor/pipeline parallelism, and quantization (INT8/FP8/INT4 GPTQ/AWQ, and NVFP4 on Blackwell/GB200, 4.08). Workflow:

HF checkpoint -> convert_checkpoint.py (choose dtype/quant, TP/PP)
             -> trtllm-build (build engine, set max batch/seq, KV cache)
             -> run via TensorRT-LLM runtime or Triton TRT-LLM backend

Stale-knowledge flag: exact script names/flags (convert_checkpoint.py, trtllm-build) change frequently. VERIFY.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Some kernels are Hopper-specific — what plugins matter and what's the A100 fallback? (4.25)

cards.cue: TensorRT is general; what specializes it for transformer LLMs?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
TensorRT-LLM uses plugins — custom fused kernels (e.g. GPT attention plugin, paged-KV, FP8 GEMM). Some tactics are Hopper-specific: FP8 GEMM plugins and FlashAttention variants that exploit Hopper's TMA/WGMMA and FP8 units. The builder selects them only on sm_90.

A100 fallback: on Ampere the builder selects INT8/FP16 fused-attention plugins instead — same fused-attention concept, no FP8 path. Build with --dtype float16 (+ INT8) rather than FP8.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Attention plugins manage the KV cache — how big is it, exactly? (4.26)

cards.cue: Some kernels are Hopper-specific — what plugins matter and what's the A100 fallback?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Per-token KV cache size (bytes):

$$\text{KV} = 2 \times n_{\text{layers}} \times n_{\text{kv\_heads}} \times d_{\text{head}} \times \text{bytes}$$

The leading 2 = keys + values. Total = × seq_len × batch. Example: 32 layers, 32 KV heads, head_dim 128, FP16 (2 bytes) → per token = 2·32·32·128·2 = 524,288 B ≈ 0.5 MiB; at 4096 tokens = 2 GiB per sequence. This is why long context/large batch is memory-bound and why GQA/MQA (fewer n_kv_heads) and KV quantization (4.16) matter.

kv_bytes = 2 * n_layers * n_kv_heads * head_dim * bytes_per_elt  # per token
total = kv_bytes * seq_len * batch

back.title: Chain →
back.html: If full attention is O(n²), how do we handle very long sequences cheaply? (4.27)

cards.cue: Attention plugins manage the KV cache — how big is it, exactly?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Sliding-window attention (Mistral) limits each token to attend to the last w tokens, bounding attention cost and KV cache to O(w) instead of O(n) — enabling long /streaming contexts. StreamingLLM keeps a few initial "attention-sink" tokens plus a recent window to preserve stability across effectively infinite streams. Trade-off: tokens beyond the window lose direct access (mitigated by layered receptive fields).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Quantize/prune/distill/serve covered for decoders — how are encoders pretrained? (4.28)

cards.cue: If full attention is O(n²), how do we handle very long sequences cheaply?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Encoders (BERT) are pretrained with MLM: randomly mask ~15% of tokens and predict them from bidirectional context. BERT's recipe: of the masked 15%, 80% → [MASK], 10% → random token, 10% → unchanged (reduces train/inference mismatch since [MASK] never appears at inference). Contrast with decoder CLM (2.15) which predicts strictly left-to-right.

# labels = -100 everywhere except masked positions
loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.view(-1, V), labels.view(-1), ignore_index=-100)

back.title: Chain →
back.html: BERT also had a second pretraining objective — what was it and is it kept? (4.29)

cards.cue: Quantize/prune/distill/serve covered for decoders — how are encoders pretrained?

back.title: Verse
back.html: BERT's second objective: given sentences A and B, predict whether B truly follows A (binary), aimed at sentence-pair tasks (NLI, QA). Later work (RoBERTa) showed NSP hurts or is unnecessary and dropped it, training MLM-only on longer sequences with larger batches. Exam-relevant nuance: NSP is historical BERT, not a modern requirement.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Optimization also covers decoding-side and search knobs — what advanced sampling affects optimization studies? (4.30)

cards.cue: BERT also had a second pretraining objective — what was it and is it kept?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Beam search keeps the top-b partial sequences by cumulative log-prob at each step, with length normalization to avoid bias toward short sequences: score = (Σ log p) / len^α. Larger beams find higher-likelihood outputs (better for translation/constrained tasks) at linear cost in b; they do not help open-ended diversity (1.11). In optimization/ablation studies beam width is a knob whose throughput cost must be measured against quality gain.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Beam is one knob; how does temperature figure into ablation studies? (4.31)

cards.cue: Optimization also covers decoding-side and search knobs — what advanced sampling affects optimization studies?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Temperature scaling (softmax with z/T) is used two ways: as a decoding knob (1.11) and as a post-hoc calibration method (fit a single T on a validation set so predicted confidence matches accuracy). Ablation studies systematically remove/vary one factor at a time (a quantization method, a sparsity level, a sampling setting) with everything else fixed, to attribute accuracy/throughput changes to that factor. Change one variable per run; hold seeds/decoding fixed for fair comparison.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Ablations vary knobs; how do we systematically search training hyperparameters? (4.32)

cards.cue: Beam is one knob; how does temperature figure into ablation studies?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
• Warmup: linearly ramp LR from ~0 over the first few % of steps to avoid early divergence (critical for transformers/post-LN and large batches).
  • Cosine decay: after warmup, decay LR following a cosine curve to a small final value — the standard LLM schedule.
  • Alternatives: linear decay, inverse-sqrt (original Transformer), constant.
from torch.optim.lr_scheduler import LambdaLR
import math
def cosine_warmup(step, warmup, total):
    if step < warmup: return step / warmup
    p = (step - warmup) / (total - warmup)
    return 0.5 * (1 + math.cos(math.pi * p))

back.title: Chain →
back.html: LR interacts with batch size — how do we scale them together? (4.33)

cards.cue: Ablations vary knobs; how do we systematically search training hyperparameters?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Linear scaling rule: when you multiply the effective batch size by k, multiply the base LR by k (with warmup), because the gradient estimate's variance drops and each step is more confident. Holds up to a critical batch size, beyond which returns diminish and LR must be tempered (or use LAMB for very large batches). Effective batch = per-device × devices × grad-accum steps (7.15).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Manual tuning is slow — how do we search hyperparameters at scale? (4.34)

back.title: Verse
back.html:
• Grid search: exhaustive; explodes combinatorially.
  • Random search: samples the space; more efficient than grid for few important dims.
  • Bayesian optimization: models the objective, proposes promising points (Optuna, Ax).
  • Population-based training (PBT): evolves a population, copying/perturbing good configs during training.

Distribute trials across GPUs/nodes (Ray Tune, NeMo/Base Command). Use early stopping (5.20) to kill weak trials fast.

INT8 integer uniform inference (A100 fallback) Turing+
FP4/NVFP4 4-bit float+microscale extreme compress inference Blackwell

cards.label: Q1 · Domain 4
cards.front: Decode latency is high and profiling shows the GPU is memory-bandwidth-bound while compute units sit idle. Which optimization helps most?

back.title: Why
back.html: Memory-bound decode is dominated by weight loading; weight-only low-bit quant shrinks weights → faster. A: W+A helps compute-bound, not this. C/D: unrelated/ worse.

cards.label: Q2 · Domain 4
cards.front: After INT8 PTQ, accuracy collapsed. Calibration used min-max on 8 random samples. Best first fix?

back.title: Why
back.html: Min-max on tiny/random data is outlier-sensitive and unrepresentative; fix calibration first (entropy/percentile, representative data) before the heavier QAT. A: premature. C/D: irrelevant.

options.html: Use entropy/percentile calibration on representative data

cards.label: Q3 · Domain 4
cards.front: A model must go to INT4 with strict accuracy. PTQ (GPTQ) still drops too much. Correct escalation?

back.title: Why
back.html: When PTQ collapses at low bit-width, QAT recovers accuracy. A: violates requirement. C/D: unrelated.

cards.label: Q4 · Domain 4
cards.front: Which is required for NVIDIA Sparse Tensor Core acceleration?

back.title: Why
back.html: Sparse Tensor Cores accelerate exactly the 2:4 pattern. A/C: unstructured doesn't qualify. D: unrelated.

back.title: Why
back.html: A100 lacks FP8 units; INT8/BF16 preserve the low-precision-GEMM concept. A: false. C: Blackwell. D: nonsense.

back.title: Why
back.html: SmoothQuant migrates activation outliers into weights, enabling W8A8. A: that's AWQ-ish/GPTQ. C/D: unrelated.

back.title: Why
