back.title: Watch out
back.html: Only the 2-of-every-4-zero pattern gets Sparse Tensor Core speedup; arbitrary/unstructured sparsity does not. Requires fine-tune to recover (4.18).

cards.label: Trap · Domain 4
cards.front: When QAT is mandatory, not optional

back.title: Watch out
back.html: QAT is required when PTQ accuracy collapses — typically INT4 or sensitive models; INT8/FP8 usually fine with PTQ (4.12). Distractors claim QAT is "always better/required."

back.title: Watch out
back.html: FP8 Tensor Cores exist on sm_89 (L4/L40S) and sm_90+ (H100, Blackwell); A100 (sm_80) has none and must fall back to INT8/BF16 (4.06, 4.25). Don't claim A100 does FP8.

back.title: Watch out
back.html: Weight-only speeds memory-bound decode; weight+activation speeds compute-bound prefill. Choosing wrong yields no speedup (4.04).

back.title: Watch out
back.html: Calibrating on non-representative data is the classic "accuracy collapsed after PTQ" cause (4.09, 4.10).

back.title: Watch out
back.html: INT8 = uniform integer steps; FP8 = floating (better dynamic range, less calibration). Not interchangeable (4.05 vs 4.06).

back.title: Watch out
back.html: Leading factor 2 (keys + values); scales with layers, kv_heads, head_dim, seq, batch. GQA/MQA reduce kv_heads (4.26).

back.title: Watch out
back.html: RoBERTa dropped NSP; don't assert it's required (4.29).

back.title: Watch out
back.html: Large-batch transformer training diverges early without warmup (4.32).

back.title: Watch out
back.html: A TensorRT engine built for A100 is not optimal/valid for H100 — rebuild per architecture (4.23).

back.title: Verse
back.html: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) continues training a pretrained model on labeled (prompt, completion) pairs, updating all weights via the CLM loss (2.15) masked to the completion (2.16). Full FT gives maximum capacity to adapt but costs memory = params + gradients + optimizer states (Adam ≈ 2× params) + activations — often prohibitive for large models (motivating PEFT, 5.10). Risk: catastrophic forgetting (5.26).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Raw SFT teaches tasks; how do we specifically make a model follow chat instructions? (5.02)

back.title: Verse
back.html: Instruction tuning is SFT on diverse (instruction, response) data rendered in the chat template (2.01, 3.10), teaching the model to follow instructions and hold multi-turn conversations. Loss is masked to assistant turns only. Quality/diversity of instructions matters more than sheer volume. This produces the "instruct"/"chat" variant from a base model.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Instruction-tuned models still may not match human preferences — how do we align to those? (5.03)

cards.cue: Raw SFT teaches tasks; how do we specifically make a model follow chat instructions?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback aligns models to preferences in three stages: (1) SFT base; (2) train a reward model (5.04) on human preference comparisons; (3) RL-optimize the policy against the reward model with PPO (5.05), regularized by a KL penalty to the SFT reference. Powerful but complex: four models in memory (policy, reference, reward, value), unstable, expensive.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: The pipeline depends on a reward model — how is it trained? (5.04)

cards.cue: Instruction-tuned models still may not match human preferences — how do we align to those?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
A reward model (RM) scores a response's quality. Trained on human preference pairs (prompt, chosen, rejected) with the Bradley-Terry loss:

$$\mathcal{L}_{RM}=-\log\sigma\big(r_\theta(x,y_{chosen})-r_\theta(x,y_{rejected})\big)$$

The RM is usually the SFT model with a scalar head. It provides the reward signal PPO optimizes. Quality/coverage of preference data caps final alignment quality.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: With a reward model, how does PPO update the policy without destroying it? (5.05)

cards.cue: The pipeline depends on a reward model — how is it trained?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Proximal Policy Optimization treats generation as RL: the policy (LLM) generates, the reward model scores, a value network estimates baselines, and a clipped surrogate objective bounds each update. A KL penalty to the frozen SFT reference keeps the policy from drifting into reward-hacking gibberish:

$$\text{reward} = r_\theta(x,y) - \beta\,\text{KL}\big(\pi_\theta \,\|\, \pi_{ref}\big)$$

Sensitive to hyperparameters; the value net doubles memory. This complexity motivates DPO.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: PPO needs a reward model and RL machinery — can we align directly from preferences instead? (5.06)

cards.cue: With a reward model, how does PPO update the policy without destroying it?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
DPO skips the explicit reward model and RL loop: it reparameterizes the RLHF objective so the optimal policy defines an implicit reward, giving a simple classification loss on preference pairs against a frozen reference:

$$\mathcal{L}_{DPO}=-\log\sigma\!\Big(\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w|x)}{\pi_{ref}(y_w|x)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l|x)}{\pi_{ref}(y_l|x)}\Big)$$

(y_w=chosen, y_l=rejected). Only policy + reference in memory; stable, no reward model, no sampling loop. The β controls deviation from the reference.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: DPO is simpler than PPO — when would I still prefer one over the other? (5.07)

cards.cue: PPO needs a reward model and RL machinery — can we align directly from preferences instead?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
• DPO: simpler, stable, cheaper (no RM/value net, no online sampling), needs a fixed preference dataset. Can overfit to the dataset and is off-policy.
  • PPO/RLHF: on-policy exploration via a reward model can exceed the static dataset and optimize non-differentiable/complex rewards, but is unstable, memory-heavy, and hard to tune.

Rule: default to DPO for preference alignment; use PPO when you need online exploration, a learned reward covering many behaviors, or reward signals you can't bake into pairs.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Both DPO and PPO have limits — what newer method drops the value network for reasoning RL? (5.08)

cards.cue: DPO is simpler than PPO — when would I still prefer one over the other?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
GRPO (from DeepSeek-R1-style reasoning training) removes PPO's value network: for each prompt it samples a group of G responses, scores them (often with a verifiable/rule-based reward), and uses the group mean/std as the baseline so the advantage is each response's reward normalized within its group:

$$A_i=\frac{r_i-\text{mean}(r_{1..G})}{\text{std}(r_{1..G})}$$

Cheaper than PPO (no value net), well-suited to reasoning tasks with automatic reward checking.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: With PPO, DPO, and GRPO on the table, how do I choose? (5.09)

cards.cue: Both DPO and PPO have limits — what newer method drops the value network for reasoning RL?

cards.front: GRPO vs PPO vs DPO decision

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Method Reward model? Value net? Data Best for
DPO no (implicit) no fixed preference pairs cheap, stable preference alignment
PPO yes (learned) yes online rollouts rich/complex rewards, exploration
GRPO reward fn (often rule-based) no grouped rollouts reasoning/verifiable rewards, cheaper RL

Escalate DPO → GRPO → PPO as reward complexity and need for online exploration rise.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Alignment methods update behavior; but most of us can't afford full FT — how do we adapt parameter-efficiently? (5.10)

cards.cue: With PPO, DPO, and GRPO on the table, how do I choose?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
LoRA freezes pretrained W₀ ∈ ℝ^{d×k} and learns a low-rank update:

$$W = W_0 + \Delta W = W_0 + \frac{\alpha}{r} BA,\qquad B\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r},\; A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times k},\; r\ll\min(d,k)$$

Only A, B train (parameters ∝ r(d+k) instead of d·k). A init random Gaussian, B init zero (so ΔW starts at 0). At inference BA can be merged into W₀ → zero added latency.

delta = (alpha / r) * (B @ A)   # add to W0

back.title: Chain →
back.html: LoRA has knobs — which matter and how are they set? (5.11)

cards.cue: Alignment methods update behavior; but most of us can't afford full FT — how do we adapt parameter-efficiently?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
• rank r: capacity of the update (4–64 typical); too low underfits, too high wastes params and risks overfit.
  • alpha α: scaling; effective scale α/r. Common heuristic α = 2r.
  • target modules: which projections get adapters — attention q_proj,k_proj,v_proj, o_proj (and often MLP). More targets = more capacity.
  • dropout: regularizes the adapter.
from peft import LoraConfig
cfg = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05,
                 target_modules=["q_proj","k_proj","v_proj","o_proj"])

back.title: Chain →
back.html: LoRA still loads the base in FP16 — how do we fine-tune when even that won't fit? (5.12)

cards.cue: LoRA has knobs — which matter and how are they set?

back.title: Verse
back.html: QLoRA quantizes the frozen base to 4-bit (NF4, a normal-float format optimal for normally-distributed weights), then trains LoRA adapters in BF16 on top. Adds double quantization (quantize the quantization constants) and paged optimizers (offload optimizer states to CPU on memory spikes). Result: fine-tune a 65B model on a single 48 GB GPU. Base stays 4-bit; gradients flow only into the BF16 adapters.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: One base can host many adapters — how do we serve them together? (5.13)

cards.cue: LoRA still loads the base in FP16 — how do we fine-tune when even that won't fit?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Because adapters are tiny and the base is shared, one deployment can serve many LoRA adapters simultaneously, routing each request to its adapter (per-task/per-tenant). The base weights load once; adapters swap cheaply (or batch heterogeneously with specialized kernels). NVIDIA supports multi-LoRA in TensorRT-LLM / NIM. Trade-off: un-merged adapters add a small per-layer compute overhead vs a merged single-task model.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: LoRA is one PEFT family — what are the alternatives? (5.14)

cards.cue: One base can host many adapters — how do we serve them together?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Adapter tuning inserts small bottleneck modules (down-project → nonlinearity → up-project, with a residual) between frozen transformer sublayers; only adapters train. Unlike LoRA (which reparameterizes existing weight matrices and can be merged), adapters add new layers, so they cannot be merged away and add inference latency. Historically first PEFT method; LoRA largely superseded it for LLMs.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: LoRA/adapters modify weights or add layers — is there a PEFT that only touches the input? (5.15)

cards.cue: LoRA is one PEFT family — what are the alternatives?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Prompt tuning / P-tuning prepend trainable continuous embedding vectors (soft prompts, 2.12) to the input; the model and all real weights stay frozen — only the prompt vectors train. Prefix tuning goes further: it prepends trainable vectors to the keys/values at every layer, not just the input embedding, giving more capacity. Extremely parameter-efficient (thousands of params), but usually less expressive than LoRA for hard tasks.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: There are two P-tuning variants — how do they differ? (5.16)

cards.cue: LoRA/adapters modify weights or add layers — is there a PEFT that only touches the input?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
• Prompt tuning / P-tuning (v1): soft prompts only at the input layer. Works well only at large scale; weak on smaller models and hard sequence-labeling tasks.
  • P-tuning v2: adds tunable prompts at every layer (deep prompt tuning, akin to prefix tuning), matching full fine-tuning across scales and tasks.

NeMo implements P-tuning; the exam may contrast "prompt tuning" (shallow) vs "P-tuning v2 / prefix" (deep).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: With four PEFT families known, how do I choose among them and full FT? (5.17)

cards.cue: There are two P-tuning variants — how do they differ?

cards.front: PEFT decision: LoRA vs adapters vs P-tuning vs full FT

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Method Trains Merge-able? Inference cost Capacity
Full FT all weights n/a none extra highest (+ forgetting risk)
LoRA/QLoRA low-rank ΔW yes zero if merged high
Adapters bottleneck layers no small latency medium
P-tuning/prefix soft prompt vecs no tiny low–medium

Rule: LoRA/QLoRA is the default (mergeable, strong, cheap). Full FT only with ample data/compute and forgetting mitigation. P-tuning for extreme parameter efficiency / many tasks. Adapters mostly legacy.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: PEFT covers task adaptation; a distinct fine-tuning goal is embeddings — how are those trained? (5.18)

cards.cue: With four PEFT families known, how do I choose among them and full FT?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Embedding models are fine-tuned so similar texts are close and dissimilar far apart. - Triplet loss: max(0, d(a,p) − d(a,n) + margin) — anchor closer to positive than negative by a margin. - InfoNCE / contrastive: treat the matching pair as positive against in-batch negatives:

$$\mathcal{L}=-\log\frac{\exp(\text{sim}(a,p)/\tau)}{\sum_i \exp(\text{sim}(a,n_i)/\tau)}$$

Temperature τ sharpens; large in-batch negatives help. Basis of retrieval/RAG embedding quality (2.24, 6.08).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Contrastive training produces embeddings — what's the standard model shape? (5.19)

cards.cue: PEFT covers task adaptation; a distinct fine-tuning goal is embeddings — how are those trained?

back.title: Verse
back.html: A bi-encoder encodes query and document separately into vectors compared by cosine — fast, precomputable, the backbone of retrieval/RAG. Contrast the cross-encoder, which jointly encodes a (query, doc) pair for a relevance score — more accurate but O(n) per query, used for re-ranking the bi-encoder's top-k. Fine-tune bi-encoders with contrastive loss (5.18) on (query, positive, negatives). NVIDIA: NeMo Retriever embedding + reranking models.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Fine-tuning risks overfitting — how do we stop training at the right time? (5.20)

cards.cue: Contrastive training produces embeddings — what's the standard model shape?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Monitor a validation metric each eval interval; stop when it fails to improve for patience consecutive checks, and restore the best checkpoint. Prevents overfitting and wasted compute. Levers: patience, min_delta (minimum improvement to count), which metric to watch. Pairs with a warmup/cosine schedule (4.32) and HP search (4.34, kill weak trials early).

if val_metric < best - min_delta:
    best, wait = val_metric, 0; save("best.pt")
else:
    wait += 1
    if wait >= patience: stop()

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Early stopping fights overfitting — what other signals reveal it? (5.21)

cards.cue: Fine-tuning risks overfitting — how do we stop training at the right time?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Signal: training loss keeps falling while validation loss rises (diverging curves). Regularizers: weight decay (L2), dropout, data augmentation, smaller LoRA rank, fewer epochs, and more/diverse data. For LLM fine-tuning, 1–3 epochs on instruction data is often enough; more epochs memorize. Label smoothing softens over-confidence.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Detecting overfitting requires the right metric — which per phase? (5.22)

cards.cue: Early stopping fights overfitting — what other signals reveal it?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Match the metric to the phase and task: - Training: loss (CLM/contrastive) for optimization. - Validation: task metric for model selection/early stopping — perplexity (LM), accuracy/F1 (classification), BLEU/ROUGE (generation), retrieval recall@k (embeddings). - Test: held-out final report; add human/LLM-judge for open-ended quality (Domain 6).

Never select the model on the test set (leakage, 3.11). Pick a single primary metric to avoid ambiguous model selection.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Metrics assess quality; a specific failure to fix in fine-tuning is hallucination — how? (5.23)

cards.cue: Detecting overfitting requires the right metric — which per phase?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Fine-tuning levers against hallucination: train on high-quality grounded data (answers tied to sources), include "I don't know" examples so refusal is learned, prefer RAG for knowledge-heavy tasks over parametric memorization (2.21, 2.23), and align with preference methods (DPO) that penalize fabrication. Over-training on narrow data can increase confident hallucination — balance with diverse data.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Fine-tuning reduces hallucination probabilistically — what enforces it at runtime? (5.24)

cards.cue: Metrics assess quality; a specific failure to fix in fine-tuning is hallucination — how?

cards.front: NeMo Guardrails for hallucination control (xref D10)

back.title: Verse
back.html: Runtime enforcement complements fine-tuning: NeMo Guardrails can add a fact-checking / self-check output rail that verifies a response against retrieved sources (or a second LLM call) and blocks/《revises unsupported claims. The guide cites integrating Cleanlab Trustworthy Language Model in NeMo Guardrails for hallucination scoring. Fine-tuning lowers the rate; guardrails catch the residue. Full guardrails treatment in 10.09–10.10.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: After mitigation, how do we quantify whether fine-tuning actually helped? (5.25)

cards.cue: Fine-tuning reduces hallucination probabilistically — what enforces it at runtime?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Measure before/after on a held-out set with the primary task metric and a regression check on general capability (to catch forgetting, 5.26). Use paired comparisons, fixed decoding/seeds, and enough samples for significance. Track both the target improvement and side-effects (safety, other tasks). Formal evaluation frameworks (Ragas, NeMo Evaluator, LLM-as-judge) are Domain 6.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: A key risk when assessing impact is losing prior abilities — what is it and how to prevent it? (5.26)

cards.cue: After mitigation, how do we quantify whether fine-tuning actually helped?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Fine-tuning on a narrow task can overwrite general capabilities — catastrophic forgetting. Mitigations: PEFT (LoRA freezes the base, structurally limiting drift), lower LR / fewer epochs, replay (mix in general/pretraining data), regularization toward the base (EWC, KL to reference — the same mechanism as RLHF's KL penalty, 5.05), and multi-task instead of sequential training. PEFT's inherent resistance to forgetting is a key reason it's the default.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Fine-tuning done; the next question is rigorous measurement — Domain 6: Evaluation.

cards.cue: A key risk when assessing impact is losing prior abilities — what is it and how to prevent it?

back.title: Recall
back.html: SFT updates all weights on (prompt, completion) with completion-masked loss, memory = params+grads+optimizer+activations (5.01); instruction tuning is SFT on diverse instructions in the chat template, assistant-masked, producing the chat variant (5.02).

back.title: Recall
back.html: SFT → reward model → PPO with KL to reference (5.03); RM trained on preference pairs with Bradley-Terry −log σ(r_chosen − r_rejected) (5.04); PPO optimizes policy with value net + clipped surrogate + KL penalty β to the frozen reference (5.05).

cards.label: WR-5a · Walk & Recall
cards.front: RLHF is unstable and won't fit four models in memory — recite the simpler chain.

back.title: Recall
back.html: DPO reparameterizes to an implicit reward, a classification loss on pairs against a frozen reference, only policy+reference in memory (5.06); pick DPO for cheap stable alignment, PPO for online exploration/complex rewards (5.07); GRPO drops the value net, using group-normalized advantage (r−mean)/std, great for verifiable reasoning rewards (5.08); escalate DPO→GRPO→PPO by reward complexity (5.09).

cards.label: WR-5a · Walk & Recall
cards.front: Which three items in this walk are most likely to be forgotten?

back.title: Most forgotten
back.html: 5.04 Bradley-Terry RM loss; 5.06 DPO = implicit reward, no RM/value net; 5.08 GRPO baseline = group mean/std (no value network).

back.title: Recall
back.html: W = W₀ + (α/r)·BA, B∈d×r zero-init, A∈r×k random, r≪min(d,k); only A,B train; merge BA into W₀ for zero added latency (5.10). Knobs: rank (capacity), alpha (α/r scale, α≈2r), target modules (attn q/k/v/o + MLP), dropout (5.11).

cards.label: WR-5b · Walk & Recall
cards.front: Even LoRA in FP16 OOMs on this model — recite.

back.title: Recall
back.html: QLoRA: 4-bit NF4 frozen base + BF16 adapters, double quantization + paged optimizers, 65B on one 48GB GPU (5.12); one base serves many adapters via multi-LoRA routing (5.13).

cards.label: WR-5b · Walk & Recall
cards.front: PEFT families and which can merge?

back.title: Recall
back.html: Adapters = bottleneck layers inserted between sublayers, cannot merge, add latency (5.14); P-tuning/prefix = trainable soft prompt vectors, input-only (prompt tuning) vs every-layer (prefix/P-tuning v2) (5.15, 5.16); decision: LoRA/QLoRA default (mergeable), full FT only with data+ forgetting mitigation, P-tuning for extreme efficiency, adapters legacy (5.17).

back.title: Recall
back.html: Contrastive/InfoNCE or triplet with temperature and in-batch negatives (5.18).

cards.label: WR-5b · Walk & Recall
cards.front: Which three items in this walk are most likely to be forgotten?

back.title: Most forgotten
back.html: 5.10 B zero-init / A random (ΔW starts at 0); 5.14 adapters cannot be merged (LoRA can); 5.16 prompt tuning (shallow) vs P-tuning v2/ prefix (every layer).

back.title: Recall
back.html: Bi-encoder encodes query/doc separately → cosine, fast, precomputable, RAG backbone; cross-encoder jointly encodes the pair, accurate but O(n)/query, used to re-rank top-k (5.19).

cards.label: WR-5c · Walk & Recall
cards.front: Val loss rising while train loss falls — recite the overfitting chain.

back.title: Recall
back.html: Early stopping on a validation metric with patience/min_delta, restore best checkpoint (5.20); the diverging curves are the overfitting signal; regularize with weight decay/dropout/fewer epochs/more data (5.21); select on validation with a single primary metric, never the test set (5.22).

cards.label: WR-5c · Walk & Recall
cards.front: Model confidently fabricates after fine-tuning — recite the mitigation chain.

back.title: Recall
back.html: Train on grounded data + "I don't know" examples + prefer RAG + DPO against fabrication (5.23); enforce at runtime with NeMo Guardrails fact-check/ self-check rail (Cleanlab TLM) (5.24); assess before/after on held-out with a general- capability regression check (5.25); watch for catastrophic forgetting — mitigate with PEFT/replay/lower LR/KL-to-reference (5.26).

cards.label: WR-5c · Walk & Recall
cards.front: Which three items in this walk are most likely to be forgotten?

back.title: Most forgotten
back.html: 5.19 cross-encoder is for re-ranking (not first- stage retrieval); 5.22 never select on the test set; 5.26 PEFT resists forgetting by freezing the base.

back.title: Answer

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Perplexity is the exponentiated average negative log-likelihood — the model's "branching factor," how surprised it is per token:

$$\text{PPL}=\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log p(x_i\mid x_{<i})\right)=\exp(\text{mean NLL})$$

Lower = better. It is a fluency/likelihood measure computed on held-out text, not a task-quality measure (a fluent model can still be wrong). Only comparable across models with the same tokenizer/vocabulary (tokenization changes N). Fixed-length models use a sliding window.

import torch
ppl = torch.exp(torch.stack(nll_per_token).mean())

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Perplexity scores likelihood, not overlap with a reference — how do we score generated text against references? (6.02)

back.title: Verse
back.html:
BLEU is precision-oriented: what fraction of the candidate's n-grams appear in the reference (with clipping to avoid repetition gaming), geometric mean over n=1..4, times a brevity penalty that punishes too-short output:

$$\text{BLEU}=BP\cdot\exp\!\Big(\sum_{n=1}^{4}w_n\log p_n\Big),\quad BP=\begin{cases}1 & c>r\\ e^{(1-r/c)} & c\le r\end{cases}$$

c=candidate length, r=reference length. No BP → a one-word correct token would score perfectly. Standard for machine translation; corpus-level.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: BLEU measures precision — what if we care about recall (did we cover the reference)? (6.03)

cards.cue: Perplexity scores likelihood, not overlap with a reference — how do we score generated text against references?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
ROUGE is recall-oriented: how much of the reference is captured by the candidate. - ROUGE-N: n-gram recall (ROUGE-1 unigrams, ROUGE-2 bigrams). - ROUGE-L: based on the Longest Common Subsequence (order-aware, gaps allowed), combined into an F-measure:

$$R=\frac{LCS(c,r)}{|r|},\quad P=\frac{LCS(c,r)}{|c|},\quad F_{L}=\frac{(1+\beta^2)RP}{R+\beta^2 P}$$

Standard for summarization. LCS needs no fixed n and rewards in-order coverage.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: BLEU/ROUGE only credit exact surface matches — how do we credit synonyms and stems? (6.04)

cards.cue: BLEU measures precision — what if we care about recall (did we cover the reference)?

back.title: Verse
back.html: METEOR aligns candidate↔reference words allowing exact, stem, and synonym matches (WordNet), computes a recall-weighted F-mean (recall weighted ~9× precision), and applies a fragmentation penalty for out-of-order chunks. Correlates better with human judgment than BLEU at the sentence level because it credits meaning-preserving variation. More expensive (needs stemmer/synonym resources, language-dependent).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: With three overlap metrics, how do I choose among them? (6.05)

cards.cue: BLEU/ROUGE only credit exact surface matches — how do we credit synonyms and stems?

cards.front: BLEU vs ROUGE vs METEOR decision

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Metric Orientation Match type Standard use
BLEU precision + brevity penalty exact n-gram machine translation
ROUGE recall (ROUGE-L = LCS) exact n-gram / subsequence summarization
METEOR recall-weighted F-mean exact + stem + synonym sentence-level, human correlation

All are surface-overlap metrics: they penalize valid paraphrases and can't judge factuality. For semantic/quality assessment, escalate to embedding-based metrics (BERTScore), LLM-as-a-judge (6.06), or humans (6.07).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Overlap metrics miss meaning — how do we score open-ended quality at scale? (6.06)

cards.cue: With three overlap metrics, how do I choose among them?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Use a strong LLM to score/compare outputs against a rubric (pointwise score or pairwise preference). Scales far cheaper than humans and correlates reasonably for open-ended quality. Known biases to control: position bias (favors first/second — randomize order), verbosity bias (favors longer), self-preference (favors its own family), and leniency. Mitigate with clear rubrics, reference answers, order swapping, and calibration against human labels.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Judges still drift from ground truth — what's the gold standard? (6.07)

cards.cue: Overlap metrics miss meaning — how do we score open-ended quality at scale?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Human evaluation is the gold standard for quality/safety: pairwise preference, Likert-scale ratings, or task success. Requires clear guidelines, multiple annotators, and inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's/Fleiss' κ). Expensive and slow → used to calibrate cheaper automatic metrics and LLM-judges, and for high-stakes final sign-off. Combine quantitative metrics + human review (NVIDIA's recommended blend).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: For RAG systems specifically, which metrics apply? (6.08)

cards.cue: Judges still drift from ground truth — what's the gold standard?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Ragas evaluates RAG pipelines along component-specific axes, mostly via LLM-judged scoring: - Faithfulness: is the answer grounded in the retrieved context (no hallucination)? - Answer relevancy: does the answer address the question? - Context precision / recall: did retrieval return the right, sufficient chunks?

Separating retrieval metrics from generation metrics localizes failures (bad retrieval vs bad generation). NVIDIA integrates Ragas with NeMo/NIM endpoints (per the guide).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Metrics tell you that it failed — how do we find why? (6.09)

cards.cue: For RAG systems specifically, which metrics apply?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Common LLM failure modes to name and detect: hallucination (fabricated facts), repetition/degeneration (loops — decoding, 1.12), refusal/over-refusal, instruction-ignoring, format violations, prompt-injection compliance, reasoning errors, bias/toxicity (Domain 10), and context failures (ignoring or misusing retrieved content). Classifying outputs into this taxonomy is the first step of error analysis.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: With a taxonomy, how do we systematically analyze errors? (6.10)

cards.cue: Metrics tell you that it failed — how do we find why?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Process: collect a representative failure sample → label each by failure mode (6.09) → quantify frequencies → find patterns (input length, topic, language, retrieval miss) → form hypotheses → target fixes (data, prompt, retrieval, fine-tuning) → re-test. NVIDIA/DLI framing: start with error analysis before adding complexity — it tells you which lever to pull. Track error rates over time as a monitoring signal (Domain 9).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Errors localized on one platform — do results hold across hardware/platforms? (6.11)

cards.cue: With a taxonomy, how do we systematically analyze errors?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Compare deployments (on-prem DGX vs cloud GPUs, A100 vs H100, different serving stacks) on both quality (task metrics — must be identical given same model/decoding) and performance (latency percentiles, throughput/tokens-per-second, cost-per-token). Quality should match across hardware; performance differs. Control everything but the variable under test: same model version, prompts, decoding params, batch, warmup.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Fair performance comparison needs standardization — what exactly must be fixed? (6.12)

cards.cue: Errors localized on one platform — do results hold across hardware/platforms?

back.title: Verse
back.html: For reproducible, fair comparison: fix random seeds, decoding params (greedy for determinism), prompt templates, dataset version, and tokenizer; report latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99, not just mean), throughput at fixed concurrency, and confidence intervals over multiple runs. Warm up before timing. Report the same metric definitions across systems (e.g. TTFT vs end-to-end latency, 8.02). Standardized harnesses prevent apples-to-oranges claims.

back.title: Verse
back.html: A robust framework integrates: dataset/benchmark management, multiple metric types (overlap + embedding + LLM-judge + human), standardized configs, versioned results, and regression tracking. NeMo Evaluator is NVIDIA's tool for running standardized LLM evals (academic benchmarks, custom tasks, LLM-as-judge) against models/endpoints. Design for reproducibility (pinned data/seeds) and comparability (same harness across model versions — ties to Domain 9 continuous benchmarking).

back.title: Verse

Integrate with the serving/monitoring stack so production traffic can be periodically re-scored (continuous benchmarking, 9.07). Store results with model+data+config versions for auditability. This closes the loop from Evaluation into Deployment and Monitoring.

back.title: Verse
back.html: Ways to split a training job across GPUs: data parallel (replicate model, split batch — DDP/FSDP), tensor parallel (split individual layers' matrices), pipeline parallel (split layers into stages), sequence parallel (split the sequence dimension), expert parallel (split MoE experts). They compose into 3D/4D parallelism. Choose based on whether the bottleneck is throughput (data) or model size (model/tensor/pipeline).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Start with the simplest: how does data parallelism sync gradients? (7.02)

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Distributed Data Parallel replicates the full model on each GPU, each processes a different micro-batch, then all-reduce averages gradients across ranks (NCCL ring all-reduce — bandwidth-optimal). Overlaps gradient communication with the backward pass (gradient bucketing). Requires the whole model + optimizer to fit on one GPU. Near-linear scaling until communication dominates.

import torch.distributed as dist
model = torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel(model, device_ids=[local_rank])
# gradients all-reduced automatically during backward()

back.title: Chain →
back.html: DDP needs the whole model per GPU — what if it doesn't fit? (7.03)

cards.cue: Start with the simplest: how does data parallelism sync gradients?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Fully Sharded Data Parallel (≈ DeepSpeed ZeRO) shards what DDP replicates: - ZeRO-1: shard optimizer states. - ZeRO-2: + shard gradients. - ZeRO-3 / FSDP: + shard parameters — each GPU holds a slice, all-gathers the full layer just-in-time for forward/backward, then frees it.

Trades extra communication for a large memory reduction, fitting models far bigger than one GPU while keeping the data-parallel programming model.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Sharding data-parallel still replicates compute per layer — how do we split a single layer's math? (7.04)

cards.cue: DDP needs the whole model per GPU — what if it doesn't fit?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Tensor Parallelism (TP) splits individual weight matrices across GPUs (intra-layer). Megatron splits attention/MLP GEMMs column- then row-wise so each GPU computes a shard and an all-reduce combines partial results per layer. High communication volume → keep TP within the NVLink domain; don't span slow inter-node links. Enables layers too big for one GPU.

GB200/NVL72 note: "within a node" traditionally meant ~8 GPUs (NVLink+NVSwitch). A GB200 NVL72 rack is a single 72-GPU NVLink domain, so TP (and EP, 7.07) can scale to far more GPUs at NVLink bandwidth than the 8-GPU rule assumes — reshaping the TP×PP×DP mapping (7.09).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: TP splits within a layer; how do we split across layers? (7.05)

cards.cue: Sharding data-parallel still replicates compute per layer — how do we split a single layer's math?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Pipeline Parallelism (PP) splits the model into stages of consecutive layers on different GPUs; activations pass stage→stage. A naive pipeline idles most GPUs (the bubble). Splitting the batch into micro-batches (GPipe / interleaved 1F1B schedules) keeps stages busy and shrinks the bubble. Bubble fraction ≈ (p−1)/(m+p−1) for p stages, m micro-batches — more micro-batches → smaller bubble. Low comm volume (only stage boundaries) → can span nodes.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Attention activations grow with sequence length — how do we parallelize that dimension? (7.06)

cards.cue: TP splits within a layer; how do we split across layers?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Sequence Parallelism (SP) splits along the sequence/token dimension, sharding the activations of the normally-replicated ops (LayerNorm, dropout) that Tensor Parallelism leaves un-split. Combined with TP (Megatron-SP), it cuts activation memory for long sequences without extra compute. For very long context, context/ring-attention variants extend this idea across GPUs.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Some models have many experts, not one FFN — how do we parallelize those? (7.07)

cards.cue: Attention activations grow with sequence length — how do we parallelize that dimension?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Mixture-of-Experts replaces the FFN with many experts; a router sends each token to top-k experts (sparse activation → more params, ~constant FLOPs/token). Expert Parallelism (EP) places different experts on different GPUs; an all-to-all shuffles tokens to their expert's GPU and back. Challenge: load balancing (add an auxiliary balancing loss) so no expert is a bottleneck.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: With all these axes, how do I decide which to use? (7.08)

cards.cue: Some models have many experts, not one FFN — how do we parallelize those?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
• Fits on one GPU, want speed → Data Parallel (DDP).
  • Optimizer/grad memory too big → FSDP/ZeRO (still data-parallel model).
  • A single layer too big → Tensor Parallel (keep within a node/NVLink).
  • Whole model too big for a node → Pipeline Parallel across nodes.
  • Long sequences → Sequence Parallel (+ TP).
  • MoE → Expert Parallel.

Order of preference by comm cost: DP/FSDP ≤ PP (low comm, cross-node) < TP (high comm, intra-node) < EP (all-to-all).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Real large-scale training combines these — how? (7.09)

cards.cue: With all these axes, how do I decide which to use?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Large LLM training composes TP × PP × DP (often + SP, + EP): e.g. TP=8 within a node (NVLink), PP across nodes, DP across the remaining replicas. Total GPUs = TP·PP·DP. Place high-communication TP on the fastest interconnect, PP on slower links, DP outermost. NeMo/Megatron-Core expose these as config knobs. Getting the mapping right to the topology is the difference between linear and terrible scaling.

GB200/NVL72: with a 72-GPU NVLink domain (7.04) you can set a much larger TP (and EP) that still stays on NVLink, shrinking cross-node PP/DP traffic — retune the mapping to the bigger domain rather than defaulting to TP=8.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Parallelism spreads work; how do we speed up the math on each GPU? (7.10)

cards.cue: Real large-scale training combines these — how?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Automatic Mixed Precision runs most ops in FP16/BF16 (fast Tensor Cores, half memory) while keeping a master FP32 copy of weights and FP32 accumulations for stability. FP16 needs loss scaling: multiply the loss before backward so small gradients don't underflow to zero, then unscale before the optimizer step (dynamic scaler adjusts the factor). BF16 needs no loss scaling (FP32 exponent range, 4.07).

scaler = torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler()
with torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.float16):
    loss = model(x).loss
scaler.scale(loss).backward(); scaler.step(opt); scaler.update()

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Mixed precision feeds Tensor Cores — how do we make sure they're actually used? (7.11)

cards.cue: Parallelism spreads work; how do we speed up the math on each GPU?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Tensor Cores accelerate matmuls only when dimensions align to their tile sizes: GEMM dims (batch, hidden, vocab) should be multiples of 8 (FP16) or 16 (INT8), and larger multiples (64/128) help. Misaligned dims (e.g. vocab 50257, odd hidden) fall back to slower paths or waste cycles on padding. Pad vocab/hidden to friendly multiples. Verify with Nsight Compute (7.22) that Tensor Core (HMMA/IMMA) pipes are active.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: FP16 vs BF16 both use Tensor Cores — which for training stability? (7.12)

cards.cue: Mixed precision feeds Tensor Cores — how do we make sure they're actually used?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Both are 16-bit Tensor Core formats. BF16 (1-8-7) has FP32's exponent range → no loss scaling, robust to overflow, the default for LLM pretraining on Ampere+. FP16 (1-5-10) has more mantissa precision but a narrow range → needs loss scaling and can still overflow on large activations/gradients. Rule: prefer BF16 for training stability; use FP16 only where required.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: On H100 there's an 8-bit training path — what is it? (7.13)

cards.cue: FP16 vs BF16 both use Tensor Cores — which for training stability?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Transformer Engine (TE) provides FP8 training/inference on Hopper+: FP8 GEMMs (E4M3 fwd, E5M2 grads, 4.06) with per-tensor scaling factors maintained via a delayed-scaling recipe (track a rolling window of amax to set scales). Wrap layers in te.Linear/te.TransformerLayer under an fp8_autocast. Big speedup + memory cut on H100 with near-BF16 accuracy.

GB200/Blackwell upgrade: the 2nd-gen Transformer Engine (sm_100) adds FP4 (NVFP4) training/inference with micro-block scaling (4.08) — finer-grained than Hopper's per-tensor delayed scaling — for even higher throughput and smaller memory. A100 fallback: use BF16 AMP (7.10/7.12) — same mixed-precision concept, no FP8/FP4 units on Ampere.

import transformer_engine.pytorch as te
from transformer_engine.common.recipe import DelayedScaling
with te.fp8_autocast(enabled=True, fp8_recipe=DelayedScaling()):
    out = te_model(x)

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Precision aside, what dominates memory and how do we manage it? (7.14)

cards.cue: On H100 there's an 8-bit training path — what is it?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Training memory = weights + gradients + optimizer states + activations. Activation memory scales with batch × sequence × hidden × layers and often dominates at long context. Levers: reduce micro-batch (+ gradient accumulation, 7.15), gradient/activation checkpointing (7.16), sequence parallelism (7.06), and lower precision. Increasing batch raises throughput and activation memory together — tune to fill the GPU without OOM.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: If we need a big effective batch but memory is tight, how? (7.15)

cards.cue: Precision aside, what dominates memory and how do we manage it?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Accumulate gradients over k micro-batches before an optimizer step to simulate a k× larger batch without the memory cost:

effective_batch = micro_batch × k × data_parallel_world_size

Do not zero grads between micro-steps; step + zero after k. Divide loss by k so the gradient magnitude matches a true large batch. Trades more forward/backward passes per update for memory headroom (pairs with the linear scaling rule, 4.33).

for i, batch in enumerate(loader):
    loss = model(**batch).loss / k
    loss.backward()
    if (i + 1) % k == 0:
        opt.step(); opt.zero_grad()

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Accumulation stores activations per micro-batch — how do we cut that memory? (7.16)

cards.cue: If we need a big effective batch but memory is tight, how?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Instead of storing every layer's activations for the backward pass, store only a few checkpoints and recompute the rest during backward. Cuts activation memory from O(L) toward O(√L) at the cost of ~1 extra forward (~30% more compute). Enables larger batches/models on limited memory — the standard OOM remedy alongside gradient accumulation.

from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint
out = checkpoint(layer, x)   # recompute activations in backward

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Memory managed; the attention GEMM is the hot compute — how is it optimized? (7.17)

cards.cue: Accumulation stores activations per micro-batch — how do we cut that memory?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Naive attention materializes the T×T score matrix in HBM → memory-bandwidth-bound and O(T²) memory. FlashAttention fuses the softmax·(QKᵀ)·V into one kernel using tiling + online softmax, keeping intermediates in SRAM and never writing the full matrix — O(T) memory, far higher throughput, IO-aware. It's the reason long context is feasible. NVIDIA ships fused attention via cuDNN / Transformer Engine.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: With tensor parallelism, how is the multi-head attention GEMM split across GPUs? (7.18)

cards.cue: Memory managed; the attention GEMM is the hot compute — how is it optimized?

back.title: Verse
back.html: In Megatron tensor parallelism, attention is split by heads: each GPU owns a subset of heads and computes their QKV projections and attention independently (column-parallel QKV), then the output projection is row-parallel with a single all-reduce to combine. Because heads are independent (1.03), this splits cleanly with communication only at the output projection. Keep head count divisible by the TP size.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Knowing all this, how do we compute whether a model+batch even fits? (7.19)

cards.cue: With tensor parallelism, how is the multi-head attention GEMM split across GPUs?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Approximate GPU memory for training (mixed precision, Adam): - Weights: P × 2 bytes (BF16). - Gradients: P × 2 bytes. - Optimizer (Adam): FP32 master + m + v ≈ P × 12 bytes. - Activations: ∝ batch × seq × hidden × layers (dominant at long context; checkpointing cuts it).

Rule of thumb: full Adam training ≈ ~16–20 bytes/param before activations, so a 7B model needs ~112–140 GB → why FSDP/parallelism/PEFT. Inference adds the KV cache (4.26) instead of optimizer states.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: When this budget is exceeded, what happens and how do we diagnose it? (7.20)

cards.cue: Knowing all this, how do we compute whether a model+batch even fits?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
CUDA OOM = requested allocation exceeds free VRAM (watch fragmentation too). Mitigations, cheapest first: reduce micro-batch, gradient accumulation (7.15), activation checkpointing (7.16), lower precision (BF16/FP8), shorter max_seq_len, FSDP/ZeRO (7.03), CPU/NVMe offload, PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True for fragmentation. Diagnose with torch.cuda.memory_summary() and the memory snapshot/ profiler.

GB200/Grace-Blackwell: the Grace CPU and Blackwell GPU share coherent, NVLink-C2C memory, so CPU offload is far cheaper than PCIe offload — large KV cache / optimizer state can spill to Grace LPDDR with much less penalty, and FP4 weights (4.08) further cut the footprint.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: OOM is one bottleneck; how do we profile the whole timeline to find others? (7.21)

cards.cue: When this budget is exceeded, what happens and how do we diagnose it?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Nsight Systems (nsys) is the system-wide timeline profiler: CPU/GPU activity, CUDA API calls, kernel launches, memcpy, NCCL comm, and gaps. Use it to find coarse problems: GPU idle bubbles, CPU-bound data loading, poor compute/comm overlap, launch gaps, host-device sync stalls. Answers "where is time going across the system." Not for per-kernel internals — that's Nsight Compute.

nsys profile -o report python train.py    # then open in Nsight Systems UI

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Once you find a slow kernel, how do you look inside it? (7.22)

cards.cue: OOM is one bottleneck; how do we profile the whole timeline to find others?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Nsight Compute (ncu) is the per-kernel profiler: occupancy, memory vs compute throughput, warp stalls, register/shared-memory usage, Tensor Core (HMMA/IMMA) utilization, and a roofline chart. Use it after Nsight Systems localizes a hot kernel, to answer "why is this kernel slow." Division of labor: Systems = timeline/ where; Compute = kernel/why.

ncu --set full -o krep python train.py

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Nsight reports occupancy — what does low occupancy indicate? (7.23)

cards.cue: Once you find a slow kernel, how do you look inside it?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Occupancy = active warps / max warps per SM. Low occupancy or low Tensor Core utilization signals underutilization, from: too-small batch/dims (not enough parallel work), register/shared-memory pressure limiting resident warps, memory-bound stalls, or misaligned dims skipping Tensor Cores (7.11). Fixes: larger batch, kernel fusion, fix alignment, reduce register spilling. Note: high occupancy is not the goal in itself — sufficient occupancy to hide latency is.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Is a slow kernel limited by compute or memory? How do we tell? (7.24)

cards.cue: Nsight reports occupancy — what does low occupancy indicate?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Arithmetic intensity = FLOPs / bytes moved. The roofline plots achievable FLOP/s vs intensity: low intensity → memory-bound (limited by HBM bandwidth); high intensity → compute-bound (limited by peak FLOP/s). LLM decode (batch 1, one token) is memory-bound (weight loading dominates) → weight-only quant helps (4.04); prefill/large-batch GEMMs are compute-bound → low-precision compute (FP8/INT8) helps. Diagnose with Nsight Compute's roofline.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Multi-GPU adds communication as a bottleneck — how do we spot it? (7.25)

cards.cue: Is a slow kernel limited by compute or memory? How do we tell?

back.title: Verse
back.html: At scale, collective communication (all-reduce, all-gather, all-to-all) can dominate. NCCL implements bandwidth-optimal collectives over NVLink/PCIe/InfiniBand. Symptoms in Nsight Systems: GPUs idle waiting on NCCL. Remedies: overlap comm with compute (DDP gradient bucketing, FSDP prefetch), place high-comm parallelism (TP) on NVLink within a node (7.04/7.09), gradient compression, and larger fused buffers. Watch for a straggler GPU serializing the collective.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Overlap needs async execution — what primitive enables it? (7.26)

cards.cue: Multi-GPU adds communication as a bottleneck — how do we spot it?

back.title: Verse
back.html: A CUDA stream is an ordered queue of GPU work; operations in different streams can run concurrently. This enables overlapping compute with H2D/D2H copies (use pinned memory + non_blocking=True) and with NCCL comm. The default stream serializes; frameworks use multiple streams internally. Missing overlap (everything on one stream, blocking copies) shows as timeline gaps in Nsight Systems.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Kernel launch overhead can also bottleneck — how do we cut it? (7.27)

cards.cue: Overlap needs async execution — what primitive enables it?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Many tiny kernels make launch overhead (CPU dispatching each kernel) the bottleneck — common in decode with small batches. CUDA Graphs capture a sequence of launches once and replay them as a single unit, removing per-launch CPU cost. torch.compile fuses ops and can use CUDA graphs automatically. Big wins for latency-bound, launch-heavy workloads (small-batch inference).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: All these tools serve one loop — what is the disciplined optimization workflow? (7.28)

cards.cue: Kernel launch overhead can also bottleneck — how do we cut it?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Disciplined loop (NVIDIA APOD: Assess, Parallelize, Optimize, Deploy): 1. Assess — profile with Nsight Systems to find the biggest bottleneck (never optimize by guessing). 2. Classify it: GPU-idle (data/comm), memory-bound, compute-bound, launch-bound. 3. Apply the matching fix (7.20–7.27). 4. Re-profile to confirm and find the next bottleneck; iterate.

Measure one change at a time; optimize the dominant cost first (Amdahl).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: An optimized, trained model must now be served in production — Domain 8: Model Deployment.

back.title: Recall

DDP all-reduces gradients via NCCL ring, needs whole model per GPU (7.02); FSDP/ZeRO shards optimizer→grads→params, all-gather just-in-time (7.03).

back.html: Gradients underflow → NaN/no learning. BF16 needs none (7.10, 7.12).

back.title: Watch out
back.html: TP is high-communication; spanning slow inter-node links kills throughput. Keep TP intra-node on NVLink (7.04, 7.09).

back.title: Watch out

back.title: Watch out

back.title: Watch out

back.title: Watch out

cards.front: Cost profiles: encoder vs decoder vs enc-dec

back.title: Verse
back.html:
• Encoder-only: one forward pass, no autoregression, no KV cache — cheapest, lowest latency (classification/embeddings).
  • Decoder-only: autoregressive — prefill (parallel) then per-token decode (serial) + KV cache; latency scales with output length.
  • Encoder-decoder: full encoder pass + autoregressive decoder + cross-attention — most expensive per request, but the encoder runs once.

Match model type to the latency/throughput/cost budget (ties to 1.05–1.07).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: For decoders, generation has two distinct phases — what are they? (8.02)

back.title: Verse
back.html:
• Prefill: process the whole prompt in parallel, build the KV cache → determines TTFT (Time To First Token). Compute-bound (big GEMM over all prompt tokens).
  • Decode: generate one token at a time, each reusing the KV cache → determines TPOT (Time Per Output Token) / inter-token latency. Memory-bandwidth-bound (loading weights per token at small batch).

End-to-end latency ≈ TTFT + (output_len − 1) × TPOT. Optimizations differ per phase (7.24).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: These phases pull latency and throughput in opposite directions — how do we balance them? (8.03)

cards.cue: For decoders, generation has two distinct phases — what are they?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Larger batches raise throughput (amortize weight loading over more sequences, better Tensor Core use) but raise per-request latency (queuing + bigger steps). Since decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, batching many sequences is nearly free on compute up to a point — the key insight enabling continuous batching (8.08). Pick an operating point on the latency-throughput curve per SLA; measure with percentiles (6.12).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: To serve this at scale we containerize — what does that pipeline look like? (8.04)

cards.cue: These phases pull latency and throughput in opposite directions — how do we balance them?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Package the model + runtime + dependencies into a container for reproducible, portable deployment. A serving pipeline = preprocess (tokenize) → model (engine) → postprocess (detokenize), often as a Triton ensemble (8.12). Containers pin CUDA/driver- compatible runtimes and enable both docker run and Kubernetes deployment. NVIDIA ships prebuilt serving containers on NGC.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Where do the model artifacts and container images come from? (8.05)

cards.cue: To serve this at scale we containerize — what does that pipeline look like?

back.title: Verse
back.html: NGC (NVIDIA GPU Cloud) is the catalog of GPU-optimized container images (PyTorch, Triton/Dynamo-Triton, TensorRT-LLM, NeMo), pretrained models, and Helm charts. Pull with docker pull nvcr.io/nvidia/.... Model artifacts (engines, checkpoints, config.pbtxt) live in a model repository the server mounts. Pin image tags for reproducibility; engines are GPU-arch-specific (4.23).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: With container and artifacts, which server serves LLMs and how is it structured? (8.06)

cards.cue: Where do the model artifacts and container images come from?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Dynamo-Triton (formerly Triton Inference Server) serves models across backends (TensorRT-LLM, vLLM, PyTorch, ONNX, Python) behind HTTP/gRPC. A model repository holds one directory per model with versioned weights/engines and a config.pbtxt declaring inputs/outputs, backend, batching, and instance groups. Features: dynamic/continuous batching, concurrent execution, ensembles, metrics endpoint.

Stale-knowledge flag: the product was renamed Triton → Dynamo-Triton; binary/ container still tritonserver. VERIFY.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: How does Triton batch incoming requests to raise throughput? (8.07)

cards.cue: With container and artifacts, which server serves LLMs and how is it structured?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Triton's dynamic batcher holds incoming requests briefly (up to max_queue_delay_microseconds) to combine them into a larger batch before running the model — raising throughput/GPU utilization. It batches at the request level and waits for the batch to finish together. Great for fixed-size/non-autoregressive models (encoders). For autoregressive LLMs with variable output lengths it's suboptimal (short requests wait for long ones) — hence continuous batching (8.08).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Why is dynamic batching not ideal for autoregressive generation? (8.08)

cards.cue: How does Triton batch incoming requests to raise throughput?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Continuous / in-flight batching (TensorRT-LLM) operates at the iteration (token-step) level: as soon as one sequence in the batch finishes, its slot is freed and a queued request joins immediately — no waiting for the whole batch. This keeps the GPU saturated despite highly variable output lengths, dramatically improving throughput and latency for LLM serving. Paired with paged KV cache for memory efficiency.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: So when do I use dynamic vs continuous batching? (8.09)

cards.cue: Why is dynamic batching not ideal for autoregressive generation?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Dynamic batching Continuous (in-flight) batching
Granularity request level token/iteration level
Waits for batch to finish together nothing — slot freed per finished seq
Best for fixed-size / encoders / non-AR autoregressive LLM generation
Backend generic Triton TensorRT-LLM / vLLM

Rule: LLM text generation → continuous batching. Fixed-shape models (embeddings, classifiers) → dynamic batching.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Some models carry state across requests — how are those batched? (8.10)

cards.cue: So when do I use dynamic vs continuous batching?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Triton's sequence batcher routes all requests of a correlation ID (a session/ stream) to the same model instance in order, preserving per-sequence state across calls — what the dynamic batcher does not do. Used for stateful/streaming models (session-based RNNs, stateful decoding, conversational state held server-side). Manages sequence start/end/ready control signals.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Batching aside, how do we run multiple models/instances at once on a GPU? (8.11)

cards.cue: Some models carry state across requests — how are those batched?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
instance_group in config.pbtxt sets how many instances of a model run and on which GPUs, enabling concurrent model execution — multiple models or multiple copies of one model serving in parallel to fill the GPU and hide per-request latency. More instances → higher throughput until memory/compute saturate. Combine with dynamic/ continuous batching.

instance_group [ { count: 2, kind: KIND_GPU, gpus: [0] } ]

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Real pipelines chain preprocess/model/postprocess — how are those composed? (8.12)

cards.cue: Batching aside, how do we run multiple models/instances at once on a GPU?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
• Ensemble: a config.pbtxt DAG wiring models together (tokenizer → model → detokenizer) so the server runs the whole pipeline in one request, avoiding client round-trips.
  • BLS (Business Logic Scripting): a Python backend model that calls other models with control flow (loops, conditionals) — for dynamic pipelines (e.g. RAG: embed → retrieve → generate) that a static ensemble DAG can't express.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Beyond raw Triton, NVIDIA packages models as microservices — what are those? (8.13)

cards.cue: Real pipelines chain preprocess/model/postprocess — how are those composed?

back.title: Verse
back.html: NVIDIA NIM (NVIDIA Inference Microservices) package an optimized model (often TensorRT-LLM engine) + Triton + an OpenAI-compatible REST API into a single container with sensible defaults, auto-selecting the best engine for the detected GPU. NIM trades some low-level control for turnkey, production-grade deployment and standard APIs. Part of NVIDIA AI Enterprise.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: When do I reach for a NIM vs configuring raw Triton myself? (8.14)

cards.cue: Beyond raw Triton, NVIDIA packages models as microservices — what are those?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
NIM Raw Dynamo-Triton
Setup turnkey, OpenAI-compatible API manual model repo + config.pbtxt
Optimization auto-selects engine per GPU you build/tune engines
Control opinionated defaults full control (backends, ensembles, BLS)
Best for standard LLMs, fast time-to-prod custom pipelines, non-standard models

Rule: NIM for supported models and speed; raw Triton for custom ensembles, unusual backends, or fine-grained control.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: However we package it, how do we scale/orchestrate it in production? (8.15)

cards.cue: When do I reach for a NIM vs configuring raw Triton myself?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Deploy the serving container as a K8s Deployment with GPU resource requests, readiness/liveness probes (Triton's /v2/health/ready) so traffic only routes to ready pods, and a Service/ingress. Scale with the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) on GPU/custom metrics (queue depth, latency). NVIDIA provides Helm charts and the GPU Operator. Use rolling updates for zero-downtime (ties to 9.13).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Not everyone runs K8s — what's the minimal bare path? (8.16)

cards.cue: However we package it, how do we scale/orchestrate it in production?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
Minimal single-node serving without orchestration:

docker run --gpus all --rm -p 8000:8000 -p 8001:8001 -p 8002:8002 \
  -v "$PWD/model_repo":/models \
  nvcr.io/nvidia/tritonserver:24.07-py3 \
  tritonserver --model-repository=/models

Ports: 8000 HTTP, 8001 gRPC, 8002 Prometheus metrics (9.01). Query with the client SDK or curl. This is the reproducible baseline every lab mirrors; K8s (8.15) wraps the same container.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Once serving, how do we watch it live? (8.17)

cards.cue: Not everyone runs K8s — what's the minimal bare path?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Dynamo-Triton exposes Prometheus metrics on port 8002: inference count, request/ queue/compute latencies, batch sizes, GPU utilization/memory, and (for TRT-LLM) LLM-specific counters. Scrape with Prometheus, visualize in Grafana. This is the bridge into Production Monitoring (Domain 9). Instrument from day one, not after an incident.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Serving evolves — how do we manage model versions safely? (8.18)

cards.cue: Once serving, how do we watch it live?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
The model repository is versioned: numbered subdirectories (1/, 2/) under each model; config.pbtxt's version policy controls which serve (latest, specific, all). This enables safe rollout/rollback and A/B or canary (9.08–9.09) by serving multiple versions simultaneously. config.pbtxt also pins backend, batching, instance groups, and I/O — the single source of truth for a served model.

version_policy { specific { versions: [2] } }

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Versioning and live metrics lead directly into Domain 9: Production Monitoring & Reliability.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: With a stack in place, which metrics actually matter? (9.02)

back.title: Verse
back.html: Classic golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation. LLM-specific: TTFT, TPOT/inter-token latency, tokens/sec throughput, queue depth, KV-cache utilization, GPU util/memory (DCGM), and quality proxies (refusal rate, guardrail triggers, user feedback). Track percentiles (p50/p95/p99), not means (6.12). These feed SLOs (9.03).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Metrics need targets — how do we set them? (9.03)

cards.cue: With a stack in place, which metrics actually matter?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
• SLI (indicator): a measured metric, e.g. "p99 TTFT" or "success rate."
  • SLO (objective): the target, e.g. "p99 TTFT < 500 ms, 99.9% of the time."
  • Error budget: 1 − SLO — the allowed failure amount; when exhausted, freeze risky changes and prioritize reliability.

SLOs turn raw metrics into actionable reliability targets and gate releases (ties to 9.13). Alert on SLO burn rate, not every blip.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Metrics tell you that something broke — how do we find why? (9.04)

cards.cue: Metrics need targets — how do we set them?

back.title: Verse
back.html: The three pillars: metrics (aggregate trends), logs (discrete events — prompts, errors, guardrail hits, with PII handling), traces (a request's path across services — tokenizer → retriever → model, via OpenTelemetry). Together they enable root-cause analysis. For LLMs, log prompt/response metadata (not raw PII), latencies per stage, and token counts. Correlate by request/trace ID.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Logs are noisy — how do we surface the anomalies automatically? (9.05)

cards.cue: Metrics tell you that something broke — how do we find why?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Detect deviations automatically: threshold/static alerts (p99 > SLO), statistical methods (z-score, EWMA, seasonal decomposition), and ML detectors for multivariate signals. Alert on rate of change and burn rate, and reduce noise with deduplication/grouping. For LLMs, watch for spikes in error rate, latency, refusal/ guardrail-trigger rate, and drift in input/output distributions (9.06). Tune to avoid alert fatigue (missed real incidents).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: A common silent failure is the world changing under the model — what is that? (9.06)

cards.cue: Logs are noisy — how do we surface the anomalies automatically?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
• Data (covariate) drift: the input distribution changes (new topics, languages, slang) while the target mapping holds.
  • Concept drift: the input→output relationship itself changes (what counts as "spam" evolves).

Detect via distribution distances (PSI, KL, embedding-space monitoring) on inputs and outputs. Drift silently degrades quality with no error thrown → triggers retraining (9.10). This is the top cause of "the model got worse over time."

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Drift signals degradation vs a baseline — how do we benchmark against prior versions? (9.07)

cards.cue: A common silent failure is the world changing under the model — what is that?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Periodically re-score the deployed model on a fixed golden eval set (reusing the Domain 6 harness) and compare to prior versions to catch regressions in quality/ latency/cost before users do. Automate in CI/CD and on a schedule; store versioned results. A regression beyond threshold blocks promotion or triggers rollback. Complements live metrics (which measure behavior, not correctness).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: To compare versions safely in production, how do we roll them out? (9.08)

cards.cue: Drift signals degradation vs a baseline — how do we benchmark against prior versions?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
• Canary: route a small % of live traffic to the new version, watch metrics, ramp up if healthy, roll back if not.
  • Shadow: send a copy of traffic to the new version without returning its responses — compare offline, zero user risk.
  • A/B: split traffic to measure a business/quality metric difference statistically.

Serve multiple versions simultaneously via the model repo version policy (8.18).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: These strategies need a clean rollback — how is that guaranteed? (9.09)

cards.cue: To compare versions safely in production, how do we roll them out?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Safe deployment requires fast, reliable rollback: keep the previous version loaded/ reachable (model repo versioning, 8.18), use K8s rolling updates with readiness gates, and automate rollback on SLO burn / regression alerts. Prefer immutable, versioned artifacts so rollback is deterministic. Practice rollback (game days). "Deploy" isn't done until "undeploy" is proven.

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Rather than manual rollback loops, how do we automate the whole lifecycle? (9.10)

cards.cue: These strategies need a clean rollback — how is that guaranteed?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Close the loop: when drift (9.06), regression (9.07), or quality-metric decline crosses a threshold, trigger retraining/fine-tuning on fresh data, re-evaluate, and (if it passes gates) promote via canary. Triggers can be scheduled, metric-based, or data-volume-based. Guard against feedback loops (training on the model's own biased outputs). This is MLOps continuous training (CT).

back.title: Chain →
back.html: Retraining and tuning need to be systematic — how? (9.11)

cards.cue: Rather than manual rollback loops, how do we automate the whole lifecycle?

back.title: Verse
back.html: Wrap retraining in a reproducible pipeline: data validation → (re)train/fine-tune → automated eval (Domain 6) → gated promotion → canary → monitor. back.title: Verse
back.html:
Audit outcomes across protected groups with group fairness metrics: - Demographic parity: equal positive rate across groups. - Equal opportunity: equal true-positive rate across groups. - Equalized odds: equal TPR and FPR across groups.

These can conflict (impossibility results) — choose per context. For generative LLMs, also probe stereotype/toxicity disparities across demographic prompts. Measure before and after mitigation.

cards.cue: How do we detect bias systematically, not anecdotally?

back.title: Verse
back.html:
NeMo Guardrails enforces policy at runtime via programmable rails, defined in the Colang language: - Input rails: block/flag malicious or off-topic prompts (jailbreak/injection, 2.25). - Dialog rails: constrain conversation to allowed topics/flows. - Retrieval rails: filter/verify retrieved context (RAG). - Output rails: block unsafe/PII/hallucinated responses (fact-check/self-check, 5.24).

Rails run independently of the model's cooperation — the enforcement layer that prompting alone (Domain 2) cannot guarantee.

cards.label: B1 · 01

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Traditional software follows rules a person wrote: if the email contains "free money", mark it as spam. That breaks as soon as the world changes or the rules get too many.

Machine learning (ML) turns this around. You give the computer many examples (emails labeled spam or not spam), and it learns the rules itself by adjusting a large set of numbers until its answers match the examples.

  • The adjustable numbers are called parameters or weights.
  • The thing that holds them and turns an input into an output is the model.
  • Adjusting the weights from examples is training.
  • Using the trained model on new inputs is inference.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is the broad goal of machines doing tasks that seem to need intelligence. ML is today's main way of getting there, and deep learning is ML with many-layered neural networks (see B3).

cards.cue: B1 — What AI, machine learning and LLMs are

cards.label: B1 · 02

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Kind What the examples look like Example
Supervised Input plus the right answer (a label) Photo → "cat"
Unsupervised Inputs only; find structure Group customers by behavior
Self-supervised The answer is hidden inside the input itself Hide a word in a sentence and predict it
Reinforcement Actions plus a reward signal A game-playing agent gets points for winning

Large language models are trained mostly with self-supervised learning: take real text, hide the next word, and ask the model to guess it. The internet provides practically unlimited "labeled" examples for free, because the label is just the next word.

cards.cue: B1 — What AI, machine learning and LLMs are

cards.label: B1 · 03

back.title: Notes
back.html:
The goal isn't to memorize the training examples but to do well on new ones. This is called generalization.

  • Underfitting: the model is too simple or undertrained; it's bad even on the training data.
  • Overfitting: the model memorizes the training data, including its noise, and does worse on new data.

To detect overfitting we hold some examples back:

  • Training set: used to adjust the weights.
  • Validation set: used during development to choose settings and decide when to stop.
  • Test set: used once at the end for an honest score.

If the training score keeps improving while the validation score gets worse, you're overfitting. This idea returns in Domain 5 as early stopping (objective 5.3).

cards.cue: B1 — What AI, machine learning and LLMs are

cards.label: B1 · 04

back.title: Notes
back.html:
A language model assigns probabilities to text. The kind behind ChatGPT, Llama and Nemotron does one thing: given some text, it predicts a probability for every possible next token (a token is a word or piece of a word; see B4).

"The capital of France is" → Paris 92% · the 2% · a 1% · …

To write a reply, the model picks a token from that distribution, adds it to the text, and repeats. That loop is called generation or decoding, and how you pick each token is sampling (Domain 1, objectives 1.4–1.5).

A large language model (LLM) is simply one with billions of parameters, trained on trillions of tokens. Scale turns out to matter: bigger models trained on more data become able to follow instructions, translate, summarize, write code and reason step by step, even though they were only ever trained to predict the next token.

cards.cue: B1 — What AI, machine learning and LLMs are

cards.label: B1 · 05

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Every exam domain is one stage of this lifecycle:

  1. Collect and clean data (Domain 3, Data Preparation).
  2. Pretrain on huge amounts of raw text to predict the next token (Domains 1, 2, 7). This is the expensive part: thousands of GPUs for weeks.
  3. Fine-tune on smaller, curated examples so it follows instructions, then align it with human preferences so its answers are helpful and safe (Domain 5).
  4. Optimize it to be smaller and faster: quantization, pruning, distillation (Domain 4).
  5. Evaluate it with metrics, benchmarks and human review (Domain 6).
  6. Deploy it as a service (Domain 8).
  7. Monitor it in production and improve it over time (Domain 9).
  8. At every step, keep it safe, fair and compliant (Domain 10).

Prompt engineering (Domain 2) is how users and developers get the most out of a model without changing its weights at all.

cards.cue: B1 — What AI, machine learning and LLMs are

cards.label: B1 · 06

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Training and running a neural network is mostly multiplying large tables of numbers (matrices). A CPU has a few very fast, very flexible cores. A GPU (graphics processing unit) has thousands of simpler cores that do the same operation on many numbers at once, which is exactly what matrix multiplication needs. NVIDIA's GPUs also have Tensor Cores, special units just for matrix math.

A modern LLM has billions of parameters, and every generated token touches all of them, so GPUs are what make LLMs practical. Domain 7 (14%) is all about using them well, and B6 covers the basics.

cards.cue: B1 — What AI, machine learning and LLMs are

cards.label: B1 · 07

back.title: Notes
back.html:
The exam is about building LLMs on NVIDIA's platform, so you'll meet these names often:

Name What it is, in one line
CUDA The programming platform for NVIDIA GPUs; almost everything runs on top of it
NGC NVIDIA's catalog of ready-made containers, models and tools
NeMo Framework for building, training, customizing and aligning LLMs

Dynamo-Triton (Triton) Server that runs models and answers requests at scale
