You don't need to know them yet. When one appears, come back to this table.

cards.cue: B1 — What AI, machine learning and LLMs are

cards.label: B1 · Flashcard
cards.front: What is the difference between training and inference?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Training adjusts the model's weights from examples; inference uses the trained weights to produce outputs for new inputs.

back.title: Answer
back.html: The adjustable numbers inside a model that training tunes so its outputs match the examples.

cards.label: B1 · Flashcard
cards.front: Why is LLM pretraining called self-supervised?

back.title: Answer
back.html: The label comes from the data itself: the model predicts the next (hidden) token of real text, so no human labeling is needed.

cards.label: B1 · Flashcard
cards.front: What is overfitting and how do you spot it?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Memorizing training data so performance on new data drops; training score keeps improving while validation score gets worse.

cards.label: B1 · Flashcard
cards.front: What are the training, validation and test sets for?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Training adjusts weights; validation chooses settings and when to stop; test gives a final honest score, used once.

cards.label: B1 · Flashcard
cards.front: What does a language model output at each step?

back.title: Answer
back.html: A probability for every possible next token in its vocabulary.

back.title: Answer
back.html: Repeatedly picking a next token from the model's probabilities, appending it, and predicting again.

cards.label: B1 · Flashcard
cards.front: Put the LLM lifecycle in order.

back.title: Answer
back.html: Data preparation → pretraining → fine-tuning and alignment → optimization → evaluation → deployment → monitoring, with safety throughout.

cards.label: B1 · Flashcard
cards.front: Why are GPUs used for LLMs?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Neural networks are mostly matrix multiplications, and GPUs run thousands of such operations in parallel (Tensor Cores specialize in them).

cards.label: B1 · Flashcard
cards.front: In one line each: NeMo, TensorRT-LLM, Triton, NIM.

back.title: Answer
back.html: NeMo trains and customizes LLMs; TensorRT-LLM makes them run fast; Triton serves models at scale; NIM packages a model, optimized engine and API in one container.

cards.label: B2 · 01

back.title: Notes
back.html:
nums = [3, 1, 4]                 # list
cfg = {"lr": 3e-4, "epochs": 3}  # dict (key → value)
for i, x in enumerate(nums):     # loop with index
    print(i, x)
squares = [x * x for x in nums]  # list comprehension

def scale(x, factor=2.0):        # function with a default argument
    return x * factor

class Counter:                   # class: data + functions together
    def __init__(self):
        self.n = 0
    def add(self):
        self.n += 1

Also know: import, with open(path) as f: for files, json.loads/json.dumps, and f-strings like f"loss={loss:.3f}". Training data for LLMs is very often JSONL: one JSON object per line, such as {"prompt": "...", "completion": "..."}.

cards.cue: B2 — Python, NumPy and PyTorch essentials

cards.label: B2 · 02

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Neural networks work on arrays of numbers. A single number is a scalar, a list is a vector (1-D), a table is a matrix (2-D), and anything with more dimensions is a tensor. The shape lists the size of each dimension.

import numpy as np
x = np.array([[1., 2., 3.],
              [4., 5., 6.]])
x.shape          # (2, 3): 2 rows, 3 columns
x.T.shape        # (3, 2): transpose swaps them
x.mean(axis=0)   # column means → shape (3,)
x @ x.T          # matrix multiply: (2,3) @ (3,2) → (2,2)
x + np.array([10., 20., 30.])   # broadcasting: the row is added to every row

Matrix multiply rule: (m, k) @ (k, n) → (m, n). The inner sizes must match. Most errors in model code are shape errors, so get into the habit of writing shapes next to each line.

Broadcasting: when shapes differ, NumPy stretches dimensions of size 1 to match. It's convenient and also a common source of silent bugs.

cards.cue: B2 — Python, NumPy and PyTorch essentials

cards.label: B2 · 03

back.title: Notes
back.html:
PyTorch is the most common framework for LLM work, and NeMo is built on it. Its tensors are like NumPy arrays with two extra powers: they can live on a GPU, and they can track gradients automatically.

import torch
x = torch.randn(4, 3)                  # random tensor, shape (4, 3)
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
x = x.to(device)                        # move to the GPU
x = x.to(torch.bfloat16)                # change the number format (dtype)
print(x.shape, x.dtype, x.device)

Every tensor has a dtype (number format: float32, float16, bfloat16, int8, …) and a device (CPU or a specific GPU). Operations need their inputs on the same device. Number formats matter a lot for memory and speed; F3 and Domain 4 cover them.

cards.cue: B2 — Python, NumPy and PyTorch essentials

cards.label: B2 · 04

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Training needs to know how changing each weight would change the error (the gradient; see B3). PyTorch computes it for you:

w = torch.tensor(2.0, requires_grad=True)
loss = (w * 3 - 12) ** 2      # we want w*3 == 12, so w should become 4
loss.backward()               # compute d(loss)/d(w)
print(w.grad)                 # -36.0: increasing w reduces the loss

loss.backward() walks back through every operation that produced loss and fills in .grad for each tensor that needs it. This is autograd, and it's why you never write derivative formulas by hand.

cards.cue: B2 — Python, NumPy and PyTorch essentials

cards.label: B2 · 05

back.title: Notes
back.html:
This is the pattern behind every training script, from this toy up to a 400-billion-parameter LLM. Learn to recognize each line.

import torch, torch.nn as nn

model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(10, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 1)).to(device)
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
loss_fn = nn.MSELoss()

X = torch.randn(1000, 10, device=device)
y = X.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True)            # the rule to learn: add up the inputs

for epoch in range(20):
    for i in range(0, len(X), 50):        # mini-batches of 50
        xb, yb = X[i:i+50], y[i:i+50]
        pred = model(xb)                  # 1. forward pass
        loss = loss_fn(pred, yb)          # 2. measure the error
        opt.zero_grad()                   # 3. clear old gradients
        loss.backward()                   # 4. compute new gradients
        opt.step()                        # 5. update the weights
    print(epoch, loss.item())

Forgetting opt.zero_grad() makes gradients add up across steps. That's a bug here, but it's exactly how gradient accumulation (Domain 7) works on purpose.

For evaluation, wrap inference in with torch.no_grad(): and call model.eval(), which turns off gradient tracking and training-only behavior such as dropout.

cards.cue: B2 — Python, NumPy and PyTorch essentials

cards.label: B2 · 06
cards.front: 6. Using a real LLM with Hugging Face

back.title: Notes
back.html:
The Hugging Face transformers library loads thousands of pretrained models in a few lines:

from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM

name = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct"                     # any small chat model works
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(name, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16).to(device)

msgs = [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain a GPU in one sentence."}]
ids = tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, add_generation_prompt=True, return_tensors="pt").to(device)
out = model.generate(ids, max_new_tokens=40, do_sample=True, temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9)
print(tok.decode(out[0][ids.shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True))

Each piece maps to an exam topic: the tokenizer (Domain 3), the chat template (Domain 2), bfloat16 (Domains 4 and 7), and temperature/top_p (Domain 1).

To get embeddings (objective 1.3), ask for hidden states: model(ids, output_hidden_states=True).hidden_states[-1] has shape (batch, tokens, hidden_size): one vector per token from the last layer.

cards.cue: B2 — Python, NumPy and PyTorch essentials

back.title: Answer
back.html: A 2-D array with 2 rows and 3 columns.

cards.label: B2 · Flashcard
cards.front: What is the shape rule for matrix multiplication?

back.title: Answer
back.html: (m, k) @ (k, n) → (m, n); the inner dimensions must be equal.

back.title: Answer
back.html: Automatically stretching size-1 dimensions so arrays of different shapes can be combined element by element.

cards.label: B2 · Flashcard
cards.front: What two things does every PyTorch tensor carry besides its values and shape?

back.title: Answer
back.html: A dtype (number format) and a device (CPU or which GPU).

back.title: Answer
back.html: Computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every tensor that requires gradients, storing it in .grad (autograd).

cards.label: B2 · Flashcard
cards.front: Name the five steps inside a training loop iteration.

back.title: Answer
back.html: Forward pass, compute loss, zero gradients, backward pass, optimizer step.

cards.label: B2 · Flashcard
cards.front: What happens if you skip optimizer.zero_grad()?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Gradients accumulate across steps; a bug normally, but deliberate in gradient accumulation.

cards.label: B2 · Flashcard
cards.front: What do model.eval() and torch.no_grad() do?

back.title: Answer
back.html: eval() switches off training-only behavior like dropout; no_grad() stops gradient tracking to save memory and time during inference.

back.title: Answer
back.html: A file with one JSON object per line; the common format for LLM training and fine-tuning data.

cards.label: B2 · Flashcard
cards.front: Which output gives per-token embeddings from a Hugging Face model?

back.title: Answer
back.html: hidden_states (with output_hidden_states=True); the last layer has shape (batch, tokens, hidden_size).

back.title: Notes
back.html:
A neuron takes some numbers in, multiplies each by a weight, adds them up with a bias, and passes the result through an activation function:

$$y = f(w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + \dots + w_n x_n + b)$$

The weights say how much each input matters. The activation adds a bend, which lets networks learn things more complicated than straight lines. Common activations:

  • ReLU: $\max(0, z)$; negative values become 0. Simple and fast.
  • GELU / SiLU (Swish): smooth versions of ReLU, used in most modern LLMs.
  • Sigmoid: squashes any number to between 0 and 1; used for yes/no probabilities.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Many neurons side by side form a layer. Written with matrices, a whole layer is one matrix multiply plus a bias: $y = f(Wx + b)$. Stack layers and you have a deep network: the output of one layer is the input to the next.

  • A layer where every input connects to every output is fully connected (nn.Linear).
  • Two linear layers with an activation between them is an MLP (multi-layer perceptron), also called a feed-forward network. Every transformer block contains one.

Without activations, stacking layers would be pointless: several matrix multiplies in a row equal one matrix multiply. The non-linearities are what give depth its power.

cards.label: B3 · 03
cards.front: 3. Loss: measuring how wrong the model is

back.title: Notes
back.html:
A loss function turns "how wrong" into a single number that training can reduce.

  • Mean squared error for predicting numbers: average of $(\text{prediction} - \text{target})^2$.
  • Cross-entropy for predicting classes, which includes the next token in an LLM. The model outputs a probability for each class; the loss is $-\log p(\text{correct class})$. If the model gives the right token probability 1, loss is 0; if it gives it 0.01, loss is $-\log 0.01 \approx 4.6$.

Language models are trained by minimizing the average cross-entropy over all tokens. Take $e$ to the power of that average and you get perplexity (Domain 6).

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Think of the loss as the height of a hilly landscape, where your position is the current setting of all the weights. Training means walking downhill.

The gradient tells you, for every weight, which direction makes the loss go up and how steeply. So you step the other way:

$$w \leftarrow w - \eta \cdot \frac{\partial \text{loss}}{\partial w}$$

$\eta$ (eta) is the learning rate, the step size:

  • Too large: you overshoot, and the loss jumps around or blows up (NaN).
  • Too small: training crawls or gets stuck.

Real training uses a learning-rate schedule: a short warmup from near zero, then a slow decay (for example, cosine). Domain 4 asks about this (objective 4.4).

back.title: Notes
back.html:
A network with a billion weights needs a billion gradients per step. Backpropagation computes them all efficiently by applying the chain rule from calculus backwards through the network, from the loss to the first layer, reusing intermediate results.

You never implement it yourself (PyTorch's autograd does, see B2), but know two facts:

  1. The forward pass must save intermediate results (activations) for the backward pass. These activations are a major user of GPU memory in training.
  2. The backward pass costs about twice the forward pass. That's where the rule of thumb "training costs about $6N$ FLOPs per token for $N$ parameters" comes from (F1).

Gradient checkpointing (Domain 7) saves memory by throwing activations away and recomputing them during the backward pass.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Batch: a group of examples processed together. The gradient is averaged over the batch.
  • Step (iteration): one weight update, from one batch.
  • Epoch: one pass through the entire training set.

Bigger batches give smoother gradients and use the GPU better but need more memory. LLM pretraining usually runs less than one epoch over a huge dataset; fine-tuning often runs 1–3 epochs over a small one.

back.title: Notes
back.html: Plain gradient descent uses the same step size for every weight. Adam and its variant AdamW (the standard for LLMs) keep two running averages per weight, of the gradient and of its square, and use them to adapt each weight's step. The catch: AdamW stores two extra numbers per parameter, so the optimizer state is often bigger than the model itself. That is why memory formulas in Domain 7 count "weights + gradients + optimizer state".

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Regularization reduces overfitting: weight decay (pull weights toward zero), dropout (randomly switch off neurons during training), more or more varied data.
  • Early stopping: stop when the validation loss hasn't improved for a set number of checks (the patience) and keep the best checkpoint (objective 5.3).
  • Normalization layers (LayerNorm, RMSNorm) keep the numbers inside the network in a sensible range, which makes deep networks trainable.
  • Residual connections add a layer's input to its output ($x + f(x)$), giving gradients a shortcut through deep stacks. Transformers use both.

cards.label: B3 · Flashcard
cards.front: What does a single neuron compute?

back.title: Answer
back.html: A weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, passed through an activation function.

cards.label: B3 · Flashcard
cards.front: Why do neural networks need activation functions?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Without non-linearities, stacked layers collapse into one linear transformation.

cards.label: B3 · Flashcard
cards.front: What is the cross-entropy loss for one prediction?

back.title: Answer
back.html: −log of the probability the model gave to the correct class (or token).

cards.label: B3 · Flashcard
cards.front: What does the gradient tell you?

back.title: Answer
back.html: For each weight, the direction and steepness in which the loss increases; training steps the opposite way.

cards.label: B3 · Flashcard
cards.front: What happens if the learning rate is too high or too low?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Too high: loss oscillates or diverges (NaN). Too low: training is very slow or stalls.

back.title: Answer
back.html: Using the chain rule backwards from the loss to compute all gradients efficiently in one pass.

cards.label: B3 · Flashcard
cards.front: Why does training need much more memory than inference?

back.title: Answer
back.html: It must store activations for the backward pass, plus gradients and optimizer state for every parameter.

back.title: Answer
back.html: Batch: examples processed together; step: one weight update; epoch: one full pass through the training data.

cards.label: B3 · Flashcard
cards.front: Why does AdamW increase memory use?

back.title: Answer
back.html: It keeps two extra values (running averages of gradient and squared gradient) for every parameter.

back.title: Answer
back.html: Stopping training when validation loss hasn't improved for a set number of checks (patience) and keeping the best checkpoint.

back.title: Answer
back.html: Add a layer's input to its output, so information and gradients can flow through very deep networks.

cards.label: B4 · 01

back.title: Notes
back.html:
A tokenizer cuts text into tokens, and each token has an ID number in a fixed vocabulary.

"Tokenization isn't hard"  →  ["Token", "ization", " isn", "'t", " hard"]  →  [3404, 2065, 2125, 956, 2653]

(The exact pieces and IDs depend on the tokenizer.) Why not use whole words or single letters?

  • Whole words: the vocabulary would be huge, and any new word, name or typo would be unknown.
  • Characters: tiny vocabulary, but sequences become very long, and attention cost grows with length.
  • Subwords (the middle ground): common words stay whole, rare words split into familiar pieces. Nothing is ever truly unknown.

Rules of thumb: in English one token is about ¾ of a word, or about 4 characters. Other languages and code often need more tokens per word, which costs more and uses more context.

cards.cue: B4 — Text as numbers: tokens, embeddings and next-token prediction

cards.label: B4 · 02

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• BPE (byte-pair encoding), used by GPT and Llama: start from single characters or bytes, then repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token until the vocabulary reaches its target size.
  • WordPiece, used by BERT: similar, but merges the pair that most increases the likelihood of the training text. Word continuations are marked with ##.
  • Unigram / SentencePiece: start from a large vocabulary and prune it; works directly on raw text including spaces, which suits many languages.

Vocabulary size is a trade-off (objective 3.3): bigger means shorter sequences but a bigger embedding table and rarer tokens; smaller means the reverse. Modern LLMs use roughly 32k–256k.

Tokenizers also add special tokens: beginning and end of text, padding, and the markers used in chat templates to separate system, user and assistant turns.

cards.cue: B4 — Text as numbers: tokens, embeddings and next-token prediction

cards.label: B4 · 03

back.title: Notes
back.html:
A token ID is just a label; the number 3404 isn't "bigger" than 956 in any meaningful way. So the first layer of the model is an embedding table: one row of numbers (a vector) per token in the vocabulary, often 4,096 numbers wide for a mid-sized LLM. Looking up a token's row gives its embedding.

These vectors are learned during training, and they end up capturing meaning: tokens used in similar ways get similar vectors. The famous example from word2vec is that king − man + woman lands near queen.

Closeness is measured with cosine similarity: the cosine of the angle between two vectors, from −1 (opposite) through 0 (unrelated) to 1 (same direction).

$$\cos(a, b) = \frac{a \cdot b}{\lVert a\rVert\,\lVert b\rVert}$$

Inside the model, each token's vector is updated layer by layer to reflect its context ("bank" next to "river" vs next to "loan"). Vectors for a whole sentence or document can be made by averaging token vectors or taking a special token's vector; models trained for this are embedding models, and they power semantic search and RAG (objective 1.6, Domain 5 §6).

cards.cue: B4 — Text as numbers: tokens, embeddings and next-token prediction

cards.label: B4 · 04

back.title: Notes
back.html:
After the transformer layers (B5), the model turns the last token's vector into one score per vocabulary entry, called logits. Softmax converts logits into probabilities that add up to 1:

$$p_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}$$

Training compares these probabilities with the real next token using cross-entropy (B3). Every position in every training text is one prediction, which is why pretraining on trillions of tokens gives trillions of training examples. This is causal language modeling (objective 2.3): each position may only look at earlier tokens.

BERT-style encoders are instead trained with masked language modeling: hide some tokens anywhere in the text and predict them using context on both sides (objective 4.7).

cards.cue: B4 — Text as numbers: tokens, embeddings and next-token prediction

cards.label: B4 · 05

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Given the probabilities, how do we pick? This is decoding (objectives 1.4–1.5):

Method How it picks Effect
Greedy Always the most likely token Deterministic; can be repetitive
Beam search Keeps the best few partial sequences Good for translation; bland for chat
Temperature Divides logits by $T$ before softmax $T<1$ sharper and safer; $T>1$ flatter and more creative
Top-k Sample only from the $k$ most likely tokens Cuts off the long tail of bad tokens
Top-p (nucleus) Sample from the smallest set whose probability adds to $p$ Adapts the cut-off to how confident the model is

Temperature near 0 behaves like greedy decoding.

cards.cue: B4 — Text as numbers: tokens, embeddings and next-token prediction

cards.label: B4 · 06

back.title: Notes
back.html: A model can only look at a limited number of tokens at once, its context window (for example 8k or 128k tokens). The prompt and the generated answer both count. Long contexts are expensive, because attention compares every token with every other and because the model keeps a KV cache that grows with every token (Domains 4 and 8).

cards.cue: B4 — Text as numbers: tokens, embeddings and next-token prediction

cards.label: B4 · 07

back.title: Notes
back.html: If a model's average cross-entropy on some text is $L$ (in nats), its perplexity is $e^{L}$. You can read it as "the model is as unsure as if it were choosing uniformly among this many tokens". A perfect model has perplexity 1; a model guessing uniformly over a 50,000-token vocabulary has perplexity 50,000. Lower is better, and numbers are only comparable between models with the same tokenizer (Domain 6).

cards.cue: B4 — Text as numbers: tokens, embeddings and next-token prediction

cards.label: B4 · Flashcard
cards.front: Why do LLMs use subword tokens instead of words or characters?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Words give huge vocabularies and unknown words; characters make sequences too long; subwords keep common words whole and split rare ones into known pieces.

cards.label: B4 · Flashcard
cards.front: How does BPE build its vocabulary?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Start from characters or bytes and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair until the target vocabulary size is reached.

cards.label: B4 · Flashcard
cards.front: How is WordPiece different from BPE?

back.title: Answer
back.html: It merges the pair that most increases training-data likelihood, not simply the most frequent pair; used by BERT, marks continuations with ##.

cards.label: B4 · Flashcard
cards.front: What is the trade-off in vocabulary size?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Larger: shorter sequences but a bigger embedding table and rarer tokens. Smaller: the reverse.

back.title: Answer
back.html: A learned vector of numbers representing a token (or text) so that similar meanings are close together.

cards.label: B4 · Flashcard
cards.front: How is similarity between embeddings usually measured?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Cosine similarity: the cosine of the angle between the vectors, from −1 to 1.

back.title: Answer
back.html: Turns a vector of scores (logits) into probabilities that are positive and sum to 1.

back.title: Answer
back.html: Causal: predict the next token from earlier tokens only (GPT). Masked: predict hidden tokens using both sides (BERT).

cards.label: B4 · Flashcard
cards.front: What does lowering the temperature do?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Sharpens the distribution, making likely tokens more likely: more predictable, less diverse output.

back.title: Answer
back.html: Top-k samples from a fixed number of best tokens; top-p from the smallest set whose probabilities add up to p, so the set size adapts.

cards.label: B4 · Flashcard
cards.front: What is the perplexity of a model guessing uniformly over V tokens?

back.title: Answer
back.html: V (perplexity is e raised to the average cross-entropy).

cards.label: B4 · Flashcard
cards.front: What counts toward the context window?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Everything the model sees in one pass: system prompt, conversation, retrieved text and the generated answer.

cards.label: B5 · 01

back.title: Notes
back.html:
In "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired", what does it mean? You know it's the animal because you looked back at the rest of the sentence. A model needs the same ability: each word's meaning depends on other words, sometimes far away.

Older models (RNNs) read one word at a time and squeezed everything seen so far into a single running memory, which was slow and forgetful over long texts. The transformer (2017) lets every token look directly at every other token in one step. That operation is self-attention.

cards.cue: B5 — The transformer, step by step in plain words

cards.label: B5 · 02

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Each token produces three vectors from its embedding, using three learned weight matrices:

  • Query (Q): what am I looking for?
  • Key (K): what do I contain, for others searching?
  • Value (V): what will I hand over if someone attends to me?

For each token, compare its query with every token's key (a dot product; bigger means more relevant), turn the scores into weights with softmax, and take the weighted average of the values. In matrix form for all tokens at once:

$$\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$

The division by $\sqrt{d_k}$ (the size of each key) keeps scores from growing with vector size; without it, softmax becomes extremely peaked and learning stalls.

Analogy: a library. Your query is your question, each book's key is its catalog entry, and its value is its content. You read mostly from the best-matching books.

cards.cue: B5 — The transformer, step by step in plain words

cards.label: B5 · 03

back.title: Notes
back.html:
One attention pattern can only capture one kind of relationship at a time. Multi-head attention runs several attentions (heads) in parallel, each with its own smaller Q, K, V, and then joins their outputs. One head might track grammar, another which noun a pronoun refers to, another nearby words. A model with width 4,096 and 32 heads gives each head 128 dimensions.

Variants that share keys and values between heads, multi-query (MQA) and grouped-query attention (GQA), shrink the KV cache and are standard in modern LLMs (L01 §2).

cards.cue: B5 — The transformer, step by step in plain words

cards.label: B5 · 04

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Attention by itself treats the input as a bag of tokens; "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would look the same. So position information is added:

  • Sinusoidal positional encodings (original paper): fixed wave patterns added to the embeddings.
  • Learned position embeddings (GPT-2, BERT).
  • RoPE (rotary position embedding, used by Llama and most modern LLMs): rotates Q and K by an angle that depends on position, so attention scores depend on relative distance.

cards.cue: B5 — The transformer, step by step in plain words

cards.label: B5 · 05

back.title: Notes
back.html:
A block is a small, repeated recipe. For each token vector $x$:

  1. Normalize, then self-attention (tokens exchange information), then add the result back: $x \leftarrow x + \text{Attn}(\text{Norm}(x))$.
  2. Normalize, then a feed-forward network (each token processed on its own; usually about 4× wider inside), then add back: $x \leftarrow x + \text{FFN}(\text{Norm}(x))$.

The "add back" steps are residual connections (B3). A model stacks many identical blocks: 32 for a 7–8B model, 80 or more for a 70B model. Roughly two-thirds of the parameters are in the feed-forward layers.

In mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, the feed-forward part is replaced by many "experts" and a router that sends each token to only a couple of them, so total size grows without every token paying for all of it (Domain 7, expert parallelism).

cards.cue: B5 — The transformer, step by step in plain words

cards.label: B5 · 06

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Family Attention rule Trained by Good at Examples
Encoder-only Every token sees every token Masked LM Understanding: classify, search, embeddings BERT, RoBERTa
Decoder-only Each token sees only earlier tokens (causal mask) Next-token prediction Generating text; the default for LLMs GPT, Llama, Nemotron
Encoder-decoder Encoder sees all input; decoder is causal and also attends to the encoder (cross-attention) Various Input→output tasks: translation, summarization T5, BART

This table is objective 1.1 in a nutshell.

cards.cue: B5 — The transformer, step by step in plain words

cards.label: B5 · 07
cards.front: 7. Generating text, and the KV cache

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Generation happens in two phases:

  1. Prefill: the whole prompt goes through the model at once. Lots of parallel math, so the GPU is busy computing.
  2. Decode: one new token per step. Each step runs the whole model again for just one token.

Without help, each decode step would recompute keys and values for every earlier token. The KV cache stores them, so each step computes K and V only for the new token. The cost is memory: the cache grows with every token, for every layer and every request. For large models serving many users, the KV cache (not the weights) often decides how many requests fit on a GPU. This is why the exam cares about GQA, KV-cache quantization, paged attention and sliding-window attention (Domains 4 and 8).

cards.cue: B5 — The transformer, step by step in plain words

cards.label: B5 · 08

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Every token's attention and feed-forward work is matrix multiplication, which GPUs do extremely well.
  • All positions in a training text are processed in parallel (unlike RNNs).
  • Performance improves predictably as you add parameters, data and compute (scaling laws; see R00).

That combination is why the same basic block now runs from phones to 100,000-GPU clusters.

cards.cue: B5 — The transformer, step by step in plain words

back.title: Answer
back.html: It lets each token directly gather information from any other token in the sequence in one step, instead of passing it along word by word.

cards.label: B5 · Flashcard
cards.front: What are the roles of query, key and value?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Query: what a token is looking for; key: what each token offers for matching; value: the information passed on when attended to.

back.title: Answer
back.html: To keep dot products from growing with vector size, which would make softmax extremely peaked and stall learning.

back.title: Answer
back.html: Each head can learn a different kind of relationship; their outputs are combined.

cards.label: B5 · Flashcard
cards.front: Why do transformers need positional information?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Attention alone ignores order; positions (sinusoidal, learned, or RoPE) let the model tell "dog bites man" from "man bites dog".

cards.label: B5 · Flashcard
cards.front: What are the two sub-layers of a transformer block?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Self-attention (tokens exchange information) and a feed-forward network (each token processed separately), each with normalization and a residual connection.

cards.label: B5 · Flashcard
cards.front: What does the causal mask do?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Stops each token attending to later tokens, so a decoder can't see the answer it's predicting.

back.title: Answer
back.html: In an encoder-decoder, the decoder's queries attend to the encoder's keys and values, reading the input.

back.title: Answer
back.html: Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel (compute-heavy); decode generates one token per step (memory-bandwidth-heavy).

cards.label: B5 · Flashcard
cards.front: What does the KV cache store and what does it cost?

back.title: Answer
back.html: The keys and values of all previous tokens so they aren't recomputed each step; it costs memory that grows with sequence length and batch size.

back.title: Answer
back.html: A feed-forward layer split into many experts with a router that sends each token to only a few, adding capacity without proportional compute.

cards.label: B6 · 01

back.title: Notes
back.html:
CPU GPU
Cores A few to a few dozen, each very powerful Thousands of simpler cores
Good at Varied tasks, branching logic, running the operating system The same arithmetic on huge amounts of data at once
Memory Large (hundreds of GB of RAM), slower Smaller (tens to ~200 GB of HBM), much faster

NVIDIA data-center GPUs you'll see in questions, oldest to newest: V100 (Volta), A100 (Ampere), H100/H200 (Hopper), B200/GB200 (Blackwell). Each generation adds faster Tensor Cores and support for smaller number formats: FP16/BF16 and TF32 on A100, FP8 on H100, FP4 on Blackwell.

cards.cue: B6 — Computers for AI: GPUs, memory, Linux, containers and clusters

cards.label: B6 · 02
cards.front: 2. GPU memory is the first limit

back.title: Notes
back.html:
A GPU's own memory (HBM, often called VRAM) must hold the model's weights, plus the KV cache when serving, plus gradients, optimizer state and activations when training.

Memory for weights = parameters × bytes per parameter.

Format Bytes 7B model 70B model
FP32 4 28 GB 280 GB
FP16 / BF16 2 14 GB 140 GB
FP8 / INT8 1 7 GB 70 GB
FP4 / INT4 0.5 3.5 GB 35 GB

So a 70B model in BF16 doesn't fit on one 80 GB GPU, but it does in INT4, or split across two GPUs. Training needs far more: with mixed-precision AdamW, about 16 bytes per parameter before activations, so a 7B model needs over 100 GB and is trained across several GPUs (Domain 7).

The other limit is memory bandwidth: how fast the GPU can read memory (about 2–8 TB/s). Generating each token reads all the weights once, so decode speed is often limited by bandwidth rather than by compute. That's why smaller formats make inference faster, not just smaller.

cards.cue: B6 — Computers for AI: GPUs, memory, Linux, containers and clusters

cards.label: B6 · 03

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• NVLink / NVSwitch: very fast links between GPUs inside a server (hundreds of GB/s per GPU). An NVIDIA DGX has 8 GPUs connected this way; a GB200 NVL72 rack connects 72.
  • InfiniBand or high-speed Ethernet: links between servers, slower than NVLink.
  • NCCL: NVIDIA's library for collective operations, such as all-reduce (every GPU ends up with the sum of everyone's gradients), which multi-GPU training relies on.

The rule of thumb: put the chattiest kind of parallelism (tensor parallelism) inside a server on NVLink, and the least chatty (data parallelism) across servers (F4, Domain 7).

cards.cue: B6 — Computers for AI: GPUs, memory, Linux, containers and clusters

cards.label: B6 · 04
cards.front: 4. The software stack on a GPU machine

back.title: Notes
back.html:
From the bottom up: the NVIDIA driver, then CUDA (the programming platform), then libraries like cuBLAS (matrix math), cuDNN (neural-network kernels) and NCCL, then frameworks like PyTorch, then tools like NeMo, TensorRT-LLM and Triton. Versions have to match, which is a big reason everyone uses containers.

Useful commands:

nvidia-smi                     # GPUs, memory used, utilization, running processes
nvidia-smi -l 1                # refresh every second
nvcc --version                 # CUDA compiler version
python -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available(), torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))"

cards.cue: B6 — Computers for AI: GPUs, memory, Linux, containers and clusters

cards.label: B6 · 05

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Almost all GPU servers run Linux, and you'll work in a terminal:

pwd; ls -la; cd /data          # where am I, what's here, move
cat file.txt; less big.log     # print, or page through, a file
grep -n "error" app.log        # search inside files
tail -f app.log                # follow a log as it grows
df -h; free -h                 # disk space, RAM
ps aux | grep python; kill 1234   # find and stop a process
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1    # restrict a program to GPUs 0 and 1

cards.cue: B6 — Computers for AI: GPUs, memory, Linux, containers and clusters

cards.label: B6 · 06

back.title: Notes
back.html:
A container packages an application with everything it needs (libraries, CUDA version, Python packages) so it runs the same everywhere. An image is the packaged template; a container is a running instance of it. Docker is the standard tool.

docker pull nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:<tag>           # get an image from NGC
docker run --gpus all -it --rm \
  -v $PWD:/workspace -p 8000:8000 \
  nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:<tag> bash               # run it with all GPUs, your folder mounted, port 8000 open
  • --gpus all needs the NVIDIA Container Toolkit installed on the host.
  • -v host:container mounts a folder, so data and models survive after the container stops.
  • -p host:container publishes a network port, which is how you reach a model server.
  • NGC (nvcr.io) is NVIDIA's registry of tested images for PyTorch, NeMo, Triton, TensorRT-LLM and NIM.

cards.cue: B6 — Computers for AI: GPUs, memory, Linux, containers and clusters

cards.label: B6 · 07

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Kubernetes (K8s) runs containers across a cluster of machines and keeps them running.

Object What it is
Pod One or more containers running together; the smallest unit
Deployment Keeps a set number of identical pods running and handles updates
Service A stable network address in front of a group of pods (load balancing)
Node A machine in the cluster
Probes Health checks: readiness (ready for traffic?) and liveness (still alive?)
HPA Horizontal Pod Autoscaler: adds or removes pods based on a metric

To use GPUs, pods request nvidia.com/gpu: 1, and the NVIDIA GPU Operator installs the drivers and plugins on the nodes. LLM servers load slowly, so readiness probes and autoscaling on queue size or latency (rather than CPU) matter (Domain 8).

cards.cue: B6 — Computers for AI: GPUs, memory, Linux, containers and clusters

cards.label: B6 · 08
cards.front: 8. Serving basics: APIs, latency and throughput

back.title: Notes
back.html:
A model server receives requests over HTTP (often an OpenAI-compatible API, as NIM offers) and returns responses, often streamed token by token.

  • Latency: time for one request. For LLMs, measure time to first token (TTFT) and time per output token (TPOT) or inter-token latency.
  • Throughput: total work per second, such as tokens per second across all users.
  • They trade off: batching many requests together raises throughput but can add latency.
  • Percentiles: report p50 (typical) and p95/p99 (the slow tail users complain about), not just the average.

cards.cue: B6 — Computers for AI: GPUs, memory, Linux, containers and clusters

cards.label: B6 · Flashcard
cards.front: How do you estimate the memory needed for a model's weights?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Parameters × bytes per parameter (FP16 = 2 bytes, INT8 = 1, INT4 = 0.5); e.g. 70B in BF16 ≈ 140 GB.

cards.label: B6 · Flashcard
cards.front: Why does quantization speed up token generation, not just save memory?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Decoding reads all weights for each token and is limited by memory bandwidth; fewer bytes means faster reads.

cards.label: B6 · Flashcard
cards.front: Roughly how many bytes per parameter does mixed-precision AdamW training need?

back.title: Answer
back.html: About 16 (weights, gradients, FP32 master weights and two optimizer moments), before activations.

cards.label: B6 · Flashcard
cards.front: Which GPU generation introduced FP8 Tensor Cores, and which FP4?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Hopper (H100) for FP8 (Ada also has FP8); Blackwell (B200/GB200) for FP4.

back.title: Answer
back.html: NVLink: fast GPU-to-GPU links inside a server; NCCL: NVIDIA's library for collective operations like all-reduce across GPUs.

back.title: Answer
back.html: Each GPU's memory use, utilization, temperature and the processes using it.

back.title: Answer
back.html: An image is the packaged template; a container is a running instance of it.

cards.label: B6 · Flashcard
cards.front: What do --gpus all, -v and -p do in docker run?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Give the container the host's GPUs; mount a host folder; publish a network port.

back.title: Answer
back.html: NVIDIA's catalog and registry (nvcr.io) of GPU-optimized containers, models and tools.

back.title: Answer
back.html: Pod: the smallest unit of running containers; Deployment: keeps N identical pods running; Service: a stable address that load-balances across them.

cards.label: B6 · Flashcard
cards.front: What is a readiness probe for?

back.title: Answer
back.html: It tells Kubernetes when a pod can receive traffic, e.g. only after the model has finished loading.

cards.label: B7 · 01

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Rung What changes Data needed Cost Use when
Prompt engineering Only the input text None to a few examples Lowest Always try first
RAG The input, filled with retrieved documents Your documents Low The model lacks facts, or facts change
Prompt learning (p-tuning) A few learned "soft prompt" vectors Hundreds of examples Low Specializing a model you can't afford to tune
PEFT (LoRA, adapters) A small set of new weights Hundreds to thousands Medium New skill, format or style
Full fine-tuning All weights Thousands or more High Big domain shift, and you have the budget
Alignment (RLHF, DPO, GRPO) All or some weights, from preferences Ranked or scored answers High Make answers helpful, safe or better reasoned

NVIDIA's blog Selecting Large Language Model Customization Techniques (SG05) is built around this ladder.

cards.cue: B7 — Building with LLMs: prompting, RAG, agents and fine-tuning

cards.label: B7 · 02

back.title: Notes
back.html:
A good prompt usually has: a role or instruction ("You are a support assistant…"), the context it needs, the task, examples of good answers, and the output format.

  • Zero-shot: instructions only. Few-shot: add a few worked examples; the model copies the pattern without any training. This is in-context learning.
  • Chain-of-thought (CoT): ask the model to reason step by step, or show examples that do. It helps on math and multi-step problems.
  • Chat templates: chat models were trained with special tokens marking system, user and assistant turns. Always format prompts with the model's own template (B2 §6).
  • Output control: ask for JSON, then validate it; or use constrained decoding, which only allows tokens that keep the output valid (objective 2.4).

cards.cue: B7 — Building with LLMs: prompting, RAG, agents and fine-tuning

cards.label: B7 · 03

back.title: Notes
back.html:
LLMs sometimes state false things fluently: they hallucinate. The model learned to produce plausible text, not to check facts, and it has no knowledge after its training date. Controls:

  • Ground it in real documents (RAG) and ask it to cite them.
  • Lower temperature for factual tasks.
  • Validate outputs, and add guardrails that check facts or block unsupported claims (Domain 10).
  • Evaluate faithfulness to the provided context (Domain 6).

cards.cue: B7 — Building with LLMs: prompting, RAG, agents and fine-tuning

cards.label: B7 · 04

back.title: Notes
back.html:
RAG gives the model an open book:

  1. Ingest: split documents into chunks (say, a few hundred tokens), turn each into an embedding with an embedding model (B4), and store them in a vector database.
  2. Retrieve: embed the user's question and find the most similar chunks. Optionally rerank them with a more precise model.
  3. Generate: put the best chunks into the prompt and ask the LLM to answer from them.

Updating knowledge is just re-indexing documents, with no retraining. NVIDIA's pieces for this: NeMo Retriever embedding and reranking NIMs, the LLM NIM, and the RAG blueprint (SG10).

cards.cue: B7 — Building with LLMs: prompting, RAG, agents and fine-tuning

cards.label: B7 · 05

back.title: Notes
back.html:
An agent is an LLM in a loop that can use tools: it decides on an action (search, call an API, run code), sees the result, and continues until the task is done. The ReAct pattern alternates "reason" and "act" steps. Agents are powerful and risky: each tool call is a chance for mistakes or misuse, so they need limits and guardrails.

Reasoning models are trained to think at length before answering, and test-time scaling means spending more compute at answer time (longer thinking, several attempts) for better answers (SG02).

cards.cue: B7 — Building with LLMs: prompting, RAG, agents and fine-tuning

cards.label: B7 · 06

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): train on example prompt → ideal response pairs. Turns a raw pretrained model into an instruction follower.
  • LoRA: instead of changing a big weight matrix $W$, learn a small update $BA$ made of two thin matrices. Trains well under 1% of the parameters, so it fits on much smaller GPUs, and one base model can switch between many adapters.
  • Alignment: teach preferences. RLHF learns a reward model from human rankings and optimizes against it; DPO learns directly from chosen/rejected pairs; GRPO compares several answers to the same prompt and rewards the better ones.
  • Risk: catastrophic forgetting, where the model gets better at your task and worse at general skills. Always compare against the base model.

cards.cue: B7 — Building with LLMs: prompting, RAG, agents and fine-tuning

cards.label: B7 · 07

back.title: Notes
back.html: Responsible deployment uses several layers, since none is perfect: a safety-aligned model, input checks (block jailbreaks and prompt injection), retrieval checks, output checks (toxic content, personal data, unsupported claims), monitoring, and human escalation. NeMo Guardrails implements these "rails" in configuration and Colang scripts (Domain 10).

cards.cue: B7 — Building with LLMs: prompting, RAG, agents and fine-tuning

cards.label: B7 · 08
cards.front: 8. How to judge whether it works

back.title: Notes
back.html: Decide what "good" means before building: accuracy on a test set, faithfulness to sources, format validity, latency and cost. Start by reading real outputs and listing what goes wrong (error analysis), then automate the checks that matter, using metrics, LLM judges and human review (Domain 6).

cards.cue: B7 — Building with LLMs: prompting, RAG, agents and fine-tuning

back.title: Answer

back.title: Answer
back.html: When you need a new behavior, format, style or skill rather than new facts.

back.title: Answer
back.html: An LLM in a loop that plans, calls tools, observes the results and continues until the task is done.

back.title: Answer

back.title: Answer

back.title: Answer

cards.label: SG01 · Paper ★★★ · Intermediate

back.title: Key idea
back.html: The paper that introduced the transformer: drop recurrence entirely and let every token attend to every other token, using scaled dot-product attention, multiple heads and positional encodings, in an encoder-decoder model for translation.

back.title: How to read it
back.html: Read The Illustrated Transformer (SG04) first. Then focus on sections 3.1–3.5 and Figure 1–2; skim the experiments. Check you can explain why scores are divided by $\sqrt{d_k}$.

back.title: Exam angle

cards.meta: Vaswani et al. (Google), 2017 · Paper · ★★★ · Intermediate · Verses 1.01–1.07

cards.label: Objective 1.1
cards.front: What does objective 1.1 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: Know the three transformer families. Encoders (BERT) read the whole input at once and are best for understanding tasks such as classification and search. Decoders (GPT, Llama) generate text left to right. Encoder-decoders (T5, original Transformer) read an input and then write a different output, as in translation or summarization.

back.title: Learn it here
back.html: verses 1.05–1.07 · L01 §4 "Choosing an architecture" · B5.

cards.cue: Analyze encoder-decoder structures and their applications.

cards.label: Objective 1.2
cards.front: What does objective 1.2 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: Explain what happens inside one transformer block: each token builds a query, key and value; attention compares queries with keys to decide which other tokens to read from; then a small feed-forward network processes each token. Residual connections and normalization keep deep stacks trainable.

back.title: Learn it here
back.html: verses 1.01–1.04 · L01 §1 "Inside the block" and §2 · B5 · F1.

cards.cue: Describe transformer architectures including self-attention mechanisms.

cards.label: Objective 1.3
cards.front: What does objective 1.3 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: Be able to write the few lines of code that run a model and take out its internal vectors, and know which vector to use: for encoders, the [CLS] token or the average over tokens; for decoders, usually the last token's hidden state or a mean over tokens.

back.title: Learn it here
back.html: verses 1.09–1.10 · L01 §5 "Extracting embeddings" · B2.

cards.cue: Develop code to extract embeddings from both encoder and decoder models.

cards.label: Objective 1.4
cards.front: What does objective 1.4 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: Know how to turn the model's next-token probabilities into text: greedy, beam search, temperature, top-k, top-p (nucleus), repetition penalties, and when each is appropriate.

back.title: Learn it here
back.html: verses 1.11–1.12 · L01 §6 "Decoding and sampling" · B4.

cards.cue: Implement advanced sampling techniques for text generation.

cards.label: Objective 1.5
cards.front: What does objective 1.5 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: The same topic from the understanding side: predict what happens to the output when you raise the temperature or shrink top-p, and why beam search gives bland text for open-ended chat.

cards.cue: Understand output sampling techniques used in decoder-based language models.

cards.label: Objective 1.6
cards.front: What does objective 1.6 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: An embedding is a list of numbers that represents a token, sentence or document so that similar meanings end up close together. Know how closeness is measured (cosine similarity) and what embeddings are used for (search, RAG, clustering).

back.title: Learn it here
back.html: verses 1.08–1.09 · B4 "Text as numbers".

back.title: Exam angle
back.html: Prefill vs decode, KV-cache memory, in-flight batching and speculative decoding; it also explains how prompt length drives cost.

back.title: In plain words

cards.label: Objective 2.2

back.title: In plain words
back.html: Zero-shot means instructions only; one-shot and few-shot add worked examples to the prompt. Know when examples help, how to pick and order them, and their cost in context length.

cards.label: Objective 2.3
cards.front: What does objective 2.3 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: Causal language modeling is next-token prediction: the model sees tokens 1…t and learns to predict token t+1, with a mask so it can't peek ahead. It's how GPT-style models are pretrained and how you continue pretraining on domain text.

cards.cue: Train decoder-based LLMs with causal language modeling as needed.

cards.label: Objective 2.4
cards.front: What does objective 2.4 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: Put code around the model: validate its output (for example, against a JSON schema), retry or repair failures, restrict which tokens it may generate so the output is always valid (constrained decoding), and ground answers in retrieved documents.

cards.cue: Design specialized LLM-wrapping modules with built-in validation and constrained decoding for improved consistency, reduced hallucinations, and better user experience.

cards.meta: Hu et al. (Microsoft), ICLR 2022 · Paper · ★★★ · Intermediate · Verses 5.10, 5.11

cards.label: Objective 4.1
cards.front: What does objective 4.1 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: Know the three ways to shrink a model and what each saves. Quantizing weights saves memory; quantizing activations too speeds up the math. Pruning removes weights, and only structured patterns (such as NVIDIA's 2:4 sparsity) actually run faster on GPUs.

cards.cue: Apply pruning, sparsity, and weight/activation quantization to reduce memory footprint and optimize model inference for hardware acceleration.

cards.label: Objective 4.2
cards.front: What does objective 4.2 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: Post-training quantization (PTQ) converts a finished model using a small calibration set; quantization-aware training (QAT) simulates low precision during training to recover accuracy. Pick the number format the GPU supports (FP16/BF16 everywhere, INT8 on A100, FP8 on H100, FP4 on Blackwell) and always measure quality before and after.

cards.cue: Choose and implement quantization strategies (post-training, quantization-aware, activation quantization) tailored for hardware and tasks (e.g., NVIDIA A100/H100 Tensor Core GPUs, FP16, INT8), and measure any accuracy trade-offs.

cards.label: Objective 4.3
cards.front: What does objective 4.3 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: Train a small "student" model to match the output probabilities (soft targets) of a large "teacher", usually mixed with the normal loss on true labels. DistilBERT is the classic example.

cards.cue: Implement knowledge distillation to create smaller, efficient models based on larger pretrained ones.

cards.label: Objective 4.4
cards.front: What does objective 4.4 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: Search learning rate, batch size, warmup and similar settings methodically (random or Bayesian search rather than guessing), run trials in parallel on many GPUs, and adjust the learning rate when you change the batch size.

cards.cue: Conduct systematic hyperparameter tuning and distributed parameter search, including learning rate schedules and batch size adjustments.

cards.label: Objective 4.5
cards.front: What does objective 4.5 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: When you compare an optimized model with the original, keep the decoding settings fixed and change one thing at a time (an ablation), so you know which change caused a quality drop.

cards.cue: Use advanced sampling (beam search, temperature scaling) and systematic ablation studies to evaluate model optimization impact.

cards.label: Objective 4.6
cards.front: What does objective 4.6 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM compile a model into a fast engine for a specific GPU. The KV cache stores past attention keys and values so each new token is cheap, but it grows with sequence length. Sliding-window and streaming attention cap that growth for long inputs.

cards.cue: Select and apply optimization methods (NVIDIA TensorRT, sliding-window/streaming attention, key-value caching) based on architecture, task, and available resources.

cards.label: Objective 4.7
cards.front: What does objective 4.7 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: Encoders like BERT are pretrained by hiding about 15% of tokens and predicting them (MLM), originally plus predicting whether two sentences follow each other (NSP, later found to matter little). Then apply the same compression ideas to encoders.

cards.cue: Train encoder-based foundation LLMs with masked language modeling (MLM) and/or next sentence prediction, and understand quantization, distillation, and model pruning concepts.

cards.meta: Avinash Selvam, Medium · Blog · ★★ · Beginner · Verses 6.02–6.05

cards.label: Objective 5.1
cards.front: What does objective 5.1 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: First teach the model to follow instructions with example conversations (SFT). Then make it prefer good answers: RLHF trains a reward model from human rankings and optimizes against it with PPO; DPO skips the reward model and learns directly from preferred/rejected pairs; GRPO scores a group of answers to the same prompt and pushes toward the better ones, without a separate value model.

cards.cue: Align models with intent via supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning from human feedback, including methods like direct preference optimization (DPO) or group relative policy optimization (GRPO).

cards.label: Objective 5.2
cards.front: What does objective 5.2 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: Contrastive training pulls matching pairs (a question and its answer passage) close together in embedding space and pushes others apart; it is how embedding models for search are trained. PEFT trains a tiny fraction of parameters: LoRA adds low-rank update matrices, adapters add small layers, p-tuning learns soft prompt vectors.

cards.cue: Apply contrastive loss for embeddings and use parameter-efficient techniques (LoRA, adapters, P-tuning).

cards.label: Objective 5.3
cards.front: What does objective 5.3 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: Watch validation loss; stop when it stops improving for a set number of checks (patience) even if training loss still falls. Choose the right metric for each stage: loss or perplexity during training, task metrics after, human or judge ratings for alignment.

cards.cue: Implement early stopping to prevent overfitting and select performance metrics for all phases.

cards.label: Objective 5.4
cards.front: What does objective 5.4 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: Fine-tuning can add or remove hallucinations and can make a model forget general skills. Compare against the base model on both the target task and general benchmarks, and prefer grounding (RAG) plus guardrails for factual accuracy.

cards.label: Objective 7.1
cards.front: What does objective 7.1 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: Know every way to split training. Data parallel (DDP) copies the model and splits the data. FSDP also splits the model's weights, gradients and optimizer state. Tensor parallel splits each layer's matrices. Pipeline parallel gives different layers to different GPUs. Sequence parallel splits along the tokens. Expert parallel puts different mixture-of-experts experts on different GPUs.

cards.cue: Configure multi-GPU and distributed training setups (DDP, FSDP, model, pipeline, tensor, data, sequence, and expert parallelism).

cards.label: Objective 7.2
cards.front: What does objective 7.2 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: Tensor Cores do matrix math much faster in FP16/BF16/FP8. Train in mixed precision (low-precision math with FP32 master weights, plus loss scaling for FP16), keep matrix sizes multiples of 8 or 16, and pick batch sizes that fill the GPU without running out of memory.

cards.cue: Apply Tensor Core and mixed-precision optimizations and batch/memory management for efficient throughput.

cards.label: Objective 7.3
cards.front: What does objective 7.3 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: Attention is a set of matrix multiplications (GEMMs) that can be split across GPUs by head (tensor parallelism) and made memory-efficient with FlashAttention. Gradient accumulation adds up gradients over several small batches before one update, so you get the effect of a big batch with little memory.

cards.cue: Distribute and optimize self-attention head general matrix multiplication (GEMM) operations and implement gradient accumulation for large models or limited GPU memory.

cards.label: Objective 7.4
cards.front: What does objective 7.4 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: Use Nsight Systems to see where time goes (GPU idle while waiting for data? communication?), Nsight Compute to study a slow kernel, and fix out-of-memory errors with smaller batches, checkpointing, lower precision or more sharding.

cards.cue: Identify and address bottlenecks using CUDA profiling and troubleshoot memory and kernel efficiency issues.

cards.label: Objective 8.1
cards.front: What does objective 8.1 ask you to be able to do?

back.title: In plain words
back.html: Encoders process the whole input in one pass, so they're fast and cheap. Decoders generate one token at a time, and each step must re-read the weights and the growing KV cache, so they are slow per token and memory-hungry. Know which phase dominates (prefill vs decode) and how to optimize each.

cards.cue: Analyze computational tradeoffs for model types (encoder, decoder, encoder-decoder) and optimize for memory and latency.

cards.label: F1 · 01

back.title: Notes
back.html:
A transformer is mostly matrix multiplies (GEMMs). For $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times k}$ and $B \in \mathbb{R}^{k\times n}$, $AB$ costs $2mkn$ FLOPs (one multiply + one add per term).

Common shapes, with batch $B$, sequence length $T$, model width $d$ (d_model), $h$ heads and head width $d_k = d/h$:

Tensor Shape
Token embeddings / residual stream $[B, T, d]$
$Q, K, V$ after head split $[B, h, T, d_k]$
Attention scores $QK^\top$ $[B, h, T, T]$ — quadratic in $T$
MLP hidden $[B, T, 4d]$ (classic)
Logits $[B, T, V]$ with vocabulary size $V$

Parameter count of a decoder block. Attention projections $W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O$ are each $d\times d$ → $4d^2$. The MLP maps $d \to 4d \to d$ → $8d^2$. So one block holds about $12d^2$ parameters, and a model with $L$ layers holds

$$N \approx 12\,L\,d^2 \;+\; V d \quad(\text{embeddings}).$$

Check: GPT-3 has $L=96$, $d=12288$: $12\cdot 96\cdot 12288^2 \approx 1.74\times10^{11}$ — the famous 175B.

FLOPs per token. A forward pass costs about $2N$ FLOPs per token (each weight is used in one multiply-add). Training costs about $6N$ (forward $2N$ + backward $4N$).

Worked example: training a 7B model on 1T tokens needs $6 \cdot 7\times10^{9}\cdot 10^{12} = 4.2\times10^{22}$ FLOPs. An H100 sustaining 400 TFLOP/s (≈40% of its ~989 dense BF16 peak) takes $4.2\times10^{22} / 4\times10^{14} \approx 1.05\times10^{8}$ s ≈ 29,000 GPU-hours.

cards.cue: F1 — The math you need for LLMs

cards.label: F1 · 02
cards.front: 2. Softmax, temperature and the log-sum-exp trick

back.title: Notes
back.html:
$$\text{softmax}(z)_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}$$

  • Adding a constant to every logit changes nothing, so implementations subtract $\max_j z_j$ first to avoid overflow (numerically stable softmax).
  • $\log\sum_j e^{z_j}$ is computed as $m + \log\sum_j e^{z_j - m}$ (log-sum-exp).
  • Temperature divides the logits: $\text{softmax}(z/T)$. $T<1$ sharpens (more deterministic), $T>1$ flattens (more diverse), $T\to 0$ approaches argmax (greedy).
  • Softmax saturates: if one logit is much larger than the rest, the output is nearly one-hot and its gradient is nearly zero. That is the whole reason for the $\sqrt{d_k}$ in attention.

cards.cue: F1 — The math you need for LLMs

cards.label: F1 · 03

back.title: Notes
back.html:
If the components of $q$ and $k$ are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, then $q\cdot k = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i$ has mean 0 and variance $d_k$ (standard deviation $\sqrt{d_k}$). With $d_k = 128$ the raw scores have standard deviation ≈ 11, softmax saturates, and gradients vanish. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ restores unit variance:

$$\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$

cards.cue: F1 — The math you need for LLMs

cards.label: F1 · 04

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• A language model outputs $p(x_t \mid x_{<t})$. Training minimizes the negative log-likelihood (cross-entropy against the one-hot next token): $\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_t \log p(x_t\mid x_{<t})$.
  • Perplexity is its exponential: $\text{PPL} = e^{\mathcal{L}}$. Interpretation: the model is as uncertain as a uniform choice among PPL tokens. A uniform model over $V$ tokens has $\mathcal{L}=\log V$ and $\text{PPL}=V$.
  • Loss in nats vs bits: divide by $\ln 2$ for bits. Perplexity depends on the tokenizer, so never compare perplexity across models with different tokenizers; use bits-per-byte or a downstream metric instead.

cards.cue: F1 — The math you need for LLMs

cards.label: F1 · 05

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Entropy $H(p) = -\sum_i p_i \log p_i$ — the average surprise.
  • Cross-entropy $H(p,q) = -\sum_i p_i \log q_i = H(p) + \text{KL}(p\,\|\,q)$.
  • $\text{KL}(p\,\|\,q) = \sum_i p_i \log\frac{p_i}{q_i} \ge 0$, zero only when $p=q$, and not symmetric.
  • Forward KL $\text{KL}(p_{data}\|q)$ is mean-seeking (covers every mode).
  • Reverse KL $\text{KL}(q\|p)$ is mode-seeking.
  • Where KL shows up: distillation loss $\text{KL}(p_{teacher}\|p_{student})$; the RLHF penalty $\beta\,\text{KL}(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{ref})$ that keeps the policy near the SFT model; drift metrics (PSI is a symmetrized KL).

cards.cue: F1 — The math you need for LLMs

cards.label: F1 · 06

back.title: Notes
back.html: $\sigma(x) = 1/(1+e^{-x})$. The Bradley–Terry model says the probability that response $y_w$ is preferred to $y_l$ is $\sigma(r(y_w) - r(y_l))$. Reward models minimize $-\log\sigma(r_w - r_l)$; DPO plugs an implicit reward $\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y|x)}{\pi_{ref}(y|x)}$ into the same formula.

cards.cue: F1 — The math you need for LLMs

cards.label: F1 · 07

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Cosine similarity $\cos(a,b) = \frac{a\cdot b}{\|a\|\|b\|}$. For unit-normalized embeddings, cosine equals the dot product, so vector databases can use inner-product search.
  • Contrastive losses (InfoNCE) are a softmax over similarities divided by a temperature $\tau$: small $\tau$ = sharper separation.

cards.cue: F1 — The math you need for LLMs

cards.label: F1 · 08

back.title: Notes
back.html:
A matrix $\Delta W = BA$ with $B\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}$, $A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times k}$ has rank at most $r$ and only $r(d+k)$ parameters instead of $dk$.

Worked example: $d=k=4096$, $r=8$ → $8\cdot 8192 = 65{,}536$ parameters vs $16{,}777{,}216$ — 0.39% of the full matrix. LoRA scales the update by $\alpha/r$ and initializes $B=0$ so training starts exactly at the pretrained model.

cards.cue: F1 — The math you need for LLMs

cards.label: F1 · 09

back.title: Notes
back.html: Backpropagation applies the chain rule layer by layer. Two facts the exam leans on: (1) the residual connection $x + f(x)$ gives gradients an identity path, which is why deep transformers train at all; (2) gradients through rounding are zero almost everywhere, which is why quantization-aware training uses the straight-through estimator (treat round() as identity in the backward pass).

cards.cue: F1 — The math you need for LLMs

cards.label: F2 · 01

back.title: Notes
back.html:
for step, batch in enumerate(loader):
    with torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
        loss = model(**batch).loss / accum_steps       # scale for accumulation
    loss.backward()
    if (step + 1) % accum_steps == 0:
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
        optimizer.step()
        scheduler.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)

Effective batch size = micro-batch × gradient-accumulation steps × data-parallel ranks. Accumulation trades time for memory: the same effective batch in more, smaller forward/backward passes.

cards.cue: F2 — How neural networks are trained

cards.label: F2 · 02

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• SGD + momentum: $v \leftarrow \mu v + g$, $\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta v$.
  • Adam: keeps a running mean $m$ and a running mean of squares $v$ of the gradient ($\beta_1 = 0.9$, $\beta_2 \approx 0.95$–$0.999$), bias-corrects them, and steps by $\eta\,\hat m / (\sqrt{\hat v} + \epsilon)$ — a per-parameter adaptive step.
  • AdamW: applies weight decay directly to the weights ($\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\lambda\theta$) instead of adding $\lambda\theta$ to the gradient. This "decoupled" decay is the LLM default (typical $\lambda = 0.1$).

cards.cue: F2 — How neural networks are trained

cards.label: F2 · 03

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Mixed-precision training with Adam stores per parameter:

Item Bytes
BF16/FP16 weights 2
BF16/FP16 gradients 2
FP32 master weights 4
Adam $m$ (FP32) 4
Adam $v$ (FP32) 4
Total (before activations) 16

Worked example: a 7B model needs $7\times10^9 \times 16 = 112$ GB just for model + optimizer state — more than one 80 GB GPU. That is why FSDP/ZeRO shards these states (Domain 7). Inference in BF16 needs only $2$ bytes/param → 14 GB, plus the KV cache.

Activations come on top and scale with batch × sequence length. For one transformer layer, the Megatron team's estimate (FP16, no recomputation) is

$$\text{activations per layer} \approx s\,b\,h\left(34 + \frac{5\,a\,s}{h}\right)\ \text{bytes}$$

with sequence $s$, micro-batch $b$, hidden size $h$ and $a$ heads. The $5as/h$ term is the stored attention matrix — exactly what FlashAttention stops storing.

Worked example: $s=4096$, $b=1$, $h=4096$, $a=32$: the $34sbh$ part is ≈0.57 GB and the attention part is ≈2.7 GB, so ≈3.3 GB per layer and ≈104 GB for 32 layers. FlashAttention drops that to ≈18 GB; full activation checkpointing keeps only each layer's input ($2sbh$ ≈ 34 MB per layer) and recomputes the rest in the backward pass.

cards.cue: F2 — How neural networks are trained

cards.label: F2 · 04

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Warmup: ramp the LR linearly from ~0 to its peak over the first few hundred to few thousand steps. Without it, Adam's early variance estimates are poor and large-batch runs diverge in the first ~100 steps.
  • Decay: cosine (or linear) decay to ~10% of peak over the rest of training.
  • Linear scaling rule: multiply the batch by $k$ → multiply the LR by $k$ (with warmup), up to the critical batch size beyond which bigger batches stop helping.
  • Symptoms: loss spikes/NaN → LR too high or no warmup; loss plateaus high → LR too low; oscillating loss late in training → decay missing.

cards.cue: F2 — How neural networks are trained

cards.label: F2 · 05

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• LayerNorm normalizes each token's features (subtract mean, divide by std, then scale and shift). RMSNorm skips the mean subtraction — cheaper, used by Llama-style models.
  • Pre-LN ($x + f(\text{LN}(x))$) is stable without warmup tricks; the original post-LN ($\text{LN}(x + f(x))$) needs warmup.
  • Gradient clipping by global norm (typically 1.0) stops one bad batch from blowing up the weights.
  • FP16 loss scaling: FP16 can't represent tiny gradients, so multiply the loss by a scale $S$, unscale the gradients before the step, skip steps that overflow, and adjust $S$ dynamically. BF16 has FP32's exponent range and needs no loss scaling.

cards.cue: F2 — How neural networks are trained

cards.label: F2 · 06

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Overfitting signature: training loss keeps falling while validation loss turns up.
  • Early stopping: evaluate every $n$ steps, keep the best checkpoint, stop after patience evaluations without improvement.
  • Regularizers: weight decay, dropout (often 0 in LLM pretraining, 0.05–0.1 in fine-tuning), data augmentation, fewer epochs (LLM fine-tunes usually need only 1–3).
  • Catastrophic forgetting: fine-tuning on a narrow task erases general skills. Fixes: lower LR, fewer steps, mix in general data (replay), PEFT (LoRA leaves base weights frozen), regularize toward the base model (KL, EWC).

cards.cue: F2 — How neural networks are trained

cards.label: F2 · 07

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Loss falls as a power law in parameters $N$, data $D$ and compute $C \approx 6ND$.
  • Chinchilla: for a fixed compute budget, the compute-optimal model uses roughly 20 training tokens per parameter. Modern models train far longer than this on purpose, because a smaller, longer-trained model is cheaper to serve.

cards.label: F3 · 01

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• A GPU is an array of streaming multiprocessors (SMs): A100 has 108, H100 SXM has 132.
  • Each SM runs warps of 32 threads in lock-step (SIMT). Many warps are resident at once so the SM can hide memory latency by switching warps. Occupancy = resident warps ÷ the SM's maximum (64 on A100/H100).
  • CUDA cores do scalar FP32/INT math; Tensor Cores do small matrix multiply-accumulates in low precision and provide almost all of the FLOPs.
  • Memory hierarchy (fast/small → slow/large): registers → shared memory / L1 (per SM, ~200 KB) → L2 (40 MB A100, 50 MB H100) → HBM (80 GB, a few TB/s) → host memory over PCIe or NVLink-C2C.

cards.cue: F3 — GPU architecture and number formats

cards.cue: F3 — GPU architecture and number formats

cards.label: F3 · 03

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Arithmetic intensity (AI) = FLOPs performed ÷ bytes moved from HBM. Attainable throughput is

$$\text{FLOP/s} = \min(\text{peak FLOP/s},\ \text{AI}\times\text{bandwidth}).$$

The ridge point is peak ÷ bandwidth: ≈153 FLOP/byte for A100 BF16, ≈295 for H100 BF16. Below it you are memory-bound; above it, compute-bound.

  • Large GEMMs (training, prefill) have high AI → compute-bound.
  • Decode multiplies a weight matrix by one token vector per sequence: each 2-byte weight is used for ~2 FLOPs per sequence in the batch, so AI ≈ batch size. At small batch, decode is memory-bound.
  • Element-wise ops (activation, dropout, norm) have AI ≪ 1 → memory-bound; that is why kernel fusion helps.

Worked example: batch-1 decode of a 7B BF16 model must read 14 GB of weights per token. At 3.35 TB/s that is ≥4.2 ms/token (≤ ~240 tokens/s) no matter how many FLOPs the GPU has. Weight-only INT4 cuts the bytes 4× — the reason it speeds up decode.

cards.cue: F3 — GPU architecture and number formats

cards.label: F3 · 04

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Every kernel launch costs a few microseconds of CPU time. Many tiny kernels leave the GPU idle between them → CUDA Graphs (capture once, replay) or torch.compile (fusion + graphs).
  • Host↔device copies over PCIe (~25–64 GB/s) are slow; use pinned memory and overlap copies with compute on separate CUDA streams.

cards.cue: F3 — GPU architecture and number formats

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Format Sign/Exp/Mantissa Max value Notes
FP32 1/8/23 ~3.4×10³⁸ baseline
TF32 1/8/10 FP32 range Ampere+ Tensor Core math mode for FP32 matmuls

Rules of thumb: fewer exponent bits = less range; fewer mantissa bits = less precision. Low-bit formats only work with scaling — per-tensor, per-channel, per-group or per-block — which is what calibration estimates.
