cards.label: F4 · 01

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Collective Before → after Used by
Broadcast one rank's tensor → every rank initial weights
Reduce sum of all ranks → one rank metrics
All-reduce every rank gets the sum DDP gradients, TP partial sums
All-gather each rank's shard → every rank has the full tensor FSDP/ZeRO-3 params, sequence parallel
Reduce-scatter sum, then each rank keeps one shard FSDP/ZeRO gradients
All-to-all each rank sends a different piece to every other rank MoE expert parallel, Ulysses attention

Identity worth remembering: all-reduce = reduce-scatter + all-gather.

cards.cue: F4 — Collective communication and multi-GPU training

cards.label: F4 · 02

back.title: Notes
back.html:
For a tensor of $S$ bytes over $N$ ranks with a ring algorithm, each rank sends and receives

  • all-reduce: $2\frac{N-1}{N}S$
  • all-gather or reduce-scatter: $\frac{N-1}{N}S$

so time ≈ bytes ÷ link bandwidth + a latency term per step. The volume per GPU barely grows with $N$ — that's why ring all-reduce scales. NCCL also uses trees and, on NVSwitch systems, in-network reductions (SHARP / NVLS).

nccl-tests reports bus bandwidth: for all-reduce, busbw = algbw × $2(N-1)/N$, so it can be compared directly with the hardware link speed.

cards.cue: F4 — Collective communication and multi-GPU training

cards.label: F4 · 03

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Link Typical bandwidth
NVLink 4 (H100), per GPU 900 GB/s
NVLink 5 (Blackwell), per GPU 1.8 TB/s
InfiniBand NDR, per 400 Gb/s NIC ~50 GB/s
PCIe Gen5 x16 ~64 GB/s

Inside a node, GPUs talk over NVLink/NVSwitch; between nodes over InfiniBand or RoCE with GPUDirect RDMA (the NIC reads GPU memory directly). Intra-node bandwidth is an order of magnitude higher, which drives the placement rule: put the chattiest parallelism on the fastest link.

cards.cue: F4 — Collective communication and multi-GPU training

cards.label: F4 · 04

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Data parallel (DDP). Every rank holds the full model and a different batch. After backward, gradients are all-reduced in ~25 MB buckets, started as soon as each bucket is ready, so communication overlaps the rest of the backward pass.

ZeRO / FSDP. Shard training state over the $N_d$ data-parallel ranks. With $\Psi$ parameters and mixed-precision Adam (12 bytes of optimizer state per parameter):

Stage Shards Memory per GPU
Baseline DDP nothing $16\Psi$
ZeRO-1 optimizer states $4\Psi + 12\Psi/N_d$
ZeRO-2 + gradients $2\Psi + 14\Psi/N_d$
ZeRO-3 / FSDP full shard + parameters $16\Psi/N_d$

Worked example (from the ZeRO paper): 7.5B parameters on 64 GPUs → 120 GB baseline, 31.4 GB (ZeRO-1), 16.6 GB (ZeRO-2), 1.9 GB (ZeRO-3). ZeRO-3 all-gathers each layer's parameters before its forward and again before its backward, and reduce-scatters its gradients — about 1.5× the traffic of DDP.

Tensor parallel (Megatron). Split each weight matrix: the first MLP matrix by columns, the second by rows, so each rank computes a partial result that needs one all-reduce per MLP and one per attention block in the forward pass (and two more in the backward). That is a collective inside every layer → keep TP within the NVLink domain. Sequence parallelism replaces each all-reduce with reduce-scatter + all-gather (same volume) and shards LayerNorm/dropout activations along the sequence.

Pipeline parallel. Split the layers into $p$ stages; send activations point-to-point between neighbours. Idle "bubble" time as a fraction of the total is

$$\frac{p-1}{m+p-1}\ \ (\approx \tfrac{p-1}{m}\text{ when } m \gg p)$$

for $m$ micro-batches. More micro-batches or an interleaved 1F1B schedule (each GPU holds $v$ non-adjacent chunks) shrink the bubble. PP tolerates slower links because it only sends activations at stage boundaries.

Expert parallel (MoE). Experts live on different GPUs; each MoE layer does an all-to-all to dispatch tokens to their experts and another to bring the results back.

Context parallel / ring attention. Split very long sequences across GPUs and pass key/value blocks around a ring.

cards.cue: F4 — Collective communication and multi-GPU training

cards.label: F4 · 05

back.title: Notes
back.html:
A typical layout: TP inside a node, PP across nodes, DP (or FSDP) outermost. Total GPUs = TP × PP × DP (× CP/EP where used).

Example: a 70B model on 64 H100s (8 nodes × 8): TP = 8 inside each node, PP = 2, DP = 4 → 8 × 2 × 4 = 64.

cards.cue: F4 — Collective communication and multi-GPU training

cards.label: F4 · 06

back.title: Notes
back.html:
torchrun --nnodes=2 --nproc_per_node=8 --rdzv_backend=c10d \
         --rdzv_endpoint=$MASTER_ADDR:29500 train.py
# inside: torch.distributed.init_process_group("nccl"); LOCAL_RANK/RANK/WORLD_SIZE from env
NCCL_DEBUG=INFO ./build/all_reduce_perf -b 8M -e 4G -f 2 -g 8   # nccl-tests

Hangs usually mean ranks called collectives in a different order or one rank crashed. Low bus bandwidth usually means traffic fell back to TCP sockets or PCIe (check the NCCL_DEBUG=INFO transport lines, NCCL_IB_HCA, NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME).

cards.label: F5 · 01

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• An image is a layered filesystem plus metadata; a container is a running instance. NVIDIA publishes GPU-ready images on NGC (nvcr.io/nvidia/...): PyTorch, NeMo, TensorRT-LLM, Triton, NIM.
  • GPUs reach containers through the NVIDIA Container Toolkit: docker run --gpus all ... (or --gpus '"device=0,1"').
  • LLM containers usually need --shm-size (or --ipc=host) because PyTorch data loaders and NCCL use shared memory.
  • The host driver must be new enough for the container's CUDA version.

cards.cue: F5 — Serving systems and operations basics

cards.label: F5 · 02

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Pod: one or more containers scheduled together. Deployment: keeps N replica pods running and does rolling updates. Service: stable network name/IP in front of pods.
  • GPUs are requested as a resource: resources.limits: nvidia.com/gpu: 1. The NVIDIA GPU Operator installs the driver, container toolkit, device plugin and DCGM exporter.
  • Probes: liveness restarts a stuck container; readiness keeps traffic away until the model is loaded (LLM servers can take minutes); startup probes give slow starters time before liveness kicks in.
  • HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler): scales replicas on a metric. CPU utilization is a poor signal for GPU inference — scale on queue depth, in-flight requests or GPU/KV-cache utilization via custom metrics.

cards.cue: F5 — Serving systems and operations basics

cards.label: F5 · 03

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• TTFT (time to first token): queueing + prefill. Dominated by prompt length.
  • TPOT / ITL (time per output token / inter-token latency): one decode step.
  • End-to-end latency ≈ TTFT + TPOT × (output tokens − 1).
  • Throughput: requests/s or output tokens/s across all users. Raising batch size raises throughput and usually raises each user's TPOT — the core serving trade-off.
  • Report percentiles (p50, p95, p99), never just the mean: tail latency is what users feel and what SLOs are written against.
  • Little's law: $L = \lambda W$ — requests in the system = arrival rate × time in system. At 20 req/s and 3 s per request, ~60 requests are in flight; that sets the batch and KV-cache capacity you need.

cards.cue: F5 — Serving systems and operations basics

cards.label: F5 · 04

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Prometheus scrapes /metrics endpoints on an interval and stores time series.
  • Metric types: counter (only goes up: requests, errors), gauge (up and down: queue depth, GPU memory), histogram (bucketed latencies).
  • Everyday PromQL:
rate(nv_inference_request_success[5m])                        # requests/s
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(latency_bucket[5m])))  # p99 latency
avg(DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL)                                     # GPU utilization
  • Grafana draws dashboards over Prometheus; Alertmanager routes alerts.
  • DCGM Exporter publishes GPU telemetry (utilization, memory, temperature, power, XID errors); Triton publishes its own metrics on port 8002.

cards.cue: F5 — Serving systems and operations basics

cards.label: F5 · 05

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• SLI: a measured ratio, e.g. fraction of requests with TTFT < 1 s.
  • SLO: the target, e.g. 99.5% over 30 days.
  • Error budget: $1 - \text{SLO}$. 99.9% over 30 days allows $0.001 \times 43{,}200 = 43.2$ minutes of badness.
  • Burn rate: how fast the budget is being spent relative to plan. A burn rate of 14.4 sustained for 1 hour consumes 2% of a 30-day budget — the classic fast-burn page.

cards.cue: F5 — Serving systems and operations basics

cards.label: F5 · 06

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Model registry: versioned artifacts with lineage (data, code, config, eval results).
  • Rolling update: replace replicas gradually; canary: send a small % of traffic to the new version and compare metrics; shadow: mirror traffic to the new version without returning its responses; A/B: split users and test a hypothesis statistically; blue/green: switch all traffic between two full environments.
  • Rollback must be one command: keep the previous artifact and config deployable.
  • Observability pillars: metrics (trends), logs (discrete events — redact PII), traces (a request's path across services, e.g. OpenTelemetry).

cards.label: F6 · 01

back.title: Notes
back.html:
From the confusion matrix (TP, FP, FN, TN):

  • Precision = TP / (TP + FP) — of what I flagged, how much was right.
  • Recall (true-positive rate) = TP / (TP + FN) — of what existed, how much I found.
  • F1 = harmonic mean $2PR/(P+R)$.
  • Accuracy misleads under class imbalance: 99% "not fraud" is 99% accurate and useless. Use precision/recall, F1, PR-AUC, or per-class metrics.
  • ROC-AUC — the probability a random positive outscores a random negative; threshold-free.
  • Calibration: do predicted confidences match observed frequencies? Measured with expected calibration error (ECE) or a reliability plot.

cards.cue: F6 — Statistics for evaluation, drift and fairness

cards.label: F6 · 02

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Every benchmark score is an estimate. For accuracy $\hat p$ on $n$ items the standard error is $\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$. At $\hat p = 0.8$, $n = 500$: SE ≈ 0.018, so a 95% confidence interval is about ±3.5 points. A 1.2-point gap is noise.
  • Bootstrap: resample the eval set with replacement ~1,000 times, recompute the metric, and take the 2.5th–97.5th percentiles as a CI. Works for any metric (BLEU, ROUGE, judge win rate).
  • Paired comparisons (both models on the same items) are far more sensitive than unpaired ones: use a paired bootstrap or McNemar's test on per-item correctness.
  • Multiple comparisons: testing 20 variants at α = 0.05 yields about one false "win". Correct for it (Bonferroni) or hold out a final test set.
  • A/B sample size: detecting a difference $\delta$ with 80% power at α = 0.05 needs roughly $n \approx 16\sigma^2/\delta^2$ per arm. Halving the effect you want to detect quadruples the traffic.

cards.cue: F6 — Statistics for evaluation, drift and fairness

cards.label: F6 · 03

back.title: Notes
back.html: Latency distributions are right-skewed; the mean is pulled up by the tail and still hides it. Report p50/p95/p99, compare the same percentiles across versions, and use enough requests for the tail (p99 needs thousands of samples to be stable).

cards.cue: F6 — Statistics for evaluation, drift and fairness

cards.label: F6 · 04

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Cohen's kappa corrects raw agreement for chance:

$$\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}$$

with observed agreement $p_o$ and chance agreement $p_e$. κ > 0.8 is strong, 0.6–0.8 substantial, < 0.4 weak — if humans can't agree, neither the rubric nor an LLM judge calibrated against it is trustworthy.

cards.cue: F6 — Statistics for evaluation, drift and fairness

cards.label: F6 · 05

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Population Stability Index (PSI) compares binned distributions of a feature (or of prompt embeddings / output lengths) between a reference window $e$ and a current window $a$:

$$\text{PSI} = \sum_i (a_i - e_i)\,\ln\frac{a_i}{e_i}$$

Rule of thumb: < 0.1 stable, 0.1–0.25 moderate shift, > 0.25 significant shift. - Kolmogorov–Smirnov test: maximum gap between two empirical CDFs, for continuous features. - KL / Jensen–Shannon divergence: JS is symmetric and bounded, handy for comparing token or topic distributions. - Data (covariate) drift changes $p(x)$ — detectable without labels. Concept drift changes $p(y\mid x)$ — needs labels or a quality proxy (feedback, judge scores).

cards.cue: F6 — Statistics for evaluation, drift and fairness

cards.label: F6 · 06

back.title: Notes
back.html:
For a protected attribute $A$ and prediction $\hat Y$:

  • Demographic parity: $P(\hat Y=1\mid A=a)$ equal across groups.
  • Equal opportunity: equal true-positive rates across groups.
  • Equalized odds: equal TPR and FPR across groups.

When base rates differ between groups, these criteria can't all hold at once; choose the one that matches the harm you care about and report it per segment.

cards.cue: F6 — Statistics for evaluation, drift and fairness

cards.label: F6 · Flashcard
cards.front: Precision vs recall in one line each?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Precision: of what I flagged, how much was right. Recall: of what existed, how much I found.

cards.label: F6 · Flashcard
cards.front: Why is accuracy misleading on imbalanced data?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Predicting the majority class scores high while missing every minority case; use precision/recall, F1 or PR-AUC.

cards.front: Standard error of an accuracy estimate p on n items?

back.title: Answer

back.title: Answer
back.html: Both models see the same items, which removes item-difficulty variance and makes differences far easier to detect.

cards.label: F6 · Flashcard
cards.front: Approximate per-arm A/B sample size for effect δ at 80% power, α=0.05?

back.title: Answer
back.html: n ≈ 16σ²/δ².

back.title: Answer
back.html: κ = (p_o − p_e)/(1 − p_e): observed agreement corrected for chance.

back.title: Answer
back.html: <0.1 stable, 0.1–0.25 moderate shift, >0.25 significant shift.

back.title: Answer
back.html: Data drift changes p(x) and needs no labels; concept drift changes p(y|x) and needs labels or a quality proxy.

back.title: Answer
back.html: Parity: equal positive-prediction rates. Equal opportunity: equal true-positive rates.

cards.label: F6 · Flashcard
cards.front: Why can't all fairness criteria hold at once?

back.title: Answer
back.html: When groups have different base rates, parity, equal opportunity and calibration conflict mathematically.

back.title: Answer
back.html: The probability that a random positive is scored above a random negative — threshold-free ranking quality.

back.title: Notes
back.html: A modern LLM is a stack of identical blocks writing into a shared residual stream. Each block has an attention sublayer (tokens exchange information) and an MLP sublayer (each token is transformed on its own). Three layouts exist — encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder–decoder — and almost everything else (positions, sampling, embeddings) is a choice made on top of that skeleton.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
def block(x):                       # x: [B, T, d]
    x = x + attn(rms_norm(x))       # tokens talk (causal mask in decoders)
    x = x + mlp(rms_norm(x))        # per-token feature transform
    return x
  • Pre-norm (norm inside the residual branch) is the modern default; it trains stably without the long warmup that post-norm needs.
  • MLP variants: classic GELU MLP ($d\to4d\to d$) or SwiGLU ($\text{SiLU}(xW_1)\odot xW_3$ then $W_2$), with hidden size ≈ $\tfrac{8}{3}d$ so the parameter count stays ≈ $8d^2$.
  • Mixture of Experts (MoE): replace the MLP with $E$ expert MLPs and a router that picks the top-$k$ per token. Total parameters grow with $E$; compute per token grows only with $k$. Mixtral 8×7B has ~47B total but ~13B active parameters per token.

cards.label: L01 · 03
cards.front: 2. Attention variants and why they matter for serving

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Variant K/V heads KV-cache size Used by
Multi-head (MHA) $h$ (one per query head) largest GPT-2, Llama-2-7B
Multi-query (MQA) 1 $h\times$ smaller PaLM, Falcon
Grouped-query (GQA) $g$ groups ($1<g<h$) $h/g\times$ smaller Llama-2-70B, Llama-3

GQA keeps most of MHA's quality while shrinking the KV cache — the main memory cost of long-context serving (Domain 4, verse 4.26). Cross-attention (queries from the decoder, keys/values from the encoder output) exists only in encoder–decoder models.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Attention is permutation-invariant, so order must be injected:

Method How Extrapolates past training length?
Sinusoidal (original) add fixed sin/cos vectors somewhat
Learned absolute add a trained vector per position no — hard maximum
RoPE rotate each (q, k) dimension pair by angle $m\theta_i$ for position $m$ with scaling tricks
ALiBi add $-\text{slope}\times\text{distance}$ to attention scores yes, well

RoPE makes $q_m\cdot k_n$ depend only on the offset $m-n$. Context extension methods (position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, YaRN) stretch RoPE's angles so a 4k-trained model can run at 32k+ with a short fine-tune.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Need Pick Why
Classification, NER, retrieval embeddings Encoder (BERT, RoBERTa, E5) bidirectional context, one forward pass
Open-ended generation, chat, code, agents Decoder (GPT, Llama, Nemotron) causal LM scales and generalizes
Translation, summarization with a clear input→output Encoder–decoder (T5, BART) encoder reads once; decoder cross-attends

Cost profile (Domain 8): encoders are cheapest (no generation loop); decoders pay a compute-bound prefill and a memory-bound decode per output token; encoder–decoders pay one encoder pass plus decoding.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel

# Encoder: masked mean pooling over the last hidden state
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
enc = AutoModel.from_pretrained("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
batch = tok(["GPUs are fast", "The cat sat"], padding=True, return_tensors="pt")
with torch.no_grad():
    h = enc(**batch).last_hidden_state                   # [B, T, d]
mask = batch["attention_mask"].unsqueeze(-1).float()
emb = (h * mask).sum(1) / mask.sum(1)                  # ignore padding
emb = torch.nn.functional.normalize(emb, dim=-1)

# Decoder: take the hidden state of the last real token (use LEFT padding)
tok_d = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2", padding_side="left")
tok_d.pad_token = tok_d.eos_token
dec = AutoModel.from_pretrained("gpt2")
b = tok_d(["GPUs are fast", "The cat sat"], padding=True, return_tensors="pt")
with torch.no_grad():
    last = dec(**b).last_hidden_state[:, -1, :]        # causal: only the last token saw everything

Why the last token? In a causal model only the final position has attended to the whole input. With right padding, position −1 is a pad token — the classic "all my decoder embeddings look the same" bug. Production retrieval uses models trained for embeddings (contrastive fine-tuning, Domain 5); NVIDIA serves these as NeMo Retriever embedding NIMs.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Worked example — logits $[2, 1, 0]$:

Temperature Probabilities
$T=0.5$ [0.867, 0.117, 0.016] — sharper
$T=1$ [0.665, 0.245, 0.090]
$T=2$ [0.506, 0.307, 0.186] — flatter

At $T=1$, top-p = 0.9 keeps the smallest set whose cumulative probability reaches 0.9: 0.665 → 0.910, so the first two tokens are kept and renormalized. Top-k = 1 is greedy.

  • Greedy: deterministic, repetitive on open-ended text.
  • Beam search: keeps the $b$ best partial sequences; good for translation/summarization with a length penalty; bland and repetitive for chat.
  • Repetition / frequency / presence penalties: push down logits of tokens already generated.
  • Typical logits-processor order (Hugging Face): repetition penalty → temperature → top-k → top-p → sample.
  • Speculative decoding: a small draft model proposes several tokens; the large model verifies them in one forward pass. The rejection-sampling acceptance rule means the output distribution is identical to the large model's, just faster.
  • temperature=0 in most APIs means greedy. Reproducibility also needs a fixed seed and deterministic kernels; batching can still change results slightly.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Megatron-Core / NeMo implement GPT, BERT, T5 and MoE models with fused kernels.
  • TensorRT-LLM and NIM expose temperature, top_p, top_k, repetition_penalty, beam_width/n, max_tokens, stop and seed on an OpenAI-compatible API.
  • cuDNN / FlashAttention kernels provide fused attention.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• "Which model for sentence classification with 20 ms latency?" → encoder.
  • "Decoder embeddings are identical for every input" → right padding; use left padding and the last non-pad token.
  • "Output is repetitive / too random" → adjust temperature, top-p, repetition penalty — not the model architecture.
  • "Model fails beyond its training length" → learned absolute positions; RoPE scaling or ALiBi extrapolate better.

back.title: Answer

back.title: Notes
back.html: Prompting is the cheapest way to adapt a model: no weights change. The domain covers four layers — (1) how to write the prompt, (2) how many examples to give, (3) how to make the model reason, and (4) how to wrap the model so its output is valid and grounded. It also includes the one training topic that belongs here: causal language modeling (2.3).

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Roles: system (rules, persona, format), user (task + data), assistant (prior turns or prefilled output).
  • Chat templates turn the role list into the exact special tokens the model was fine-tuned on (<|start_header_id|>, [INST], <|im_start|>). Using the wrong template quietly degrades quality — always call tokenizer.apply_chat_template(...).
  • Delimiters (XML tags, triple backticks) separate instructions from untrusted data.
  • Specificity beats cleverness: state the audience, format, length and what to do when information is missing ("If the answer is not in the context, say I don't know").

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Zero-shot: instruction only. Works well for instruction-tuned models on common tasks.
  • Few-shot: 2–8 input→output demonstrations. The model infers format and label space in context; no weights change (in-context learning).
  • Choosing exemplars: similar to the query (retrieve them by embedding), cover every label, balanced, and in the exact output format. Order matters — models over-weight the last examples (recency bias) and majority labels.
  • Cost: every exemplar is paid for on every request (tokens, TTFT). When examples stop fitting or stop helping, move to fine-tuning (Domain 5).

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Technique How When
Chain-of-thought (CoT) few-shot examples with worked reasoning multi-step math/logic on large models
Zero-shot CoT append "Let's think step by step" quick boost without exemplars
Self-consistency sample $k$ CoT paths at $T>0$, majority-vote the final answer accuracy matters more than cost ($k\times$ tokens)
ReAct interleave Thought → Action (tool call) → Observation tasks needing search, calculators, APIs
Tree of Thoughts search over branching partial solutions puzzles/planning, expensive
Test-time scaling spend more inference compute (longer reasoning, more samples, verifiers) reasoning models (o1/R1-style)

CoT helps mostly on large models; on small models it can hurt. Self-consistency needs sampling — greedy decoding gives the same path $k$ times.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Instead of hand-written text, train a few virtual token embeddings prepended to the input while the model stays frozen:

  • Prompt tuning: trainable embeddings at the input layer only.
  • P-tuning: a small prompt encoder (LSTM/MLP) generates the virtual tokens; NeMo supports it for multi-task adaptation.
  • Prefix tuning: trainable key/value prefixes at every layer.

These suit small labeled datasets and many tasks sharing one frozen model (each task stores only a tiny prompt). They are covered again under PEFT (Domain 5).

back.title: Notes
back.html:
The decoder is trained to predict token $t$ from tokens $<t$:

$$\mathcal{L} = -\sum_{t} \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t})$$

logits = model(input_ids).logits                 # [B, T, V]
shift_logits = logits[:, :-1, :]                 # predict position t+1 from t
shift_labels = input_ids[:, 1:].clone()
shift_labels[prompt_mask[:, 1:]] = -100          # SFT: don't train on the prompt
loss = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(
    shift_logits.reshape(-1, shift_logits.size(-1)), shift_labels.reshape(-1),
    ignore_index=-100)
  • Teacher forcing: during training the model always sees the true previous tokens, which is why all positions train in parallel.
  • Loss masking (label −100) on prompt and padding tokens for instruction tuning.
  • Packing concatenates short examples into full-length sequences (with document masks or position resets) so no compute is wasted on padding.
  • Hugging Face models shift labels internally when you pass labels=input_ids — don't shift twice.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Asking for JSON in the prompt works most of the time. Production systems need always:

  1. Constrained (guided) decoding: compile a JSON schema, regex or grammar into a state machine and, at every step, mask the logits of tokens that would break it. The output is guaranteed to parse. Available in NIM / TensorRT-LLM / vLLM (backends such as XGrammar and Outlines) as guided_json, guided_regex, guided_choice.
  2. Validation layer: parse and validate against a schema (e.g. Pydantic); check business rules (IDs exist, numbers in range); on failure, retry with the error message in the prompt, fall back, or escalate.
  3. Grounding checks: verify that claims are supported by retrieved context; refuse or abstain when not.
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError

class Ticket(BaseModel):
    category: str
    priority: int

def extract(text, llm, retries=2):
    prompt = f"Return JSON with category and priority (1-4).\n<ticket>{text}</ticket>"
    for _ in range(retries + 1):
        raw = llm(prompt, guided_json=Ticket.model_json_schema(), temperature=0)
        try:
            t = Ticket.model_validate_json(raw)
            if 1 <= t.priority <= 4:
                return t
            error = "priority must be 1-4"
        except ValidationError as e:
            error = str(e)
        prompt += f"\nYour last answer was invalid: {error}. Try again."
    raise RuntimeError("extraction failed")

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Why models hallucinate: they generate plausible continuations, not verified facts; knowledge is frozen at training time and rare facts are poorly stored.
  • Mitigations, cheapest first: instruct abstention, lower temperature for factual tasks, supply context (RAG), require citations, verify with a second pass or a fact-checking rail, and fine-tune for faithfulness when needed.
  • RAG pipeline: chunk documents (e.g. 256–1,024 tokens with overlap) → embed → vector index → retrieve top-k for the query → (optionally) rerank with a cross-encoder → put the passages in the prompt → generate with citations. Quality depends on retrieval: measure context precision/recall (Domain 6). Models attend less to the middle of very long contexts ("lost in the middle"), so rank the best passages first.
  • Prompt injection: instructions hidden in user input or retrieved documents ("ignore previous instructions…"). Defenses: delimit untrusted data, least-privilege tools, input/output rails (Domain 10), and never let retrieved text grant permissions.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• NIM for LLMs: OpenAI-compatible chat API with guided decoding parameters.
  • NeMo Retriever embedding and reranking NIMs for RAG; NeMo Guardrails for topic, injection and grounding rails.
  • NeMo for p-tuning / prompt tuning and SFT with loss masking.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Few examples, a few hundred labels, one frozen model serving many tasks → prompt learning (p-tuning) or LoRA, not full fine-tuning.
  • "JSON is sometimes malformed" → constrained decoding + a validation/retry wrapper, not just a stronger prompt.
  • "Model invents policy details" → RAG with citations and an abstention instruction.
  • Self-consistency questions always involve sampling several reasoning paths and voting.

back.title: Notes
back.html: Model quality is bounded by data quality. The domain has three parts: clean and curate (remove junk, duplicates, PII; understand distributions and imbalance), organize (formats, splits without leakage, sharding), and tokenize (pick or train a tokenizer and vocabulary size).

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Normalize text: Unicode NFC/NFKC, fix mojibake (e.g. with ftfy), strip boilerplate HTML, normalize whitespace; keep casing unless the model is uncased.
  • Missing data: drop rows when rare and random; impute (median, mode, "unknown" token) when informative; never impute using statistics computed on the test split.
  • Scaling (tabular features feeding classifiers or reward models): standardize (z-score) or min–max; fit the scaler on train only.
  • Class imbalance: look at label counts first. Fix with class-weighted loss, over/under-sampling, focal loss, or more data; judge with per-class precision/recall and F1, not accuracy.
  • Distributions to inspect: document length, tokens per document, language mix, source/domain mix, label balance, duplicate rate, toxicity/quality score histograms.
  • GPU EDA: RAPIDS cuDF runs pandas-style dataframe work on the GPU; python -m cudf.pandas script.py accelerates existing pandas code with no changes.

cards.label: L03 · 03
cards.front: 2. Curation at scale with NeMo Curator

back.title: Notes
back.html:
A typical pretraining/fine-tuning curation pipeline (NeMo Curator runs each stage on GPUs with Dask/RAPIDS):

  1. Download and extract (Common Crawl WARC → text, PDFs, code).
  2. Language identification (fastText lid) and splitting by language.
  3. Heuristic quality filters — Gopher/C4-style rules: word count bounds, mean word length, symbol-to-word ratio, fraction of lines ending in punctuation, repeated n-gram/line fractions, "lorem ipsum"/boilerplate markers.
  4. Classifier quality filters — a fastText or small transformer classifier trained to tell "reference-quality" text from random web text (FineWeb-Edu-style educational scores).
  5. Deduplication — exact (hash of normalized text), fuzzy (MinHash + LSH), semantic (embedding clustering, SemDeDup).
  6. PII redaction and safety filtering — detect emails, phone numbers, IDs; mask or drop; filter toxic content.
  7. Decontamination — remove documents that overlap benchmark test sets (e.g. 13-gram matches) so evaluation isn't inflated.
  8. Blend and shuffle — choose the mix of sources (web, code, books, math) by weight.

MinHash + LSH in one paragraph. The probability that two documents share the same MinHash value equals their Jaccard similarity $s$ (of shingle sets). With $b$ bands of $r$ hashes each, a pair becomes a candidate with probability $1-(1-s^r)^b$, an S-curve whose threshold is ≈ $(1/b)^{1/r}$. Tune $b$ and $r$ to target near-duplicates at $s\approx0.8$.

Why dedup matters: duplicates waste compute, increase memorization (and privacy leakage), and skew evaluation when test items leak into training.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Formats: JSONL, one record per line. SFT records usually look like {"messages": [{"role": "user", ...}, {"role": "assistant", ...}]} or {"input": ..., "output": ...}; preference data has prompt, chosen, rejected.
  • Splits without leakage: deduplicate before splitting; split by document, user, conversation or time, not by random line; stratify labels; keep a frozen test set that no one tunes against.
  • Scale: Megatron/NeMo convert tokenized data to memory-mapped indexed datasets (.bin + .idx) and shard across files so many workers stream in parallel.
  • Packing: concatenate short samples up to the sequence length to avoid padding waste; use attention masks or position resets so samples don't attend to each other.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Why subwords: word vocabularies explode and can't handle new words; characters make sequences too long. Subwords give a fixed vocabulary with no out-of-vocabulary words.

BPE (byte-pair encoding) — worked example. Corpus: low×5, lower×2, newest×6, widest×3, split into characters. Count adjacent pairs and merge the most frequent:

  1. e s (6 + 3 = 9) → es
  2. es t (9) → est
  3. est </w> (9) → est</w>
  4. l o (7) → lo
  5. lo w (7) → low …

The learned merge list, applied in order, is the tokenizer. Byte-level BPE (GPT-2, Llama 3) starts from the 256 bytes, so any string is encodable and there is never an unknown token.

WordPiece (BERT) merges the pair that most increases likelihood: $\text{score}(a,b) = \frac{\text{count}(ab)}{\text{count}(a)\,\text{count}(b)}$, and marks word-internal pieces with ##.

Unigram LM (T5, often via SentencePiece) starts from a large vocabulary and prunes the pieces whose removal least hurts corpus likelihood; it can sample alternative segmentations (subword regularization).

SentencePiece is a library that trains BPE or Unigram directly on raw text, treating whitespace as a symbol (▁), so it's language-agnostic (no pre-tokenizer needed for Chinese or Japanese).

Vocabulary size trade-off:

Larger vocabulary Smaller vocabulary
fewer tokens per word (lower fertility) → shorter sequences, more text per context longer sequences, more compute per document
bigger embedding and output layers ($V\times d$ each) smaller model
rare tokens get few training updates better-trained embeddings

Worked example: $V = 128{,}256$ and $d = 4096$ → 525M parameters in the embedding table (and the same again in an untied output layer).

Fertility (tokens per word) varies by language: English-centric vocabularies can spend 2–4× more tokens on Hindi or Telugu text, which raises cost and shortens the effective context. Measure fertility on your target data before choosing a tokenizer.

Special tokens: BOS/EOS, PAD, UNK (WordPiece/Unigram), [CLS]/[SEP]/[MASK] (BERT), chat-role tokens. Adding tokens means resizing embeddings (model.resize_token_embeddings(len(tokenizer))) and training them.

from tokenizers import Tokenizer, models, trainers, pre_tokenizers
tok = Tokenizer(models.BPE(unk_token=None))
tok.pre_tokenizer = pre_tokenizers.ByteLevel(add_prefix_space=False)
trainer = trainers.BpeTrainer(vocab_size=32000, special_tokens=["<s>", "</s>", "<pad>"])
tok.train(["corpus.txt"], trainer)
print(len(tok.encode("Tokenization fertility matters").ids))

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• NeMo Curator: GPU-accelerated extraction, language ID, heuristic and classifier filters, exact/fuzzy/semantic dedup, PII redaction, decontamination.
  • RAPIDS cuDF / cuML: GPU dataframes and clustering for EDA and semantic dedup.
  • NeMo / Megatron data tools: preprocess JSONL into indexed .bin/.idx datasets.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• "Validation score is suspiciously high" → leakage: duplicates across splits or split by line instead of by document/user.
  • "Model memorizes and regurgitates text" → deduplicate (fuzzy) and redact PII.
  • "Same text costs far more tokens in language X" → tokenizer fertility; retrain or extend the vocabulary.
  • BPE = frequency of pairs; WordPiece = likelihood score; Unigram = prune from large.

cards.label: L04 · 01

back.title: Notes
back.html: Optimization shrinks memory and latency while keeping accuracy. Three families compose: quantization (fewer bits per number), pruning/sparsity (fewer numbers), and distillation (a smaller model that imitates a larger one). Around them sit the inference-engine tools (TensorRT, TensorRT-LLM, KV caching, windowed attention) and the experimental discipline to prove a change helped (hyperparameter search, ablations).

cards.cue: L04 — Model Optimization (17%, the heaviest domain)

cards.label: L04 · 02

back.title: Notes
back.html:
$$q = \text{round}(x/s) + z, \qquad \hat x = s\,(q - z)$$

Symmetric INT8 (weights): $x = [-1.23, 0.31, 2.54]$, $\max|x| = 2.54$ → $s = 2.54/127 = 0.02$, $z = 0$ → $q = [-62, 16, 127]$ → $\hat x = [-1.24, 0.32, 2.54]$ (error ≤ $s/2$ = 0.01).

Asymmetric UINT8 (skewed activations in $[-0.5, 3.5]$): $s = 4/255 \approx 0.0157$, $z = \text{round}(0.5/s) = 32$. Real 0 maps exactly to $q = 32$, so zero padding and ReLU outputs stay exact.

Granularity: one scale per tensor (coarse, cheap) → per output channel (standard for weights) → per group of e.g. 128 weights (needed for INT4) → per block of 16/32 (NVFP4, MXFP4).

Outliers are the whole problem. Beyond ~6.7B parameters, a few activation channels reach values ~20× larger than the rest (LLM.int8 paper). A per-tensor INT8 scale sized for them leaves ordinary values with only a handful of levels. The fixes: keep outlier channels in FP16 (LLM.int8), migrate them into the weights (SmoothQuant), use finer granularity, or use FP8's wider dynamic range.

Memory for weights of a 70B model: BF16 140 GB · FP8/INT8 70 GB · INT4 35 GB (plus a few % for scales) · NVFP4 ≈ 35–40 GB.

cards.cue: L04 — Model Optimization (17%, the heaviest domain)

cards.label: L04 · 03
cards.front: 2. What to quantize, for which bottleneck

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Bottleneck Quantize Why it helps
Memory-bound decode, small batch weights only (INT4 AWQ/GPTQ, W4A16) fewer bytes read per token; math stays FP16
Compute-bound prefill / large batch weights + activations (FP8, INT8 SmoothQuant, W8A8) GEMMs run on low-precision Tensor Cores
Long context / many users KV cache (FP8/INT8) cache is the dominant memory at long context

Hardware: INT8 on Turing/Ampere+; FP8 on Ada/Hopper+ (not A100); NVFP4 on Blackwell.

cards.cue: L04 — Model Optimization (17%, the heaviest domain)

cards.label: L04 · 04

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• PTQ (post-training quantization): no retraining. Run a few hundred representative samples through the model to measure ranges (calibration), compute scales, done in minutes.
  • Calibrators: max/min-max (outlier-sensitive), percentile (clip e.g. 99.99%), entropy/KL (TensorRT's default for INT8 — pick the clipping threshold that minimizes KL between the FP32 and quantized distributions), MSE.
  • QAT (quantization-aware training): insert fake-quant (quantize→dequantize) ops, fine-tune, and backprop with the straight-through estimator so the weights learn to tolerate rounding. Needed when PTQ loses too much (INT4 W+A, very sensitive tasks).
  • Decision rule: FP8 / INT8 weight-only → PTQ almost always fine; INT4 weights → use GPTQ/AWQ (still PTQ); aggressive W4A4/INT4 activations or accuracy-critical → QAT.
  • Measure the trade-off: accuracy on the task metric (not just perplexity), throughput, latency and memory, on the same eval set before and after.

cards.cue: L04 — Model Optimization (17%, the heaviest domain)

cards.label: L04 · 05

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Method Quantizes Trick
GPTQ weights (INT4/INT3, groups of 128) quantize one column at a time and update the remaining weights with the inverse Hessian ($H = 2XX^\top$ from calibration inputs) to cancel the error
AWQ weights (INT4) ~1% of weight channels matter most — those that see large activations; scale them up before quantizing to protect them; no backprop
SmoothQuant weights + activations (W8A8) per channel $s_j = \max|X_j|^\alpha / \max|W_j|^{1-\alpha}$ (α ≈ 0.5); divide activations by $s$, multiply weights by $s$ — the product is unchanged but activations become easy to quantize
FP8 (Transformer Engine / ModelOpt) weights + activations per-tensor scales from amax history (delayed scaling)

cards.cue: L04 — Model Optimization (17%, the heaviest domain)

cards.label: L04 · 06

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Unstructured (zero individual weights by magnitude): high sparsity possible, but dense hardware gets no speedup.
  • Structured (remove heads, channels, whole layers): smaller dense model, real speedup everywhere, bigger accuracy hit → retrain or distill.
  • 2:4 semi-structured: exactly 2 zeros in every group of 4 weights. Ampere+ Sparse Tensor Cores skip them for up to 2× GEMM throughput (end-to-end gains are smaller). Prune, then fine-tune to recover (NVIDIA ASP / TensorRT Model Optimizer).
  • One-shot LLM pruning: SparseGPT (Hessian-based reconstruction), Wanda (score = $|W|\cdot\|X\|$, no weight update).
  • Sparsity and INT8 compose: sparse INT8 engines in TensorRT.

cards.cue: L04 — Model Optimization (17%, the heaviest domain)

cards.label: L04 · 07

back.title: Notes
back.html:
$$\mathcal{L} = \alpha\,T^2\,\text{KL}\big(p^{teacher}_T \,\|\, p^{student}_T\big) + (1-\alpha)\,\text{CE}(y, p^{student})$$

  • The soft targets at temperature $T$ carry "dark knowledge" (which wrong answers are almost right); $T^2$ keeps gradient scales comparable.
  • Logit distillation (above), feature distillation (match hidden states), sequence-level distillation (fine-tune the student on teacher-generated outputs — the common LLM route, i.e. synthetic data).
  • DistilBERT: 40% smaller, 60% faster, ~97% of BERT's GLUE score.
  • NVIDIA Minitron: prune a trained model (width and depth) and distill it back using a small fraction of the original training tokens — e.g. Nemotron-4 15B → 8B and 4B.

cards.cue: L04 — Model Optimization (17%, the heaviest domain)

cards.label: L04 · 08

back.title: Notes
back.html:
TensorRT takes an ONNX model or network definition and builds an engine: layer and tensor fusion, precision selection (FP16/INT8/FP8), kernel auto-tuning for the exact GPU, and optimization profiles (min/opt/max shapes) for dynamic inputs. An engine is tied to the GPU architecture and TensorRT version — rebuild when either changes.

trtexec --onnx=model.onnx --fp16 --saveEngine=model.plan \
        --minShapes=input:1x128 --optShapes=input:8x128 --maxShapes=input:32x128

TensorRT-LLM adds LLM-specific pieces: fused attention (FMHA/XQA) kernels, paged KV cache, in-flight batching, tensor/pipeline parallel engines, quantization via TensorRT Model Optimizer (FP8, INT4-AWQ, W4A8, NVFP4, FP8 KV cache), speculative decoding.

# VERIFY flags against your TensorRT-LLM version (they change often)
python examples/quantization/quantize.py --model_dir ./llama --qformat fp8 \
       --kv_cache_dtype fp8 --calib_size 512 --output_dir ./ckpt_fp8
trtllm-build --checkpoint_dir ./ckpt_fp8 --output_dir ./engine \
       --max_batch_size 64 --max_input_len 4096 --max_seq_len 8192

Newer releases also offer a Python LLM API and trtllm-serve (PyTorch backend) that skip the explicit engine-build step.

cards.cue: L04 — Model Optimization (17%, the heaviest domain)

cards.label: L04 · 09

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Per token, the cache holds keys and values for every layer:

$$\text{bytes/token} = 2 \times n_{layers} \times n_{kv\,heads} \times d_{head} \times \text{bytes}$$

Model Layers KV heads $d_{head}$ FP16 bytes/token 4k-token sequence
Llama-2-7B (MHA) 32 32 128 512 KB 2 GB
Llama-3-8B (GQA) 32 8 128 128 KB 0.5 GB
Llama-3-70B (GQA) 80 8 128 320 KB 1.25 GB

Multiply by concurrent sequences to size a server. Levers: GQA/MQA, FP8 KV cache (½), paged allocation (no fragmentation), prefix reuse, and bounded attention:

  • Sliding-window attention (Mistral, Longformer): attend to the last $W$ tokens only, so the cache is a fixed-size rolling buffer.
  • StreamingLLM / attention sinks: keep the first few tokens plus a recent window; the model stays stable on unbounded streams without retraining.

cards.cue: L04 — Model Optimization (17%, the heaviest domain)

cards.label: L04 · 10

back.title: Notes
back.html: BERT masks ~15% of tokens; of those, 80% become [MASK], 10% a random token, 10% stay unchanged (so the model can't rely on seeing [MASK]). Next-sentence prediction (NSP) was dropped by RoBERTa as unhelpful; RoBERTa also used dynamic masking, more data and bigger batches.

cards.cue: L04 — Model Optimization (17%, the heaviest domain)

cards.label: L04 · 11

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Schedules: warmup then cosine/linear decay; tune peak LR on a log scale.
  • Batch size: linear scaling rule with warmup; watch the critical batch size.
  • Search strategies: grid (few dims only), random (better than grid in high dimensions), Bayesian (TPE/GP model of the objective), Hyperband/ASHA (successive halving: stop bad trials early), PBT (population-based training: copy weights and perturb hyperparameters of good trials during training).
  • Distributed search: Ray Tune or Optuna with a shared study database; one trial per GPU or node; a fixed budget. NeMo's Auto Configurator searches parallelism and micro-batch settings for throughput.
  • Ablations: change one factor at a time, fix everything else (data, eval set, decoding settings, seeds), run ≥3 seeds and report mean ± std. Decoding settings (beam width, temperature) change metrics too — ablate them separately from model changes.
  • Beam search for evaluation: add a length penalty (GNMT: $((5+|y|)/6)^\alpha$) so beams don't favor short outputs; memory and compute scale with beam width.

cards.cue: L04 — Model Optimization (17%, the heaviest domain)

cards.label: L04 · 12

back.title: Notes
back.html: TensorRT · TensorRT-LLM · TensorRT Model Optimizer (PTQ, QAT, sparsity, distillation) · Transformer Engine (FP8/FP4 training) · NeMo (distillation, Minitron pruning, Auto Configurator) · Triton/NIM for serving the result.

cards.cue: L04 — Model Optimization (17%, the heaviest domain)

cards.label: L04 · 13

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• The bottleneck decides the method: memory-bound → weight-only; compute-bound → W+A.
  • "Accuracy collapsed after INT8 PTQ" → better calibration data/method first, then SmoothQuant/per-channel, then QAT.
  • "Unstructured 50% sparsity gave no speedup" → dense kernels ignore scattered zeros; use 2:4 or structured pruning.
  • "Engine built on A100 is slow/invalid on H100" → rebuild per GPU architecture.
  • "KV cache OOM at long context" → GQA, FP8 KV cache, paged KV, sliding window.

cards.cue: L04 — Model Optimization (17%, the heaviest domain)

cards.label: 4.02 · Flashcard
cards.front: Symmetric INT8 scale for weights with max |x| = 2.54?

cards.label: 4.02 · Flashcard
cards.front: Why use an asymmetric zero-point for activations?

back.title: Answer
back.html: It maps the real skewed range onto all 256 levels and represents real 0 exactly.

cards.label: 4.03 · Flashcard
cards.front: Why does INT4 need per-group scales?

back.title: Answer
back.html: With only 16 levels, one scale per tensor or channel can't cover outliers; groups of ~128 localize the range.

back.title: Answer
back.html: Quantize weight columns one at a time and use the inverse Hessian from calibration activations to update the remaining weights and cancel the error.

cards.label: 4.14 · Flashcard
cards.front: How does AWQ choose what to protect?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Weight channels that see large activations (~1%) are salient; it scales them up before quantization.

back.title: Answer
back.html: s_j = max|X_j|^α / max|W_j|^(1−α), α≈0.5; divide activations and multiply weights by s.

cards.label: 4.10 · Flashcard

back.title: Notes
back.html: Fine-tuning changes weights. Pick the objective (SFT, preference optimization, RL), the parameter budget (full vs PEFT), and the guard rails on the process (early stopping, metrics, forgetting and hallucination checks). The exam rewards knowing which combination fits a scenario's data, hardware and goal.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Stage Data What it learns
Pretraining trillions of raw tokens language and knowledge
SFT / instruction tuning prompt → ideal response (thousands–millions) follow instructions, format, persona
Preference optimization (RLHF-PPO, DPO) prompt + chosen + rejected what humans prefer (helpful, harmless)
RL with verifiable rewards (GRPO) prompts + an automatic checker reasoning that reaches correct answers

SFT trains the causal-LM loss on responses only (prompt tokens masked). Small, clean, diverse data beats large noisy data (LIMA: ~1,000 curated examples).

back.title: Notes
back.html:
1. SFT a policy $\pi_{SFT}$.
  2. Train a reward model on preference pairs with the Bradley–Terry loss $-\log\sigma(r_\phi(x,y_w) - r_\phi(x,y_l))$.
  3. Optimize the policy with PPO on $r_\phi(x,y) - \beta\,\text{KL}(\pi_\theta\,\|\,\pi_{ref})$.

PPO keeps four models in play: policy, frozen reference, reward model and value (critic) network — expensive in memory and fiddly to tune. The KL term stops reward hacking (exploiting reward-model flaws, e.g. ever-longer or sycophantic answers).

back.title: Notes
back.html:
DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop. It treats the policy's log-ratio to the reference as an implicit reward and trains directly on preference pairs:

$$\mathcal{L}_{DPO} = -\log\sigma\!\Big(\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w|x)}{\pi_{ref}(y_w|x)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l|x)}{\pi_{ref}(y_l|x)}\Big)$$

  • Only policy + frozen reference; a supervised-style loss; stable.
  • $\beta$ (≈0.1) sets how far the policy may drift from the reference: larger β = stay closer.
  • Works offline on a fixed preference dataset; can't explore new behaviors the way online RL can. Variants: IPO, KTO (unpaired thumbs-up/down), ORPO, SimPO.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Group Relative Policy Optimization (DeepSeekMath, DeepSeek-R1):

  1. For each prompt, sample a group of $G$ responses.
  2. Score each with a reward — often a rule-based verifier (is the math answer right? do the unit tests pass?).
  3. Advantage $A_i = \frac{r_i - \text{mean}(r)}{\text{std}(r)}$ — the group is the baseline.
  4. PPO-style clipped update plus a KL penalty to the reference.

No value network → far less memory than PPO, and verifiable rewards resist reward hacking. Best for reasoning, math and code where correctness can be checked.

Choose When
SFT you have ideal responses; first step always
DPO you have preference pairs; want simple, stable alignment
PPO online RL with a learned reward; maximum control, maximum cost
GRPO rewards are checkable (math, code, format); want RL without a critic

back.title: Notes
back.html:
LoRA: freeze $W_0$, learn $\Delta W = \frac{\alpha}{r}BA$ with $B$ zero-initialized.

  • Worked example: Llama-2-7B, $r=16$ on $W_q,W_k,W_v,W_o$ (4096×4096) in 32 layers → $16\cdot 8192 \cdot 4 \cdot 32 \approx 16.8$M trainable parameters (0.25% of 7B). Optimizer state becomes negligible; memory is dominated by the frozen BF16 base (14 GB) and activations.
  • Typical settings: $r$ = 8–64, $\alpha$ = $r$ to $2r$, dropout 0.05, target all attention and MLP projections for best quality. LR is higher than full fine-tuning (~1e-4 to 2e-4).
  • Merge $W_0 + \frac{\alpha}{r}BA$ for zero inference overhead, or keep adapters separate to serve many.
  • QLoRA: base weights in 4-bit NF4 (NormalFloat, suited to normally distributed weights), double quantization of the scales, paged optimizers to survive memory spikes; LoRA adapters train in BF16. Fine-tunes a 65B model on one 48 GB GPU.
  • Multi-LoRA serving: one base model in GPU memory, many small adapters selected per request and batched together (supported by NIM and TensorRT-LLM).

Other PEFT methods:

Method Trains Inference cost Notes
LoRA / QLoRA low-rank ΔW none once merged default choice
Adapters (Houlsby) bottleneck MLPs inserted in each block extra layers → latency can't be merged
Prompt tuning / P-tuning virtual token embeddings longer input tiny per task; weaker on small models
Prefix tuning / P-tuning v2 key/value prefixes at every layer longer KV stronger than input-only prompts
Full fine-tuning everything none best ceiling; most memory; highest forgetting risk

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Train a bi-encoder so that a query and its relevant passage are close:

$$\mathcal{L} = -\log\frac{\exp(\text{sim}(q,p^+)/\tau)}{\exp(\text{sim}(q,p^+)/\tau) + \sum_j \exp(\text{sim}(q,p_j^-)/\tau)}$$

  • In-batch negatives: every other passage in the batch is a negative, so bigger batches give more negatives.
  • Hard negatives (similar but wrong, mined with BM25 or the current model) teach fine distinctions.
  • Temperature $\tau$ ≈ 0.01–0.1. Triplet loss is the margin-based alternative.
  • Bi-encoder (embed separately, fast ANN search) for retrieval; cross-encoder (score the pair jointly, slow, accurate) for reranking the top-k.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Early stopping: evaluate every N steps, keep the best checkpoint, stop after patience evaluations without improvement.
  • Overfitting signals: validation loss rising while training loss falls; outputs copy training phrasing; general benchmarks drop.
  • Metrics per phase:
Phase Watch
Pretraining train/val loss, perplexity, tokens/s, MFU
SFT val loss on held-out responses, task metrics (EM, F1, ROUGE, pass@k), instruction-following
Preference / RL reward and reward margin, KL to reference, win rate vs baseline, response length
Pre-deployment regression suite, safety evals, latency/cost

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Fine-tune on grounded examples (answer from supplied context, cite it) and include unanswerable examples whose target is "I don't know".
  • RAFT: train with the relevant document plus distractors so the model learns to use context selectively.
  • Preference pairs where the factual answer beats a fluent fabrication (DPO).
  • Be careful teaching new facts through SFT: research finds it can increase hallucination; put fresh knowledge in retrieval instead.
  • Assess impact before shipping: target-task metrics, general benchmarks (catch forgetting), safety/refusal behaviour, and a fixed regression set — always against the base model with identical decoding settings.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• NeMo Framework / NeMo AutoModel: SFT and PEFT (LoRA, QLoRA, adapters, p-tuning) at scale with Megatron parallelism.
  • NeMo RL (successor to NeMo-Aligner): DPO, PPO/RLHF, GRPO — VERIFY current names.
  • NeMo Customizer microservice: managed fine-tuning jobs; NIM serves LoRA adapters.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• One 24–48 GB GPU and a 13B–70B model → QLoRA.
  • Many customers, one base model → multi-LoRA serving.
  • Preference data, no RL infrastructure → DPO. Verifiable math/code rewards → GRPO.
  • "Embedding search returns near-misses" → contrastive fine-tuning with hard negatives, then a cross-encoder reranker.
  • "Fine-tuned model forgot general skills" → lower LR / fewer steps, mix in general data, LoRA, KL regularization.

back.title: Answer

back.title: Answer

back.title: Answer
back.html: NF4 4-bit base weights, double quantization of the scales, paged optimizers (adapters in BF16).

cards.front: Why can't Houlsby adapters be merged like LoRA?

back.title: Answer
back.html: They're extra nonlinear layers in the forward path, not an additive change to an existing weight matrix.

cards.label: 5.18 · Flashcard

back.title: Answer

cards.label: 5.23 · Flashcard
cards.front: Where should brand-new facts go — SFT or retrieval?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Retrieval; teaching unknown facts via SFT can increase hallucination.

back.title: Notes
back.html: Evaluation answers three questions: is the model good at the task (quality metrics), where and why does it fail (error analysis), and is it fast and cheap enough on this platform (performance benchmarking). Each needs a fixed, versioned eval set and a repeatable harness.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Family Examples Good for Blind spot
Likelihood perplexity, bits-per-byte pretraining progress, same-tokenizer comparisons says nothing about usefulness
N-gram overlap BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, chrF translation, summarization with references paraphrases score low
Embedding similarity BERTScore, cosine to reference semantic overlap can reward fluent wrong answers
Task accuracy exact match, F1 (QA), pass@k (code), multiple-choice accuracy closed-form answers needs a gold answer
Judges LLM-as-judge, human rating, pairwise win rate open-ended quality, helpfulness, safety bias, cost, variance
RAG metrics Ragas faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision/recall retrieval + generation pipelines depend on judge LLM quality

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Candidate "the cat sat on the mat", reference "the cat is on the mat":

  • BLEU (precision-oriented): clipped unigram precision 5/6, bigram precision 3/5 (the cat, on the, the mat), … combined as a geometric mean times a brevity penalty $BP = e^{1-r/c}$ when the candidate is shorter than the reference (here 1). Without BP, a one-word output could score perfect precision.
  • ROUGE-L (recall-oriented): the longest common subsequence is the cat on the mat (5 tokens) → recall 5/6, precision 5/6, F ≈ 0.83. ROUGE-N counts n-gram recall.
  • METEOR aligns unigrams using exact, stem and synonym matches, weights recall over precision and penalizes fragmented alignments — closer to human judgment than BLEU.

Choose: translation → BLEU/chrF (+ COMET if allowed); summarization → ROUGE; either with paraphrase tolerance → METEOR or BERTScore; anything open-ended → judges.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Generate $n$ samples per problem, count $c$ that pass the tests, and use the unbiased estimator

$$\text{pass@}k = 1 - \frac{\binom{n-c}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}}.$$

With $n=10$, $c=3$: pass@1 = 0.3.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Modes: single-answer grading against a rubric (1–10), pairwise comparison (A vs B), reference-guided grading.
  • Known biases and controls:
  • Position bias → evaluate both orders (A/B and B/A) and count only consistent wins.
  • Verbosity bias → instruct to ignore length; compare length-controlled win rates.
  • Self-preference → use a judge from a different model family.
  • Weak rubric → specific criteria with examples of each score.
  • Validate the judge: score a sample that humans also labeled and report agreement (accuracy or Cohen's κ). Low human–judge agreement means the judge can't be trusted yet.
  • Human evaluation stays the gold standard for high-stakes launches: clear guidelines, multiple raters, inter-annotator agreement.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Metric Measures Needs
Faithfulness fraction of answer claims supported by the retrieved context question, answer, contexts
Answer relevancy how directly the answer addresses the question question, answer
Context precision are the relevant chunks ranked at the top? question, contexts, reference
Context recall does the retrieved context contain what the reference answer needs? contexts, reference

Low faithfulness → generation problem (hallucination). Low context recall → retrieval problem (chunking, embeddings, top-k). Diagnose the component before changing the model.

back.title: Notes
back.html: MMLU (57-subject multiple choice), GSM8K (grade-school math), HumanEval/MBPP (code, pass@k), HellaSwag/ARC (commonsense), TruthfulQA (imitative falsehoods), IFEval (verifiable instruction following), MT-Bench (multi-turn, judged), Chatbot Arena (human pairwise votes → Bradley–Terry/Elo ratings). Public benchmarks can leak into training data (contamination) — pair them with private, task-specific evals.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
1. Collect failures from the eval set and production samples.
  2. Read them and tag each with a cause — open coding — until categories stabilize.
  3. Typical taxonomy: retrieval miss · wrong reasoning · hallucinated fact · format/schema violation · ignored instruction · over-refusal · unsafe output · truncation/length · tokenization/language issue.
  4. Count per category and slice (by language, input length, customer, topic).
  5. Fix the biggest, cheapest bucket first; add the examples to the regression set.

back.title: Notes
back.html: Keep everything fixed except the thing being compared: model version and precision, prompt set and input/output lengths, decoding parameters, tokenizer, concurrency, warmup. Measure TTFT, inter-token latency, output tokens/s and requests/s at several concurrency levels, report p50/p95/p99, and plot throughput against latency. NVIDIA GenAI-Perf (now evolving into AIPerf) and perf_analyzer generate this load against Triton, NIM or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint; MLPerf Inference defines standardized scenarios.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Harness: versioned datasets + prompt templates + decoding config + metrics + a results store. Open-source: EleutherAI lm-evaluation-harness; NVIDIA: NeMo Evaluator (academic benchmarks, custom datasets, LLM-as-judge, RAG and agent evals as a microservice/SDK).
  • CI/CD gate: every candidate model runs the suite; block promotion if a key metric regresses beyond a tolerance (with confidence intervals, not single numbers).
  • Scale: run evals in parallel against a served endpoint (NIM/Triton), cache generations, and re-score cheaply when only the metric changes.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• "BLEU rewards a one-word output" → the brevity penalty is missing.
  • "Judge always prefers the first answer" → position bias; swap and aggregate.
  • "RAG answers are fluent but unsupported" → faithfulness metric; fix grounding.
  • "Scores differ between two platforms" → check that decoding params, precision and prompts were identical before blaming the hardware.
  • Perplexity comparisons across different tokenizers are invalid.

back.title: Answer
back.html: Faithfulness: answer claims supported by context (generation). Context recall: context covers the reference answer (retrieval).

back.title: Answer
back.html: 1 − C(n−c, k)/C(n, k) for n samples with c correct.

cards.label: 6.11 · Flashcard

back.title: Answer

cards.label: 6.14 · Flashcard
cards.front: What makes an eval a CI gate?

back.title: Answer
back.html: It runs automatically on every candidate and blocks promotion when key metrics regress beyond a tolerance.

back.title: Notes
back.html: Four skills: spread the work across GPUs (parallelism), shrink the numbers (mixed precision), fit the memory (accumulation, checkpointing, sharding, fused attention), and find the bottleneck (profiling). The recurring exam move is to read a symptom — OOM, low utilization, NCCL wait, divergence — and name the lever.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Does the model + optimizer state fit on one GPU?
├─ yes → DDP (replicate; all-reduce gradients). Add grad accumulation for a bigger batch.
└─ no  → shard state first: FSDP / ZeRO-2 → ZeRO-3
         Still too big per layer, or too slow? → tensor parallel inside the node (NVLink)
         Too many layers for one node?         → pipeline parallel across nodes
         Very long sequences?                  → sequence / context parallel
         MoE model?                            → expert parallel (all-to-all)

Throughput check — model FLOPs utilization (MFU):

$$\text{MFU} = \frac{6N \times \text{tokens/s per GPU}}{\text{peak FLOP/s per GPU}}$$

Worked example: 7B model at 8,000 tokens/s per H100 → $6\cdot7\times10^9\cdot8000 = 3.36\times10^{14}$ FLOP/s = 336 TFLOP/s → 34% MFU of ~989 TFLOP/s. Well-tuned large runs reach roughly 40–55%.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• AMP (torch.autocast): matmuls and convolutions in FP16/BF16, reductions and softmax in FP32, FP32 master weights in the optimizer.
  • FP16 needs a GradScaler (dynamic loss scaling). BF16 doesn't — prefer it on Ampere and later.
  • TF32 is enabled for FP32 matmuls on Ampere+ (torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32) — free speedup with FP32 range.
  • FP8 with Transformer Engine (Hopper+): swap in te.Linear / te.TransformerLayer and wrap the forward in te.fp8_autocast(...). The hybrid format uses E4M3 in the forward pass and E5M2 for gradients; delayed scaling picks each tensor's scale from a history of recent absolute maxima (amax).
  • Blackwell: the 2nd-gen Transformer Engine adds MXFP8 and NVFP4 recipes with micro-block scaling.
import transformer_engine.pytorch as te
from transformer_engine.common.recipe import DelayedScaling, Format
recipe = DelayedScaling(fp8_format=Format.HYBRID, amax_history_len=16, amax_compute_algo="max")
layer = te.TransformerLayer(hidden_size=4096, ffn_hidden_size=16384, num_attention_heads=32).cuda()
with te.fp8_autocast(enabled=True, fp8_recipe=recipe):
    y = layer(x)

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Total ≈ parameters + gradients + optimizer states + activations (+ KV cache at inference) — see F2 for the 16 bytes/param rule and the activation formula.

OOM mitigation ladder (cheapest first):

  1. Smaller micro-batch + gradient accumulation (same effective batch).
  2. FlashAttention / fused attention (no $T\times T$ matrix in memory).
  3. Activation checkpointing — full (store only layer inputs, ~30% more compute) or selective (recompute only the attention core: most memory, few FLOPs).
  4. BF16 / FP8 weights and activations.
  5. FSDP / ZeRO stage up (optimizer → gradients → parameters).
  6. Tensor / pipeline parallelism.
  7. CPU/NVMe offload (ZeRO-Offload) — slowest; far cheaper on Grace-Blackwell with coherent NVLink-C2C memory.

Also rule out: fragmentation (PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True), holding references to graph tensors (losses.append(loss) instead of loss.item()), and eval without torch.no_grad(). Inspect with torch.cuda.memory_summary() or a memory snapshot (torch.cuda.memory._record_memory_history()).

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Standard attention writes the $T\times T$ score and probability matrices to HBM and reads them back — memory-bound and $O(T^2)$ memory. FlashAttention tiles Q, K, V into on-chip SRAM, computes softmax incrementally with a running max and sum (online softmax), writes only the output, and in the backward pass recomputes attention from saved softmax statistics. It is exact, not an approximation.

  • FlashAttention-2: better parallelism across the sequence and warps, fewer non-matmul FLOPs.
  • FlashAttention-3: Hopper features (warp specialization, TMA, asynchronous pipelines, FP8).
  • Under tensor parallelism, attention heads are split across GPUs — each rank computes attention for $h/\text{TP}$ heads with no communication until the output projection.

back.title: Notes
back.html: Tensor Cores need 16-bit or lower inputs and friendly shapes: hidden, FFN and vocab sizes divisible by 8 (FP16/BF16) or 16 (INT8/FP8), ideally by 64; pad the vocabulary (e.g. to a multiple of 128); keep tokens per micro-batch large enough to fill the GPU. Small or odd GEMMs show up in Nsight Compute as low Tensor-pipe utilization.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
# Timeline: CPU threads, CUDA API, kernels, memcpy, NCCL, NVTX ranges
nsys profile -t cuda,nvtx,osrt,cublas,cudnn --capture-range=cudaProfilerApi \
     -o train_report python train.py
# Kernel deep dive: throughput vs speed-of-light, occupancy, stalls, roofline
ncu --set full -k regex:gemm -c 5 -o gemm_report python infer.py

Annotate phases with NVTX (torch.cuda.nvtx.range_push("forward") / range_pop()) and capture a few steady-state steps, not the warmup.

What you see in Nsight Systems Likely cause Fix
Gaps between kernels, CPU busy Python/launch overhead CUDA Graphs, torch.compile, bigger kernels
GPU idle while waiting for data data loader more workers, pinned memory, prefetch, GPU preprocessing (DALI)
Long NCCL kernels not overlapped exposed communication bucket overlap, bigger buckets, fewer ranks per collective, TP on NVLink
Synchronous cudaMemcpy pageable memory, .item() in loop pin_memory=True, non_blocking=True, avoid sync points
Many tiny element-wise kernels no fusion fused kernels, torch.compile
What you see in Nsight Compute Meaning
High memory throughput %, low compute % memory-bound — fuse, reduce bytes (lower precision), improve reuse
High compute %, low memory % compute-bound — use Tensor Cores / lower precision
Both low latency-bound — low occupancy, stalls, too-small grid
Low achieved occupancy registers or shared memory per thread limit resident warps

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• CUDA streams run independent work concurrently: copy the next batch (pinned memory, non_blocking=True) while computing this one; NCCL runs on its own stream so gradient all-reduce overlaps the backward pass.
  • CUDA Graphs capture a sequence of kernels once and replay it with one launch — ideal for decode steps with static shapes. torch.compile(mode="reduce-overhead") uses them; mode="max-autotune" also searches kernel configs.
  • The APOD loop: Assess (profile), Parallelize, Optimize, Deploy — then measure again.

back.title: Notes
back.html: Megatron-Core / NeMo (TP, PP, SP, CP, EP, distributed optimizer) · Transformer Engine (FP8/FP4) · NCCL + nccl-tests · Nsight Systems / Nsight Compute · DCGM for fleet telemetry · cuDNN fused attention.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• "Fits, but want more throughput" → DDP (+ accumulation), not model parallelism.
  • "Doesn't fit" → FSDP/ZeRO first, then TP within node, then PP across nodes.
  • "TP across nodes is slow" → TP belongs on NVLink; use PP/DP across nodes.
  • "Loss becomes NaN in FP16" → loss scaling or switch to BF16.
  • "GPU utilization is 40% and the timeline has gaps" → input pipeline or launch overhead, not the GEMMs.
  • Nsight Systems = where time goes (system timeline); Nsight Compute = why a kernel is slow.

back.title: Answer
back.html: (6 × parameters × tokens/s per GPU) ÷ peak FLOP/s per GPU.

back.title: Answer

back.title: Answer
back.html: Computing softmax block by block with a running max and running sum, so the full row never has to be in memory.

back.title: Answer
back.html: Systems: whole-application timeline (where time goes). Compute: per-kernel metrics (why a kernel is slow).

cards.label: 7.24 · Flashcard
cards.front: Kernel shows high memory throughput and low compute throughput — what is it?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Memory-bound; fuse ops, use lower precision, improve data reuse.

cards.label: 7.27 · Flashcard
cards.front: When do CUDA Graphs help most?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Many small kernels with static shapes, e.g. LLM decode steps, where launch overhead dominates.

cards.label: 7.20 · Flashcard
cards.front: Training loop memory grows every step until OOM — common Python cause?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Keeping references to loss tensors (and their graphs), e.g. appending loss instead of loss.item().

cards.label: 7.25 · Flashcard
cards.front: Gradient all-reduce shows up as a long idle gap after backward — fix?

back.title: Answer
back.html: Overlap it with backward via DDP bucketing (tune bucket size) and make sure NCCL uses NVLink/InfiniBand.

back.title: Notes
back.html: Serving an LLM is a memory-bandwidth problem with a latency SLO attached. Prefill is compute-bound and sets TTFT; decode is memory-bound and sets inter-token latency (ITL/TPOT). Batching trades a little latency for a lot of throughput, and the KV cache decides how many requests fit.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
$$\text{E2E latency} \approx \text{TTFT} + (\text{output tokens} - 1)\times\text{ITL}$$

Lever TTFT ITL Throughput
Bigger batch / more concurrency ↑ ↑ slightly ↑↑
Lower precision (FP8/INT4 weights) ↓ ↓ ↑
Tensor parallelism ↓ ↓ per-GPU ↓
Prefix (KV) caching ↓↓ for shared prompts — ↑
Chunked prefill smoother fewer ITL spikes ↑
Speculative decoding — ↓ (at low batch) small ↑ or ↓ at high batch
Disaggregated prefill/decode ↓ tail ↓ tail ↑ at scale

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Llama-3-70B: 80 layers, 8 KV heads (GQA), head dim 128.

  • KV bytes per token $= 2 \times L \times n_{kv} \times d_h \times \text{bytes} = 2\cdot80\cdot8\cdot128\cdot2$ = 320 KB in FP16, 160 KB in FP8.
  • On 2× H100 80 GB with TP=2 and FP8 weights (~70 GB), leave ~10% for activations and the runtime → ~80 GB for KV.
  • 80 GB ÷ 160 KB ≈ 500k tokens of cache ≈ 120 concurrent 4k-token sequences.

Paged KV (vLLM PagedAttention, TRT-LLM paged KV cache) allocates this in fixed blocks so memory isn't wasted on reserved-but-unused max lengths.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Dynamic batching (Triton): waits up to max_queue_delay_microseconds to group requests into one batch. Good for fixed-cost models (encoders, embeddings, rerankers).
  • In-flight / continuous batching (TRT-LLM, vLLM): the batch is re-formed every decode step — finished sequences leave, new ones join. Essential for generative LLMs whose output lengths vary.
  • Sequence batcher: routes all requests of a stateful sequence to the same model instance (correlation ID).

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Model repository layout:

model_repository/
└── llama_ensemble/
    ├── config.pbtxt
    └── 1/                 # version directory
        └── model.plan     # or model.onnx, model.pt, model.py (Python backend)

name: "embedder"
backend: "tensorrt"
max_batch_size: 64
dynamic_batching { preferred_batch_size: [16, 32]  max_queue_delay_microseconds: 2000 }
instance_group [ { count: 2, kind: KIND_GPU } ]
version_policy: { latest: { num_versions: 1 } }

  • Ensembles chain models as a DAG in config; BLS (Business Logic Scripting, Python backend) adds loops and conditionals.
  • Concurrent execution: instance_group.count runs multiple copies per GPU.
  • Backends: TensorRT, TensorRT-LLM, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, Python, vLLM.
  • Tuning: perf_analyzer / GenAI-Perf for load, Model Analyzer to sweep batch size and instance count against latency constraints.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
A NIM is a container with the model, an optimized engine selected for the detected GPU (TensorRT-LLM, vLLM or SGLang profiles) and an OpenAI-compatible API.

export NGC_API_KEY=...
docker run --rm --gpus all --shm-size=16g \
  -e NGC_API_KEY -v ~/.cache/nim:/opt/nim/.cache -p 8000:8000 \
  nvcr.io/nim/meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct:latest
curl localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hi"}]}'

NIM vs raw Triton: NIM when you want a supported model fast with an OpenAI API and enterprise support; raw Triton + TRT-LLM when you need custom models, custom pipelines (ensembles/BLS) or full control of engine builds.

back.title: Notes
back.html: Once deployed, a model can fail in two ways: the system degrades (latency, errors, saturation) or the model degrades (drift, quality regressions). Monitor both, define SLOs, ship changes gradually, and make rollback boring.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Layer Signals Source
Golden signals latency (p50/p95/p99), traffic (RPS, tokens/s), errors (4xx/5xx, timeouts), saturation (queue time, GPU memory, KV-cache use) Triton/NIM metrics, gateway
LLM-specific TTFT, ITL, output tokens per request, cost per 1k tokens, refusal rate, guardrail trigger rate server + app logs
GPU fleet utilization, SM clock, memory, power, temperature, ECC/XID errors, NVLink errors DCGM exporter
Quality judge score on sampled traffic, thumbs up/down, task success, hallucination flags eval pipeline
Data input length distribution, language mix, topic mix, embedding drift feature logs

Stack: Prometheus scrapes → Grafana dashboards → Alertmanager alerts; OpenTelemetry for traces spanning gateway → retriever → LLM → guardrails; structured logs with request IDs (and PII redaction).

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• SLI — a measured ratio, e.g. fraction of requests with TTFT < 500 ms.
  • SLO — the target, e.g. 99.9% over 30 days.
  • Error budget = $1 - \text{SLO}$: 0.1% of 30 days = 43.2 minutes of allowed badness. Burn it fast → freeze risky launches; alert on burn rate, not single blips.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Anomaly detection: static thresholds for hard limits; rolling z-scores or seasonal baselines for traffic and latency; alert on sustained deviation.
  • Data drift — the input distribution $P(x)$ changes (new product, new language).
  • Concept drift — the right answer $P(y\mid x)$ changes (new policy, new facts).
  • Detecting drift: PSI or KL divergence on binned features (input length, topic), KS test on continuous features, distance between embedding centroids, and falling quality scores on sampled traffic.

PSI $= \sum_i (a_i - e_i)\ln\frac{a_i}{e_i}$ over bins, with expected $e$ and actual $a$ proportions. Rule of thumb: < 0.1 stable, 0.1–0.25 moderate shift, > 0.25 significant.

Worked example: short/medium/long prompts moved from 50/30/20% to 30/30/40%: $(0.3-0.5)\ln(0.6) + 0 + (0.4-0.2)\ln 2 = 0.102 + 0.139 = 0.24$ → moderate drift; investigate.

cards.label: L09 · 05
cards.front: 4. Safe change: canary, shadow, A/B, rollback

back.title: Notes
back.html:
Strategy Users see new model? Use it to
Shadow no — copies of traffic, responses discarded test load and compare outputs with zero user risk
Canary small % (1→5→25→100) catch regressions with limited blast radius
A/B test split cohorts measure business impact with statistical significance
Blue/green switch all at once, old stack kept warm instant rollback

Automate promotion gates (error rate, p95 latency, judge score vs baseline) and automatic rollback when a gate fails. Rollback requires the previous model, engine, config and prompt versions to be kept and addressable.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• Re-run the performance benchmark (GenAI-Perf) and the quality suite on every new engine, driver, container or model — regressions often come from the stack, not the weights.
  • Retraining triggers: sustained drift above threshold, quality below SLO, new labeled data volume, or a schedule. Retrain → evaluate against the champion → canary.
  • Automated tuning pipelines: sweep serving configs (batch size, instance count, TP degree, precision) with Model Analyzer or similar and pick the best config meeting the SLO.

back.title: Notes
back.html: A model registry (MLflow, NGC private registry, W&B) records for every version: training data snapshot, code commit, hyperparameters, eval results, engine build flags, approval status. Lineage lets you answer "which data produced this output?" — the base of audit trails, model cards and incident review.

back.title: Notes
back.html: Multiple replicas across nodes/zones, health-checked load balancing, request timeouts and retries with backoff, circuit breakers, rate limits per tenant. Under overload, degrade gracefully: route to a smaller/quantized fallback model, shorten max_tokens, disable expensive features (reranking), or serve cached answers — rather than failing everything.

back.title: Notes
back.html:
• "Accuracy dropped but latency and errors look fine" → model/data drift, not infrastructure.
  • "Want to test a new model with zero user impact" → shadow deployment.
  • "Measure business impact of a new model" → A/B test.
  • "99.9% availability monthly — how much downtime?" → ~43 minutes.
  • "Regression appeared after a container upgrade" → continuous benchmarking would have caught it; roll back the container.

back.title: Answer
back.html: Latency, traffic, errors, saturation.

back.title: Answer

back.title: Answer
back.html: Data: P(x) changes. Concept: P(y|x) changes — the correct answer itself changes.

back.title: Answer
back.html: < 0.1 stable, 0.1–0.25 moderate, > 0.25 significant shift.

back.title: Answer
